ABBEY: Canada is home to historic abbeys like [Saint‑Benoît‑du‑Lac](https://www.abbaye.ca/) in Quebec and [St. Peter’s Abbey](https://stpetersabbey.ca/wp/) in Saskatchewan, the oldest Benedictine monastery in the country. These monastic communities have preserved centuries-old traditions while contributing to local culture through art, agriculture, and hospitality. Visitors can admire their serene architecture and learn about the daily life of monks. Abbeys offer a quiet glimpse into Canada’s rich spiritual and cultural history.
ACORN: After the decisive Battle of Vimy Ridge during the First World War, Canadian soldier, Lieutenant Leslie Miller, gathered acorns from oak trees amongst the rubble and wreckage. Miller brought the acorns back home to Scarborough, Ontario and planted the trees as a legacy to those who perished. The acorns from those trees were then repatriated and planted back in France in 2018. Lieutenant Leslie Miller's Vimy Oaks are now growing on Vimy Ridge, and today approximately 1,000 descendant Vimy Oaks have been planted across Canada as commemorative trees. Check out the [Vimy Oaks Legacy](https://vimyoakslegacy.ca/) website to learn more!
ACRES: Canada’s vast landscape covers over 2 billion acres, with millions dedicated to fertile farmland. While Canada officially uses the metric system, the acre remains a popular way to measure land, especially in farming and real estate. These acres grow much of the food enjoyed across the country and around the world – from wheat and canola to fruits and vegetables. Canada’s farmland is a vital part of the nation’s economy, culture, and connection to the land.
ADAPT: On the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, we’re proud to highlight the [Straz Strong Foundation](https://www.strazstrongfoundation.com/), created by Humboldt Broncos crash survivor Ryan Straschnitzki. Straz Strong helps people adapt by supporting access to adaptive sports, technologies, and opportunities that promote independence and inclusion. Their work showcases the strength of communities that come together to break barriers and champion resilience across Canada.
AFTER: Did you know that 1 in 3 of those visiting food banks are children? Food Banks Canada's [After The Bell](https://foodbankscanada.ca/after-the-bell/) program provides nutritious, child-friendly food packs throughout the summer when school-centered supports are not available so kids can soar on the swings and splash in the community pool with their friends. Participating food banks receive packs that contain shelf-stable items such as milk, hummus, crackers, cereal, oatmeal and sunflower seeds and they also receive grant money to supplement the food packs. The goal in 2024 is for the program to deliver 200,000 packs in 215 communities across Canada.
AGATE: Canada is home to stunning agates, including the famous Thunder Bay Agate, known for its deep red and orange hues from iron oxidation! These colourful nodules form in volcanic rock and can be found along Lake Superior's north shore, as well as in British Columbia, Alberta, and the Maritimes. Rockhounds love hunting for these hidden gems - finding an agate is like holding a piece of Earth's history in your hand!
AGENT: [Camp X](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/camp-x) - a popular name that reflects the secrecy surrounding its activities - was a training school for covert agents and a radio communications centre that operated on the shores of Lake Ontario between Whitby and Oshawa during the Second World War. It was the first such purpose-built facility constructed in North America.
ALBUM: The Juno Award for [Album of the Year](https://junoawards.ca/nomination/2024-album-of-the-year-charlotte-cardin/) is an annual award presented by the Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences for the best album released in Canada. It has been awarded since 1975. Arcade Fire, Celine Dion, Michael Bublé and The Weeknd are the artists with the most wins in this category with three each; Dion is the most nominated artist with 12 nominations.
ALERT: Alert, in the Qikiqtaaluk Region of Nunavut, Canada, is the northernmost continuously inhabited place in the world, on Ellesmere Island (Queen Elizabeth Islands) just 817 kilometres from the North Pole. Alert was named after HMS Alert, a British ship that wintered in the area from 1875-76.
ALIVE: The 52nd annual [Canadian Finals Rodeo](https://www.cfr.ca/) wraps up today at Rogers Place in Edmonton, Alberta! Held October 7–10 under the banner “Where the West Comes Alive,” the championship brings Canada's top rodeo competitors together for four days of thrilling action, including bull riding, barrel racing and saddle bronc riding. With live music, western festivities and thousands of cheering fans, the event brings the spirit of Canada's rodeo tradition to life!
ALLEY: Each spring along the eastern coast of Newfoundland and Labrador, it's prime time for spotting icebergs. With many little towns along a thousand kilometres of coastline, this area known as "Iceberg Alley" is an outstanding location for viewing roving blue natural ice sculptures that float down from Greenland and Canada's Arctic. The massive chunks of broken glaciers are only 10% visible since most of the iceberg is submerged and floating on its side.
ALLOY: An alloy is a mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and another element, designed to enhance strength, durability, or other properties. In Canada, alloys are essential in industries from aerospace and automotive manufacturing to construction and energy. Alloys of copper, nickel, and steel are also used in everyday items like Canadian coins, highlighting how these metal blends are both practical and integral to Canadian life.
ALTAR: Canada has several famous altars, mostly found in its historic churches and cathedrals. These altars are known not just for their religious significance but also for their architectural and artistic beauty. A few notable examples include the altars at Notre-Dame Basilica and Basilica of Saint Joseph's Oratory in Montreal, and the St. Michael's Cathedral Basilica altar in Toronto. These altars not only serve as the focal points for worship but also stand as significant artistic and architectural landmarks in Canada's religious and cultural landscape.
AMBER: Canada is home to rare and fascinating amber deposits, including finds at Cedar Lake in Manitoba, where ancient tree resin has been preserved for millions of years. Amber has also been discovered in other parts of the country, offering a glimpse into prehistoric forests and the insects and plant life they once contained. These golden fossils provide a natural time capsule of Canada’s distant past.
ANGEL: Abigail Becker (1830–1905), known as the Angel of Long Point, was a Canadian woman credited with saving the lives of numerous sailors caught in storms along the shores of Long Point, located on Lake Erie in Ontario. When the storms had passed, she would wade in the water as far as she could to rescue trapped seamen from their doomed ships.
ANIME: Did you know that [Anime North](https://www.animenorth.com/) is Canada's largest fan-run anime convention? Founded in 1997 by Toronto anime enthusiast Donald Simmons, it began as a one-day event with around 600 attendees. Today, it attracts tens of thousands of fans annually to celebrate anime, manga, music, games, and Japanese culture. This year's convention takes place from May 23-25, 2025, at the Toronto Congress Centre.
ANKLE: The [town of Macklin](https://macklin.ca/), Saskatchewan is home to the world's largest bunnock! A bunnock is an anklebone of a horse, and is used in a game of the same name. Within the 9.8-metre high fibre-glass horse anklebone replica, there is also a tourist information booth. Every year since 1992, Macklin hosts a world championship bunnock tournament that brings out over 1,000 competitors each August long weekend, doubling the town's population.
APPLE: The McIntosh (nicknamed the “Mac”) is the national apple of Canada. John McIntosh discovered the original McIntosh sapling on his Dundela farm in Upper Canada in 1811. Many years later, Apple Inc. named the Macintosh computer line after the fruit.
ARENA: The largest indoor arena in Canada is the Montreal Canadiens’ Bell Centre with a capacity of 21,700. The largest open air stadium is Edmonton’s Commonwealth Stadium, home to CFL’s Edmonton Elks, able to hold 56,302.
ARROW: Canada's response to the threat of Soviet nuclear bombers was the Avro Arrow. A marvel of engineering, it was a twin-engine, all-weather supersonic interceptor. Only five Avro Arrow planes were ever built, yet this innovative jet fighter put Canada on top of the aviation world in the 1950s.
ASPEN: Aspen are a deciduous, hardwood tree of the genus Populus, belonging to the willow family. Trembling aspen and largetooth aspen are native to Canada; the former, found from the treeline to northern Mexico, is the most widely distributed tree in North America. Trembling aspen grows on most soils, doing best on well-drained, moist, sandy or gravelly loams. As a fast-growing pioneer tree species, it is ideal for quickly restoring a wide range of forest functions after disturbances.
ATLAS: The Armstrong Whitworth Atlas was a British single-engine two-seat biplane. It served as an army co-operation aircraft for the Royal Canadian Air Force in the 1920s and 1930s. April 1, 2024 marked 100 years of service for the Royal Canadian Air Force as a distinct military element. The [RCAF Centennial](https://rcaf2024arc.ca/) is an opportunity to showcase Air Force personnel and their accomplishments, demonstrate air and space power, enhance the reputation of the RCAF, and proudly honour its distinguished history and heritage.
AUGER: Ice fishing is a popular winter pastime in Canada that is enjoyed on many Canadian lakes! Small holes are drilled through the frozen lake surfaces using ice augers, allowing for the fun activity of fishing during the winter months! Billed as the "Ice Fishing Capital of Canada," more people fish on Lake Simcoe, Ontario in winter than all other seasons combined.
AWARE: [Moose Hide Campaign Day](https://moosehidecampaign.ca/), observed on the third Thursday of May each year, is a national day of action led by the Indigenous-led grassroots movement focused on engaging men and boys in ending violence towards women and children. The day is all about building awareness of the role we all play in creating safer communities. Being aware means recognizing harm, choosing respect, and committing to change. What began with a small square of moose hide as a symbol of safety, respect, and healing has grown into a powerful movement across Canada, united by awareness and action.
AXIAL: The Axial Seamount, an undersea volcano in the Pacific Ocean, influences the west coast's marine ecosystem. The Axial Seamount may sit off the coast of the United States, but it's still part of a unique underwater volcanic chain that Canada helps study! This active submarine volcano lies along the Juan de Fuca Ridge, a tectonic boundary just west of Vancouver Island. Canada's involvement in ocean research, particularly through programs like [Ocean Networks Canada](https://www.oceannetworks.ca/), helps monitor activity in the Axial Seamount and other geological features in the Pacific Ocean. The insights from this research help scientists understand undersea volcanic activity and potential impacts on the Canadian coast.
AXLES: Canada’s early auto industry relied on strong, durable axles to keep vehicles rolling across rugged roads. In the 1920s and 1930s, factories in Ontario and Quebec built cars and trucks with heavy-duty axles that could handle both city streets and rural trails. These simple yet vital components were essential to the growth of Canada’s automotive industry and its expanding national transportation network.
AZURE: The word azure means bright sky-blue, a colour seen across Canada’s vast skies and lakes. In heraldry, azure also appears in [The Coat of Arms of Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/official-symbols-canada.html#a1) on the shield, representing the royal emblems of Ireland (a harp) and France (three fleurs-de-lis). Together with symbols from England and Scotland, these elements reflect the historical nations that shaped Canada’s founding.
BACON: Canadian bacon comes from the loin of the pig instead of the side or belly.
BADGE: On Canadian Armed Forces Day (celebrated on the first Sunday in June), we recognize the dedication and service of Canada's military personnel. In the Canadian Armed Forces, a badge carries deep meaning - reflecting a unit's identity, honouring its history, and building pride among those who wear it. From regimental crests to specialized qualification badges, each one tells a story of dedication and service to Canada. Many incorporate iconic symbols like maple leaves, beavers, or crowns, proudly connecting each badge to Canada's heritage.
BAGEL: The Montréal bagel is one of Canada's most iconic and coveted snacks. It is a distinctive variety of handmade bagel that traditionally has a prounounced sweet taste and a chewy and dense texture, and is always baked in a wood-fired oven. The bagel first arrived in Montréal with the wave of Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe in the early 1900s.
BAKER: [Baker Lake](https://www.bakerlake.ca/), or Qamani’tuaq in Inuktitut, meaning “where the river widens,” is a remote hamlet near the geographic centre of Canada. Nunavut’s only inland community sits at the mouth of the Thelon River and is renowned for its vibrant Inuit art scene, with internationally celebrated artists including Jessie Oonark and Marion Tuu’luq.
BANDS: Today is [National Indigenous Veterans Day](https://www.veterans.gc.ca/en/remembrance/people-and-stories/indigenous-veterans), a time to honour the First Nations, Inuit, and Métis peoples who have served in uniform. Thousands of Indigenous veterans from communities and bands across Canada volunteered in both World Wars, Korea, and beyond – often travelling far from home to defend a country that did not yet grant them full rights. Their courage, resilience, and leadership are now formally recognized and remembered each November 8, as Canadians pay tribute to the vital role Indigenous veterans have played in our shared history.
BANJO: The Banjo Bowl is the annual rematch game between the Winnipeg Blue Bombers and Saskatchewan Roughriders of the Canadian Football League after the Labour Day Classic. The game has been sold out every year since 2005. As of the 2023 season, Winnipeg leads the series 12–7. The Blue Bombers will host the CFL's Western Final this Saturday, after the team secured the top spot in the division for the third season in a row.
BANKS: Today is National Food Bank Day! Held on the first Friday in September, National Food Bank Day encourages you to commit to contributing to the cause that believes no one should go to bed hungry. Founded in 1989, [Food Banks Canada](https://foodbankscanada.ca/) is a national organization working to reduce food insecurity countrywide. Food Banks Canada's mission is to provide national leadership to relieve hunger today and prevent hunger tomorrow.
BARGE: The McBarge, officially named the Friendship 500, was a floating McDonald's restaurant built for Expo 86 in Vancouver. This sleek, futuristic barge served Big Macs with a waterfront view, but after the fair, it was left adrift, moving from site to site along the B.C. coast. Despite hopes for restoration, the McBarge met a sad fate in March 2025 when it sank near Maple Ridge. While its golden arches faded, its legend lives on as one of Canada's most unique fast-food relics.
BARNS: Canada is home to countless barns scattered across its vast agricultural landscape, serving as iconic symbols of rural life and farming heritage. Barns have played a crucial role in Canada's agricultural history, providing shelter for livestock, storage for crops, and a place for farmers to work and gather. From the iconic red barns of the Canadian prairies to the picturesque white barns of rural Quebec, each barn tells a story of hard work, resilience, and connection to the land. When you're driving through the countryside, keep an eye out for these charming structures that stand as enduring symbols of Canada's agricultural heritage.
BASIC: From fresh produce to pantry staples, [Food Basics](https://www.foodbasics.ca/) has been a familiar name in Ontario grocery aisles since 1995. The discount supermarket chain built its reputation around offering Canadians the basics they need every day at prices that help stretch the grocery budget. Today, Food Basics has more than 150 stores across Ontario.
BASIN: Canada is home to numerous basins, including Canada Basin in the Arctic, Basin Head Beach in Prince Edward Island, the Sudbury Basin in Ontario, and the Western Canada Sedimentary Basin which underlies 1.4 million square kilometres across Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia.
BATHE: From coast to coast, Canadians have long sought out steamy, mineral-rich waters to bathe in and unwind. At Liard River Hot Springs in northern BC, you can soak beneath a canopy of boreal forest. In the Rockies, Radium and Banff Upper Hot Springs offer stunning alpine views. Even the Yukon boasts Takhini Hot Springs, where bathers compete in a frozen hairdo contest each winter! Wherever you roam, there's a hot spring waiting to to help you relax - Canada's natural spa experience.
BEACH: Canada is home to the two longest freshwater beaches in the world: Wasaga Beach (14 km) on the Georgian Bay in Ontario and Sauble Beach (11 km) on the Bruce Peninsula, along the eastern shore of Lake Huron.
BEERS: Canadians spent $9.2 billion on beer in 2020 ($325 per adult), which equates to 2.3 billion litres of beer.
BELLS: It's time to ring in the New Year! Churches, cathedrals and towers across Canada will be ringing the bells tonight at midnight to signal the start of 2023. There are 11 carillons in Canada, ranging from the historic Hamilton cathedral to the more modern Exhibition Place carillon in Toronto. The Peace Tower Carillon on Parliament Hill in Ottawa is the most frequently played and the best known carillon. It has 53 bells, and was inaugurated on July 1, 1927 to mark the 60th anniversary of Confederation. The Cathedral of the Transfiguration in Markham, Ontario contains one of the world’s largest sets of bells. They were cast in bronze and weigh in at a whopping 32,000 pounds (over 14,500kg)!
BELLY: In the heart of St. John's, Newfoundland, [YellowBelly Brewery](https://www.yellowbellybrewery.com/) serves up more than just great beer - it pours out history! Housed in one of the city's oldest buildings, this brewery gets its name from the 'Yellowbellies,' a term historically tied to Irish immigrants and their role in the Irish Rebellion of 1798. The building itself dates back to the early 1800s and even survived the devastating Great Fire of 1892. Today, visitors can enjoy a pint while soaking in the rich past of this legendary spot - where history and hops go hand in hand!
BELTS: Wampum are tubular purple and white beads made from shells. Wampum are used primarily by Indigenous peoples of the Eastern Woodlands for ornamental, ceremonial, diplomatic and commercial purposes. Belts made of wampum were used to mark agreements between peoples. Wampum belts and other wampum bead artifacts continue to hold significance for Indigenous peoples and any treaties or agreements they might represent.
BENCH: In the House of Commons, MPs with leadership roles sit on the front bench, while everyone else sits on the back bench. Backbenchers may not wear the cabinet title, but they’re far from idle, reviewing legislation in committees, introducing private members’ bills, and taking part in Question Period. In the 45th Canadian Parliament, all 343 MPs, including the backbench, keep the work of democracy moving every day.
BERTH: A berth is a docking spot in a port or harbour where ships load and unload cargo or passengers. With the world's longest coastline, Canada relies on berths at major ports like Vancouver, Halifax, and Montreal to keep trade and travel moving. Berths also serve ferries, cruise ships, and naval vessels- from Halifax's naval base to Marine Atlantic's ferries in Newfoundland. Whether for commerce, travel, or defence, berths keep Canada connected by sea!
BEZEL: A bezel is a frame that holds a gem, watch face, or even a coin – adding both protection and style. In Canada, bezels are a popular way to turn meaningful items into wearable keepsakes, from Indigenous-made jewelry to custom-crafted pendants. The Royal Canadian Mint even offers sterling silver bezel kits, allowing collectors to transform special coins into necklaces, brooches, or keychains, letting Canadian craftsmanship shine one coin at a time. Canada was the first country in the world to introduce coloured coin technology back in 2004, starting with the iconic poppy quarter. From glow-in-the-dark dinosaurs to shimmering maple leaves, Canadian coins are known for pushing boundaries – and bezels help keep that beauty on full display.
BICEP: Canadian arm wrestling legend Devon Larratt is known around the world for his powerful biceps and unmatched technique! Born in Victoria, British Columbia, Larratt served in the Canadian Armed Forces before becoming a dominant force in professional arm wrestling. With multiple world titles and viral matchups under his belt, he's helped put Canada on the map in this intense sport of strength and strategy.
BIKER: [Canadian bikers](https://cyclingcanada.ca/) have pedaled their way to impressive Olympic success! In cycling events, Canada has celebrated numerous achievements. [Clara Hughes](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/clara-hughes/) stands out as a dual-season Olympian, winning two bronze medals in road cycling at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, adding to her Winter Olympic medals in speed skating. [Catharine Pendrel](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/catharine-pendrel/) earned a bronze in mountain biking at the 2016 Rio Olympics, showcasing Canada's strength in off-road events. And let's not forget [Lori-Ann Muenzer](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/lori-ann-muenzer/), who made history by winning gold in track cycling at the Athens 2004 Olympics. Sixteen years later, [Kelsey Mitchell](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/kelsey-mitchell/) won gold in the sprint event at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics. Other notable Canadian cyclists who have raced to Olympic glory include Curt Harnett, Brian Walton, Lauriane Genest, Alison Sydor, Marie-Hélène Prémont, and Steve Bauer.
BIKES: Did you know Toronto, Ontario makes one of the world's best racing bikes? Using the same tools and techniques as Formula One teams, Toronto-based Cervélo builds what have been called some of the world's fastest and lightest bikes. At the 2008 Olympics in Beijing, athletes riding Cervélo bikes won 10 medals, while in 2008, Carlos Sastre rode a Cervélo bike to win the Tour de France.
BILLS: In Canada, law-making is one of the most significant responsibilities of Parliament. A bill is a proposed law that is introduced in either the House of Commons or the Senate. A bill can become law only once the same text has been approved by both Houses of Parliament and has received royal assent.
BINGO: The game of Bingo has been a beloved pastime in Canada for decades! In fact, the first official Canadian Bingo hall opened in the 1940s in British Columbia, and the game quickly became a popular way to raise money for charities, schools, and local communities. Whether played at a community centre or as a family game night favourite, Bingo remains a fun way to bring Canadians together! From coast to coast, Canadians have enjoyed shouting "Bingo!" as a way to win big and support their communities at the same time.
BIRCH: The white birch is the most widely distributed of native birch trees, and grows in every region of Canada. The bark has long been used for making canoes and ornaments.
BIRDS: Point Pelee National Park is Canada's smallest National Park by size, but it comes to life in a big way every May for the annual [Festival of Birds](https://www.festivalofbirds.ca/). In spring, birds return from their winter migration to nest and breed, pass through before heading further north, or are permanent year-round residents of this southernmost point of mainland Canada. Over 370 species of birds can be found at Point Pelee National Park. This event is one of the biggest and best attended bird festivals in the country. Celebrate spring migration at the 2024 Festival of Birds from May 1 to May 20.
BLADE: Today marks the start of the [Western Hockey League](https://chl.ca/whl/) (WHL) regular season in Canada! The [Saskatoon Blades](https://chl.ca/whl-blades/) are a Canadian major junior ice hockey team based in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. Founded in 1964, the Blades were a charter team of the then-Western Canada Junior Hockey League in 1966, and are the only club that has played every season in the league in its original location. The team has twice hosted the Memorial Cup tournament, in 1989 and in 2013.
BLAND: Despite the name, Blanding’s turtles aren’t bland at all! This bright-eyed freshwater species, found in southern Ontario, Quebec, and parts of the Maritimes, has a striking yellow throat and domed shell. Sadly, these turtles are endangered, and conservation efforts across Canada are helping protect their wetlands and nesting sites so they can continue to thrive.
BLING: Hotline Bling by Canadian artist Drake became one of the defining hits of 2015, reaching No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 and dominating charts around the world. Known for its minimalist production and instantly recognizable music video, the track spent weeks in the top tier of the charts and earned multiple Grammy wins, further cementing Drake’s global influence as a Canadian music powerhouse.
BLITZ: Today is the [110th CFL Grey Cup](https://www.greycupfestival.ca/)! When you hear the term blitz you probably think of football, but The Canadian Wildlife Federation and the Nature Conservancy of Canada use [Bioblitzes](https://cwf-fcf.org/en/explore/bioblitz/) to help determine the health of an ecosystem. A Bioblitz is a participatory search for species within a limited area and a limited timeframe that takes a "snapshot" of as many living things as possible. Biodiversity - literally the variety of life - is an indicator that an area is ecologically stable and healthy. Through use of the [iNaturalist Canada app](https://inaturalist.ca/), the species records are compiled into a single data set to help researchers, scientists and policy-makers to help them make informed decisions about wildlife management.
BLOCK: The Centre Block is the main building of the Canadian parliamentary complex on Parliament Hill, in Ottawa, Ontario, containing the House of Commons and Senate chambers, as well as the offices of a number of members of parliament, senators, and senior administration for both legislative houses.
BLUES: The [Maple Blues Awards](https://www.mapleblues.ca/) is Canada’s national blues awards program. Its goal is to promote blues music across Canada and to recognize outstanding achievement in the field. The Maple Blues Awards have been presented by the Toronto Blues Society since their inception in 1997.
BONES: Known as the "Dinosaur Capital of the World", the town of Drumheller, Ablerta has some of the richest deposits of fossils and dinosaur bones in the world! In Alberta's Red Deer River valley, home to Dinosaur Provincial Park, more than 1,000 complete skeletons of extinct dinosaurs have been found since the late 1800s.
BOOKS: Happy National Read a Book Day! Reading is one of the most popular pastimes in Canada, with over 80% of adults admitting to reading for pleasure. There are so many incredible books written by famous Canadian authors, and today is a great day to pick up your favourite Canadian book! Check out [CBC Books](https://www.cbc.ca/books) to learn more about books in Canada!
BOOST: Launched in Sherwood Park, Alberta in 1999, [Booster Juice](https://boosterjuice.com/) has grown from a single Prairie shop into a nationwide Canadian success story. Its smoothies, boosters, and fresh juices offer a quick pick-me-up for Canadians on the go. It’s a true homegrown brand delivering a refreshing boost across the country.
BOOZE: Canada is known for its thriving alcohol industry, producing a wide variety of spirits, wines, and beers enjoyed by people around the world. From award-winning whiskies to crisp ice wines harvested in the vineyards of Ontario's Niagara region, Canada offers a diverse and flavourful selection of alcoholic beverages. Whether you're enjoying a glass of Canadian wine or enjoying a cold craft beer from one of Canada's many breweries, the alcohol industry in Canada is sure to quench your thirst and leave you wanting more!
BORER: In Canada, the emerald ash borer and bronze birch borer are two well-known tree borers found in our forests. The emerald ash borer is an invasive species that affects ash trees, while the bronze birch borer is native to North America and targets birch trees. Both insects live beneath the bark, where they tunnel through wood and disrupt the flow of water and nutrients, making them important considerations in Canadian forest health and tree management.
BOWER: The word bower comes from the classic card game Euchre, a longtime favourite in Canada! In Euchre, the "right bower" (jack of the trump suit) and "left bower" (jack of the same colour) are the top two cards. With its simple rules, quick rounds, and team play, Euchre has become a go-to game in homes, cottages, and legion halls across the country. It's a true staple of Canadian card culture!
BRACE: The modern lingual brace has Canadian roots. Saskatchewan-born orthodontist Dr. Craven Kurz earned his dental degree from McGill University in 1968 before moving to California, where he pioneered braces that attach to the back of the teeth. Developed in the 1970s for patients who wanted a less visible treatment, his innovation helped make “invisible” orthodontics a reality.
BRAID: Although the cultures and traditions of Indigenous Peoples are diverse, the importance of long hair is the same for all Nations. It is a long-standing practice within many First Nations for both women and men to wear their hair in braids. It is seen as a symbol of their connection to culture and Indigenous roots. For some, braids are a symbol of strength and wisdom, and it represents a connection to their ancestors, the Earth and the Creator.
BRAKE: In 1901, Canadian court clerk Louis Joseph Lacoste from Montreal patented a hull-mounted ship brake meant to help slow and control vessels, even pitching it to the British Admiralty and getting it tested on a U.S. Navy battleship. The design featured large steel "doors" or wings mounted amidships that swung out into the water to act as a hydrodynamic brake and improve turning radius - adding a unique chapter to Canada’s long history of maritime innovation.
BRAND: Canada is home to many iconic brands and locally owned companies that reflect the country’s creativity, innovation, and regional pride. From everyday essentials to globally recognized names like Tim Hortons, Lululemon, Canada Goose, Aritzia, and Roots, Canadian brands span food, fashion, retail, and outdoor gear. Together, they are a strong part of the national identity, showcasing homegrown quality and entrepreneurial spirit and connecting communities in every part of the country.
BRAVE: On November 11th, we remember and honour all the individuals who have and continue to serve in Canada's military services. Attending Remembrance Day ceremonies on November 11th is a well known way to honour the brave men and women who served Canada in times of war, military conflict and peace. For more than 100 years, millions of Canadians have proudly served our country in uniform. On this Remembrance Day, we honour those brave soldiers who fought for our country and made the ultimate sacrifice. Lest we forget.
BREAD: Bannock or fry bread is a form of bread that served as a staple in the diets of early settlers in Canada. It's believed Scottish fur traders introduced it, but many Indigenous communities had pre-colonial versions of bannock: Inuit call it "palauga", Mi’kmaq "luskinikn", and Ojibwe "ba‘wezhiganag". A delicious bread that has been made and enjoyed in Canada for hundreds of years, bannock is now frequently found at gatherings and festivals. Read more about bannock on [The Canadian Encyclopedia](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/bannock).
BREAK: Canadian fitness icons Hal Johnson and Joanne McLeod hosted over 300 episodes of the show [BodyBreak](https://bodybreak.com/) which focused on how exercise can be incorporated into daily life. Every show ended with the tagline "Keep Fit and Have Fun!", encouraging everyone to stay active and have fun doing it!
BREWS: Happy International Beer Day! Beer is the most popular alcoholic beverage in Canada, in terms of both volume and dollar value. Beer was introduced to Canada by European settlers in the seventeenth century. The first commercial brewery was La Brasseries du Roy started by New France Intendant Jean Talon, in Québec City in 1668.
BUDDY: On the east coast predominantly (but also heard nationwide), buddy is a way to talk about a person in Canada without using a name. When you call someone "bud" or "buddy" in Canada, that person could literally be your best friend or a total stranger. It is a friendly colloquialism used as a term of endearment or camaraderie. Peace By Chocolate even has a special edition [Hey Buddy chocolate bar](https://peacebychocolate.ca/products/92g-hey-buddy-canada-bar)!
BUGLE: Bugles have been used for centuries to communicate commands, signals, and alerts on the battlefield, and Canadian military units have employed bugle calls as part of their tradition and discipline. During World War I and World War II, bugle calls were instrumental in coordinating troop movements, signaling attacks, and conveying orders in the heat of battle. Today, bugle calls continue to be an integral part of Canadian military ceremonies, including [Remembrance Day services](https://www.canada.ca/en/department-national-defence/services/military-history/history-heritage/remembrance-ceremony/11.html), where the haunting notes of 'Last Post' and 'Reveille' pay tribute to the sacrifices of Canadian soldiers. The bugle remains a symbol of honour, duty, and tradition in Canada's military heritage.
BUILD: Tomorrow (November 27th) marks the 100th anniversary of the Civic campus of [The Ottawa Hospital](https://www.ottawahospital.on.ca/en/)! The original red brick hospital was built in 1924 and was the dream of Harold Fisher, Ottawa’s mayor at the time, who envisioned a state-of-the-art building that would bring together three community hospitals struggling under an aging infrastructure and a deadly influenza pandemic. That defining moment in history went on to improve the lives of every citizen of Ottawa and helped lay the foundation for a century of healthcare advances in Canada. Now, a century later, on the heels of another pandemic, a $500-million fundraising campaign is underway to help build a new hospital campus right in the heart of the very community where Mayor Fisher first dared to dream. Discover how you can support the [Campaign to Create Tomorrow](https://ohfoundation.ca/campaign-to-create-tomorrow/) and help The Ottawa Hospital Foundation build Canada’s most technologically advanced research hospital, reshaping the future of healthcare.
BUMPS: Did you know the Goosebumps TV series, based on R.L. Stine’s popular children’s books, was filmed in Canada? Many episodes were shot in Ontario, including locations in and around the Greater Toronto Area, which helped create the show’s eerie suburban atmosphere. Canadian settings played a key role in bringing the spooky stories to life for young viewers in the 1990s.
BUOYS: Buoys are floating markers used to guide navigation and monitor ocean conditions. In Canada, buoy systems play an important role in tracking weather, waves, and marine safety across the country’s vast coastlines. Scientific buoys deployed by organizations like Fisheries and Oceans Canada help collect real-time ocean data used for forecasting, research, and environmental monitoring.
BURST: The countdown is on to 2024! In skies across Canada and around the world at midnight tonight, there will be fireworks bursting and producing beautiful displays of light and colour to ring in the new year. Cheers to the New Year!
BYLAW: From coast to coast, Canada is home to some wonderfully strange and amusing bylaws that reflect the quirks and character of its communities. In Dawson City, Yukon, it's illegal to disturb a moose, including honking at one! In Calgary, Alberta, you're not allowed to put your feet on benches, planters, or sculptures in public spaces. And In Souris, Prince Edward Island, you can't build a snowman taller than 30 inches on a corner lot – safety first, even for frosty friends! These odd rules show how unique (and Canadian!) our local bylaws can be.
CABIN: Cabin is another name for a cottage, and Canada has no shortage of weekend getaway spots!
CABLE: In 1909, one of the first transatlantic telegraph cables made landfall in Halifax, Nova Scotia, creating a physical communications link between North America and Europe. Another cable linked St. John's to New York, and previously cables ran between Ireland and Heart's Content, Newfoundland in the 1850s and 1860s. Within 20 years, seven more cables connected Europe and North America via Signal Hill. Halifax was the Atlantic seaboard's primary cable ship port and service call depot for the transatlantic cable. Large spools of cable were stored in the bottom of Cable Wharf. As one of the last original structures on the harbour, Cable Wharf is a rare gem among the constantly changing Halifax Waterfront.
CAJUN: Happy [National Acadian Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/celebrate-canada/acadian-day.html)! On August 15, we celebrate the culture, history, and resilience of Acadian communities across Canada. After the Deportation of the Acadians in the 1700s, many were exiled from their Maritime homeland. Some eventually settled in Louisiana, where the word “Acadian” evolved into “Cajun.” While Cajun and Acadian cultures have distinct histories, Cajun traditions remain a vibrant reminder of Canada’s Acadian roots – rich in music, food, language, and pride that still echoes from the Maritimes to the bayou.
CAMEL: The [Sopwith Camel](https://www.canada.ca/en/air-force/services/aircraft/sopwith-camel.html) became the most successful British fighter of the First World War. Several Canadian aces used the Camel as their mount. Very manoeuvrable, it could be tricky to fly in the hands of a novice pilot. For experienced pilots, however, the aircraft proved to be a superb fighter. The guns were mounted on the forward fuselage with their breeches enclosed in a faired metal cowling - a "hump" that gave the Camel its name.
CAMPS: Over 5.7 million Canadian adults camp each year and the camping industry contributes a total of $4.7 billion annually to Canada's economy.
CANAL: The 202 km of Rideau Canal with 47 locks is the oldest, continuously operated canal system in North America.
CANES: While candy canes bring sweetness and festive charm to the holiday season, Canada is also home to a revolutionary cane designed for accessibility. At just 14 years old, Canadian student Riya Karumanchi invented the SmartCane, an innovative device to aid visually impaired individuals. Her design incorporates advanced features like ultrasonic sensors, GPS integration, and haptic feedback to detect obstacles and enhance navigation. Her invention has since received widespread recognition, securing funding from major tech companies like Microsoft and Google, and establishing Riya as a young leader in accessibility innovation. Much like the joy candy canes bring, the SmartCane embodies Canadian ingenuity, spreading hope and empowerment globally.
CANOE: In Canada, the canoe has long been associated with the fur trade and the romantic figure of the voyageur.
CANON: In literature, a canon is a collection of works considered especially important or enduring, and Canada has many that stand out. From beloved classics like Lucy Maud Montgomery's Anne of Green Gables to influential contemporary novels such as Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale, the Canadian literary canon also includes powerful works by Indigenous authors whose stories reflect the depth and diversity of this land. Together, these books remain cornerstones of Canadian storytelling.
CANUCK: The word Canuck is a proud and playful nickname for Canadians! While its origins are debated, it has been used since at least the 19th century to describe people from Canada. From Johnny Canuck, a folk hero who stood up to tyranny, to the Vancouver Canucks hockey team, the word has become a symbol of Canadian identity. It even inspired the name of our game - Canuckle - a fun and truly Canadian word game!
CAPER: The "Canadian Caper" was the joint covert rescue by the Canadian government and the CIA of six American diplomats who had evaded capture during the seizure of the United States embassy in Tehran, Iran, on November 4, 1979. An article written about these events was published in Wired in 2007. The article was used loosely as the basis of the 2012 film Argo.
CAPES: Canada is home to some stunning coastal landscapes adorned with picturesque capes! Along its vast coastline, Canada boasts numerous capes that offer breathtaking views of the surrounding seas and landscapes. One iconic example is Cape Breton Island's Cabot Trail in Nova Scotia, where rugged cliffs meet the Atlantic Ocean, creating a dramatic and awe-inspiring vista. Cape Scott Provincial Park on Vancouver Island is renowned for its remote wilderness and rugged coastline, while Cape Columbia located on Ellesmere Island in the Qikiqtaaluk Region of Nunavut is the northernmost point of land of Canada and offers incredible views of the Canadian Arctic. Cape Spear in Newfoundland and Labrador holds the distinction of being the easternmost point in North America. Canada's capes provide endless opportunities for adventure and discovery!
CARDS: [Kelvington, Saskatchewan](https://www.townofkelvington.com/) is known as "Canada's Hockey Factory"! A giant hockey cards monument was built to celebrate Kelvington's famous hockey players, including Lloyd Gronsdahl, Barry Melrose, Joe Kocur, Wendel Clark, Kerry Clark, and Kory Kocur.
CARGO: Did you know that Canada is home to one of the world's largest cargo ports? The [Port of Vancouver](https://www.portvancouver.com/), located in British Columbia, is not only Canada's largest port but also the third-largest port in North America by total tonnage. Serving as a vital gateway for trade between North America and Asia, the Port of Vancouver handles a diverse range of cargo, including containerized goods, bulk commodities, automobiles, and more. With state-of-the-art facilities and strategic transportation networks, the port plays a crucial role in supporting Canada's economy and global trade.
CAROL: For the past several weeks, the most popular songs around have been Christmas carols. Many of our favourites have European roots, but one that is still sung can claim to be the first Canadian Christmas carol. The "Huron Carol" (or "Twas in the Moon of Wintertime") was written by Jean de Brébeuf, a Jesuit missionary at Sainte-Marie among the Hurons in Canada. Brebeuf's hymn, written in both Huron and French, is now over 380 years old. The song remains a common Christmas hymn in Canadian churches, and it has become a cherished part of Canadian Christmas.
CARTS: Carts were essential for travel and trade in early Canada, and the [Red River Cart](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/red-river-cart) is one of the most famous. Developed by the Métis during the settlement of the Prairies in the mid- to late-1800s, these two-wheeled wooden carts could carry up to 450 kg of goods across long distances, pulled by oxen or horses. The cart takes its name from the Red River, along which the Red River Colony was settled, and the Métis had their own Michif words for it, including aen wagon and aen charet. These carts became a lasting symbol of Métis ingenuity and resilience on the frontier.
CARVE: With its many carved pumpkins, sculptures and special effects, [Pumpkins After Dark](https://pumpkinsafterdark.com/) brings magic across Canada. Pumpkins After Dark is Canada’s award-winning outdoor Halloween event, with locations in Burnaby, Calgary, Edmonton, Milton and Ottawa. Featuring over 10,000+ hand-carved pumpkins, this one-of-a-kind walk-through experience is the must-see event of the spooky season.
CATCH: Prince Edward Island offers anglers the chance to catch one of the world's mightiest big-game fish - the bluefin tuna! The first bluefin landed on P.E.I. was out of North Lake Harbour in 1967. By 1970s the catch rates had increased and a charter business began on the island. North Lake soon became known as one of the few places you could catch a fish weighing over 1000 pounds and was coined the "Tuna Capital of the World" because of all the world record catches.
CAUSE: Happy National Philanthropy Day! Every year on November 15, this day pays tribute to the extraordinary contribution that those involved in the philanthropic process have made to our communities. In 2012, Canada became the first - and remains the only - country in the world to recognize this day. Philanthropy is the spirit of giving without expectation of reward. Canadians continue to be inspired by the dedication of volunteers who devote themselves to improving the lives of others. Philanthropy helps build strong communities and active civic participation by bringing people together to serve a common goal and support a cause. Join us in recognizing the extraordinary generosity and dedication of donors, volunteers and charities.
CAVES: Canada is home to some spectacular natural caves waiting to be explored! While Canada may be known for its vast wilderness and towering mountains, it also boasts a hidden underground world filled with breathtaking caverns and geological wonders. Some notable examples include the Bonnechere Caves and Bruce Peninsula Caves in Ontario, the Canmore Caverns in Alberta, the Horne Lake Caves on Vancouver Island, and the Castleguard Cave in Banff National Park, the longest cave in Canada. Whether you're spelunking through narrow passageways or admiring dazzling rock formations, exploring caves in Canada is an unforgettable adventure that reveals the hidden beauty beneath the surface of the Great White North.
CEDAR: Canada has the world’s largest stock of standing western redcedar trees. The western redcedar is the arboreal emblem of the province of British Columbia.
CHAIN: Did you know that a group of lynx is called a "chain"? The Canada lynx, a native species to Canada, is known for its distinctive tufted ears and large, padded paws that act like snowshoes in the winter. These elusive cats are most commonly found in the boreal forests of Canada, where they primarily hunt snowshoe hares. While lynx are typically solitary animals, the term "chain" is used to describe a group of them when they do come together. Seeing a chain of lynx in the wild is a rare and remarkable sight, reflecting the rich biodiversity of Canada's wilderness.
CHALK: [Chalk River Laboratories](https://www.cnl.ca/) is a Canadian nuclear research facility in Deep River, about 180 km north-west of Ottawa. It is a site of major research and development to support and advance nuclear technology, particularly CANDU reactor technology. Until the shutdown of its nuclear reactor in 2018, CRL produced a large share of the world's supply of medical radioisotopes.
CHANT: Today is [National Indigenous Peoples Day](https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1100100013718/1708446948967)! On June 21, we recognize and celebrate the history, heritage, resilience and diversity of First Nations, Inuit and Métis across Canada. Chants play a vital role in Indigenous culture in Canada, used in ceremonies, healing, and storytelling for generations. These rhythmic vocalizations help preserve history, connect communities, and honour ancestors. Chants, alongside traditional songs, are a way for Indigenous peoples to maintain their cultural identity and pass knowledge from one generation to the next. They are a powerful form of expression and resilience within Canada’s rich cultural mosaic.
CHASE: For over 5,500 years, Indigenous Peoples of the Plains used a strategic chase to guide bison toward cliffs known as buffalo jumps. At [Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump](https://headsmashedin.ca) in Alberta, hunters built stone cairns to funnel herds toward a steep drop. Now a UNESCO World Heritage Site with a museum dedicated to Blackfoot culture, it showcases the skill, planning, and cooperation behind one of history's most effective hunting techniques.
CHEER: In 1606, Samuel de Champlain created the Order of Good Cheer in Port-Royal, Nova Scotia. The Order of Good Cheer was a winter supper club, created to pass the winter months joyously and to combat French settlers from dying of scurvy. Each member of the Order of Good Cheer had to take his turn hunting, fishing, and trading with the Mi’kmaq to create a lavish meal. The night would begin with a ceremonial procession to the table with members carrying the dishes to the feast. The feast leader would lead the procession and he would have the honour of wearing the chain of the Order and a large napkin over his shoulder. To create a lively and fun atmosphere, the dinners would be filled with lots of story-telling, singing and music. Cheers! We hope your day is full of Christmas cheer!
CHEST: Our chest rises and falls with every breath - something we often take for granted. Respiratory therapists across Canada are the experts who help keep those breaths strong and steady. Represented by the [Canadian Society of Respiratory Therapists](https://www.csrt.com/about-respiratory-therapists/) (CSRT), they care for people with conditions affecting the lungs and chest in hospitals, communities, and beyond. This week from October 19-25, the CSRT celebrates Respiratory Therapy Week, honouring the dedication and vital work of Canada’s respiratory therapists!
CHICK: Happy Easter from Canuckle! From chocolate treats to springtime farm visits, the chick is a beloved Easter symbol across Canada. These fluffy little birds represent new life and fresh beginnings - perfect for a holiday that celebrates renewal, hope, and the arrival of spring. They're a cute reminder of the season's fresh start!
CHIEF: In many Indigenous cultures in Canada, chiefs are the leaders of bands, clans and/or First Nations. Chiefs act as cultural and spiritual leaders and also serve as links between their people and the municipal, provincial and federal governments. RoseAnne Archibald is the current National Chief of the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) in Canada.
CHILD: Canada declared November 20th as [National Child Day](https://nationalchildday.org/) to celebrate the rights of children. It was chosen in recognition of Canada's commitment to upholding the rights of children, and to commemorate the day the United Nations adopted the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) on November 20, 1989.
CHILL: In 2001, Canada took the lead to promote an international standard for wind chill. A team of scientists and medical experts from Canada and the US worked together to develop the current wind chill index. This index represents the degree of "chill" that your skin senses, and is based on the loss of heat from the face. Wind chills below -70 have been recorded in northern communities in Canada. On January 13, 1975 at Kugaaruk, Nunavut, the air temperature was -51C and the winds were 56km/h, producing a bone-chilling wind chill of -78!
CHIME: The Peace Tower’s 53 bells chime high above Parliament Hill, ringing out everything from O Canada to classic folk tunes. Played like a giant piano, this grand carillon is one of the largest in the world! Since 2008, Canada’s official Dominion Carillonneur, Dr. Andrea McCrady, has performed thousands of live recitals from the tower, keeping this uniquely Canadian tradition ringing loud and proud in the heart of Ottawa with every chime.
CHINOOK: A chinook is a warm, dry wind that sweeps down the eastern slopes of the Rockies, famous for sudden temperature swings on the Prairies. Interior chinooks—often called “snow eaters”—can raise winter temperatures dramatically in hours, melting snow and giving locals a mid-winter reprieve. Coastal chinooks, on the other hand, are milder, carrying moisture from the Pacific and influencing weather along British Columbia’s coast.
CHIVE: [Wild chives](https://naturaledge.watersheds.ca/plants/wild-chives/) are native to Canada and grow naturally across much of the country, from British Columbia to Newfoundland and into the North. Indigenous peoples have traditionally used the onion-flavoured plant as both food and medicine, including remedies for coughs, colds and wounds. Their distinctive pink-purple flowers bloom across Canada from early to late summer.
CHOCK: A chock is a wedge used to keep wheels or sleds from rolling, and in Canada’s snowy north, chocks are essential for sleds and dog teams. Chocks can be made of wood, rubber, metal, plastic, or even ice, helping adventurers and mushers stay safe on slippery trails. This simple tool proves that even the smallest pieces can have a big impact in the great outdoors!
CHOIR: Canada's world-renowned and oldest-surviving mixed-voice amateur choir, the [Toronto Mendelssohn Choir](https://www.tmchoir.org/), was founded in 1894 by Augustus Stephen Vogt. It is one of Canada's oldest, largest, and most recognized choral ensembles, renowned for over 125 years for delivering the highest standard of musical performance.
CHORD: Canada has a long tradition of bringing musicians together, and [Four Chords & The Truth](https://fourchordsandthetruth.com/) is one of the country’s most beloved showcases for songwriters. Launched in Toronto in 2015, this unique event invites artists to share their music “in the semi-round,” taking turns performing songs and telling the stories behind them. The result is an intimate night where every chord struck carries a bit of truth – a perfect harmony of Canadian creativity and storytelling.
CHUTE: The Canadian Forces Parachute Team, the SkyHawks, is Canada’s only military parachute demonstration team. It has been representing Canada and the Canadian Forces for more than 50 years, providing parachute demonstration jumps to over 75 million spectators worldwide under the team’s signature Canadian flag parachutes.
CIDER: In Canada, the history of cider could be traced back to explorers like Captain Cook and the Hudson's Bay Company. Cider was used to help prevent scurvy! It may have been the British that first brought cider to Canada, but production flourished in Quebec.
CIGAR: Wordle launched its global word-game craze with CIGAR as its very first answer, a spark that eventually inspired Canuckle’s own Canadian twist. That origin story has a fun modern echo thanks to [Dominion Cigar](https://www.dominioncigar.com/), a Canadian owned and operated company, which released "[The Canuckle](https://www.dominioncigar.com/canuckle/)" cigar this past summer. A perfectly Canadian coincidence linking our puzzle beginnings with a homegrown maker. On New Year’s Eve, it’s a playful way to honour endings, new beginnings, and the words that tie them together.
CIVIC: Canadian citizens have the civic duty to serve on a jury if called to do so and the civic responsibility to vote in Canadian elections. Federal election voter turnout in Canada rose sharply in the 2015 federal election to 68.3% of eligible voters, the highest turnout since 1993. Voter turnout decreased to 67% in 2019 and to 62.2% in 2021.
CIVIL: [Canada History Week 2023](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/history-week.html) takes place from November 20 to 26. This year’s theme is the History of Black Achievement in Canada. The week encourages Canadians to reflect upon and engage with Canada’s past. Viola Desmond was a Canadian civil and women's rights activist and businesswoman of Black Nova Scotian descent. In 1946, she challenged racial segregation at a cinema in New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, by refusing to leave a whites-only area of the Roseland Theatre. Viola was forcibly removed and jailed, sparking the civil rights movement in Canada. #HistoryWeek2023
CLAMS: Happy [National Acadian Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/celebrate-canada/acadian-day.html)! Acadian food is part of Canada's French heritage, and it's got a distinct history and flavours which are intertwined with neighbouring Québec. Fried clams or "coques frites" is a delicious traditional Acadian dish enjoyed by many in Canada's Maritime provinces. With an abundance of fresh seafood, there’s no better place to dig in to some battered fried clams along with a side of crispy fries. You’ll be happy as a clam when you try this dish!
CLANS: Many Indigenous communities across Canada are organized into clans, which play an important role in identity, governance, and kinship. Ribbon skirts often honour these connections, with colours and patterns reflecting clan affiliations, personal stories, or ancestral ties. On January 4th, as we celebrate National Ribbon Skirt Day, we recognize the strength and unity of Indigenous clans, which continue to inspire the designs and meanings behind these beautiful garments.
CLASS: On October 5th, we celebrated [World Teachers' Day](https://www.ctf-fce.ca/events/2024-world-teachers-day-celebration), a day to recognize the incredible role teachers play in shaping the minds of the next generation across the country! Canada is home to over 500,000 teachers who bring passion and dedication to the classroom each day. In fact, Canada is known for its strong public education system, consistently ranking among the best in the world. Whether they're in small rural schools or bustling urban centres, teachers in Canada ensure students have access to quality education from coast to coast.
CLAWS: Lobster fishing is a major industry in Canada, especially in the Atlantic provinces, and lobster claws are considered a delicacy. Shediac, New Brunswick is home to the world's largest lobster! Using two giant fiberglass claws to defend its claim as "Lobster Capital of the World," Shediac's 35 ft. long lobster sits atop a terraced rock perch with a lifesized bearded fisherman. It was sculpted by artist Winston Bronnum in 1989 and is maintained by Moncton artist Jared Betts. The [Shediac Lobster Festival](https://www.shediaclobsterfestival.ca/) runs from July 1-9 and welcomes you with open claws!
CLERK: The [Clerk of the Privy Council](https://www.canada.ca/en/privy-council/corporate/clerk.html) is the professional head of the Public Service of Canada. As the deputy minister for the Privy Council Office (the Prime Minister's department), the clerk is the senior civil servant in the Government of Canada and serves as the secretary to the Cabinet.
CLIMB: Did you know that sport climbing is making its second appearance in the 2024 Paris Olympics? This dynamic and challenging sport has gained popularity worldwide, including in Canada. [Canadian sport climbers](https://olympic.ca/sports/sport-climbing/) have been making their mark on the international stage, with athletes like [Sean McColl](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/sean-mccoll/) and Alannah Yip leading the way. Both climbers have represented Canada in various international competitions, showcasing their skills and determination.
CLOWN: Richard Pochinko (1946–1989) was a notable Canadian clown trainer who developed a new style of mask/clown performance training, known as the "Pochinko Method" or the Canadian Clowning technique. Originally from Selkirk, Manitoba, he was based primarily in Toronto, Ontario and founded the city's Theatre Resource Centre. Pochinko's technique for which he is known combined both European and First Nations traditions of masked and clown performance.
COACH: Henry Ruttan was a prominent businessman, inventor, and politician in Upper Canada who revolutionized railway travel. In 1858, he patented an innovative system for heating and cooling railway coaches, which was adopted by several railway companies across North America. His system used the motion of the train to force outside air through ducts and a wash tank, where the air was cleaned, humidified, and cooled. During winter, the system was adapted to heat the air entering the cars, making train travel more comfortable year-round. Ruttan’s invention was a game-changer for passenger comfort and a brilliant example of Canadian ingenuity!
COINS: Canada has some iconic coins, including the $1 loonie and the $2 toonie. DYK: In 2017, the Canadian Mint ran a contest and Canadians chose "Churchill" as the toonie polar bear's official name, a reference both to Winston Churchill and to the common polar bear sightings in Churchill, Manitoba. Canada has even commemorated the coins with monuments: the "Big Loonie" in Echo Bay, Ontario and the "Giant Toonie" in Campbellford, Ontario.
COMET: The de Havilland Comet is the world's first commercial jet airliner. On May 29th 1953, the first of two 40 passenger de Havilland Comets arrived in Ottawa. With the arrival of this aircraft, the Royal Canadian Air Force became the first air force in the world to operate jet transports and the first operator to make scheduled trans-Atlantic crossings.
COMIC: Today is International Read Comics in Public Day! Did you know that comic book characters Wolverine and Deadpool are both from Canada? Many other Canadian superheroes have appeared on comic book stands over the years, including Johnny Canuck, Nelvana of the Northern Lights, Captain Canuck, Northguard & Fleur de Lys, and Northstar and Weapon Alpha (aka Guardian), members of Alpha Flight, a team of Canadian superheroes. Although not Canadian himself, Superman was co-created by a Canadian: Toronto-born artist Joe Shuster created the superhero with American writer Jerry Siegel.
CONES: Snow-dusted evergreens are a hallmark of Canadian Christmas, and their cones play a surprisingly festive role. Pine cones are often gathered, painted, glittered, or scented with cinnamon to make ornaments, wreaths, and table centrepieces. Across Canada, these natural treasures help bring a rustic, wintry charm to Christmas décor, connecting homes to the snowy landscapes outside.
COOKS: Celebrity Cooks was one of Canada’s first cooking shows, airing from 1975 to 1987 and hosted by Bruno Gerussi of The Beachcombers fame. It mixed celebrity guests with easy, tasty recipes, inspiring a generation of home cooks. Since then, Canadian chefs have kept the country’s culinary scene vibrant, from Stephen Yan of the Canadian-produced Wok with Yan to Chuck Hughes, Lynn Crawford, Mark McEwan, Matty Matheson, Michael Smith, Anna Olson, Susur Lee, and Rob Feenie. These chefs showcase Canada’s diverse culinary talent on TV, in restaurants, and in cookbooks.
COPPER: Copper is one of Canada’s most important mined metals, used in construction, electronics, and power infrastructure. With major mines across the country, Canadian copper helps power everything from homes and hospitals to electric vehicles and renewable energy systems. It also crowns the roofs of Parliament Hill in Ottawa, where weathered copper has given Canada's iconic parliamentary buildings their distinctive green hue for generations.
COUGH: In 1919, Toronto pharmacist William Knapp Buckley bought a pharmacy and by March of 1920 he had discovered several natural ingredients that had a positive impact on coughs and colds; Buckley's Mixture was born. [Buckley's](https://www.buckleys.ca/) cough syrup is known for its famous campaign slogan: "It tastes awful. And it works."
COURT: The Supreme Court of Canada is the highest court in the judicial system of Canada. It comprises nine justices, whose decisions are the ultimate application of Canadian law.
COVES: Canada is full of hidden gems along its coastline, and some of the most famous are its coves. From the iconic lighthouse at [Peggy's Cove](https://novascotia.com/listing/peggys-cove-lighthouse-and-village/) to the turquoise waters of Green Bay Cove, these small, sheltered inlets have long been havens for wildlife, fishermen, and adventurers alike. Whether along the Atlantic, Pacific, or Arctic coasts, Canada's coves showcase the country’s diverse natural beauty, revealing serene hideaways tucked along its shores.
CRABS: Canada is the largest producer of snow crab in the world, accounting for about two-thirds of the global supply! The provinces of Newfoundland and Quebec provide Canada and the world with hundreds of tonnes of snow crab each year. Snow crabs have white flesh with a tinge of pink and a slightly salty flavour offering the perfect balance of sweet and briny.
CRAFT: In the past decade, Canada has seen a rapidly growing number of craft breweries popping up. Craft breweries have become so popular in Canada that a new association, Canadian Craft Brewers Association, was formed in May 2019. Sales of craft beer increased tenfold from 2008 to 2018, and it now accounts for 6% of the Canadian market. December 10th is National Lager Day! Lagers are some of the most popular beer styles in the world and Canada is no exception. Celebrate with a craft lager from your favourite Canadian brewery!
CRANE: The Whooping Crane is the tallest bird in North America and the rarest crane species. They stand nearly five-feet tall and are easily recognizable with their snowy white plumage and crimson cap. The only self-sustaining wild population of whooping cranes breeds in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park, which straddles the Northwest Territories and Alberta border.
CRAVE: [Crave](https://www.crave.ca/) is a popular Canadian streaming service offering a wide range of content and programming. Launched by Bell Media in 2014, Crave provides Canadians with access to a rich library of movies, TV shows, and original content. It has become a go-to platform for Canadian viewers craving top-quality entertainment, including hit series like "Game of Thrones," "The Handmaid's Tale," and Canadian originals like "Letterkenny." With its extensive selection and exclusive offerings, Crave has cemented itself as a key player in the Canadian streaming landscape.
CRAZY: "The Crazy Canucks" was the nickname for a group of World Cup alpine ski racers from Canada who rose to prominence in the 1970s and 1980s. Together, Ken Read, Steve Podborski, Dave Irwin and Dave Murray were a cultural phenomenon known as the Crazy Canucks; a team of world class skiers who were the first to challenge the Europeans for downhill supremacy in the sport they’d dominated for decades. "Jungle" Jim Hunter is considered to be the original Crazy Canuck before the core four, and Todd Brooker was the last member of the Crazy Canucks.
CREST: With its striking crest, the hooded merganser is one of Canada’s most distinctive waterfowl. Both males and females can raise or lower their fan-shaped crests, using them for display and communication. The male’s bold black-and-white crest is especially eye-catching during breeding season, helping it stand out on lakes and wetlands across the country. Even its scientific name reflects this feature, drawing from Greek words meaning “crest” and “diver,” a perfect match for this skilled, fish-catching duck.
CRIED: [The Girl Who Cried Pearls](https://www.nfb.ca/film/the-girl-who-cried-pearls/) made history in 2026 by winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film. Produced by the National Film Board of Canada, the stop-motion film was created by Montréal-based directors Chris Lavis and Maciek Szczerbowski, and is set in early 20th-century Montréal. Featuring Canadian voice actor Colm Feore, it’s a powerful example of homegrown storytelling earning global recognition.
CRIER: Before newspapers or social media, Canadian towns relied on the town crier to spread the news. Ringing a bell and shouting “Hear Ye! Hear Ye!”, they announced royal proclamations, local events, and important updates. Today, town criers are a cherished part of Canada’s history, keeping this lively tradition alive at festivals and ceremonies!
CRISP: How do Canadians like their coffee? Crisp! Coffee Crisp is a chocolate bar made in Canada consisting of layers of vanilla wafer and coffee-flavoured soft candy, covered in milk chocolate. It's a unique Canadian treat, and it rarely ventures beyond Canada's borders. The candy has largely been made exclusively for Canadian markets - over 150 million Coffee Crisp bars are produced every year in the Nestlé Canada factory in Toronto.
CROOK: A shepherd’s crook is the curved staff traditionally used to guide and protect sheep. Sheep farming has long been part of Canada’s agricultural story, from the rolling hills of the Maritimes to ranches across the Prairies, helping provide wool, milk, and meat for communities across the country!
CROPS: Canada is the world’s largest grower and exporter of flax seed, canola, oats, mustard seeds, pulses (peas, beans, and lentils) and durum wheat.
CROWN: As of 2019, there were 47 Crown corporations in Canada, including CBC, Canada Post, VIA Rail, the Royal Canadian Mint, and the Bank of Canada.
CRUDE: Canada has the 3rd largest oil reserves in the world and is the 4th largest oil producer and exporter.
CRUSH: In Newfoundland and Labrador, Crush isn’t just a drink – it’s a cultural icon! While most Canadians know the classic Orange Crush, Newfoundlanders enjoy unique flavours like Pineapple, Lime, and Birch Beer. These colourful cans are a staple at family gatherings, corner stores, and summer picnics, and many who leave the island still crave the sweet, fizzy taste of home.
CRUST: March 14th is known as Pi Day because the date (3/14) represents the mathematical constant π (pi), which begins with 3.14. Pi is essential in calculating the circumference of circles, making it a perfect day to celebrate round things like pies! In Canada, pies come in all flavours, from the savoury tourtière of Quebec to the sweet and sticky butter tarts found across the country. A pie's crust is just as important as its filling, with bakers perfecting their flaky, golden layers. So on Pi Day, whether you're enjoying a slice of sugar pie, blueberry pie, or a warm tourtière, take a moment to appreciate the delicious, mathematical magic of pie!
CUBIC: Canada is one of the world's top producers of diamonds, with mines in the Northwest Territories, Ontario, and Quebec. Diamonds, which are also the birthstone for April, form deep underground in a cubic crystal structure, giving them their signature sparkle! The first Canadian diamond mine, Ekati, opened in the Northwest Territories in 1998, and today, Canada is known for its high-quality, ethically sourced gems.
CURSE: The Oak Island mystery is a series of stories and legends concerning buried treasure and unexplained objects found on or near Oak Island in Nova Scotia. Since the 18th century, attempts have been made to find treasure and artifacts. Hypotheses about artifacts present on the island range from pirate treasure to Shakespearean manuscripts to the Holy Grail or the Ark of the Covenant. A "curse" on the treasure is said to have originated more than a century ago and states that seven men will die in the search for the treasure before it is found. This intriguing tale has been the subject of the popular TV series "The Curse of Oak Island," which follows brothers Rick and Marty Lagina as they explore the island's mysteries.
CYCLE: Today is World Bicycle Day! It's a global celebration supported by the United Nations held each year on June 3rd and aims to promote physical activity and the use of bicycles for transportation. Canada boasts an extensive network of cycling infrastructure, ranging from urban bike lanes to scenic rural trails. By participating in World Bicycle Day, Canadians can raise awareness about the benefits of cycling, encourage their fellow citizens to take up this healthy and eco-friendly habit, and advocate for continued improvements to cycling infrastructure in their communities.
DAILY: Daily Planet was a Canadian television program featuring daily news, discussion and commentary on the scientific aspects of current events and discoveries. The show first aired on January 1, 1995, the same day as the premiere of Discovery Channel Canada, under the name @discovery.ca with Jay Ingram as the host. Ingram previously hosted the science program Quirks and Quarks on CBC Radio One from 1979 (when he took over the show from David Suzuki) to 1992.
DANCE: Canada is a country rich in multicultural heritage and culture, part of which is dance. Long before we called this land Canada, Aboriginal dancers were practising dance. Powwow dances are beautiful expressions of Indigenous spirituality, history and culture. When more people began immigrating to Canada in the 1900s, they brought with them bits of rich heritage and culture from all over the globe. This influx of international talent is what led to the creation of most of our dance institutions today, including the National Ballet of Canada and the Royal Winnipeg Ballet, Canada's oldest ballet company and the longest continuously operating ballet company in North America. Sikh-Canadian Gurdeep Pandher of the Yukon, has been spreading joy, hope and positivity across Canada with his Bhangra dancing - a traditional folk dance of Punjab. Check out [www.gurdeep.ca](https://gurdeep.ca/) and get ready to dance!
DEEDS: November 13th is [World Kindness Day](https://www.randomactsofkindness.org/world-kindness-day)! The purpose of World Kindness Day is to highlight and encourage good deeds in your community. In Canada, the Chevrolet Good Deeds Cup seeks to inspire young Canadians to do good by transforming the positive values learned through hockey into Good Deeds within their communities. The program has made an incredible impact in communities coast to coast to coast amounting more than 1,000 Good Deeds and over $600,000 to charities.
DENIM: The Canadian Tuxedo is an outfit consisting of a denim jacket or jean shirt worn with denim jeans, or denim-on-denim. The term originated in 1951 after Bing Crosby was refused entry to a Vancouver hotel wearing double denim.
DEPOT: In early Canadian history, a depot was more than just a storage spot – it was a lifeline. Trading depots were key hubs during the fur trade era, where Indigenous peoples, voyageurs, and European traders exchanged goods like furs, tools, and textiles. Major depots, such as those run by the Hudson’s Bay Company and North West Company, helped shape trade routes and settlements across Canada. These depots laid the groundwork for many towns and cities we know today!
DERBY: It's the final weekend of the 2023 [Calgary Stampede](https://www.calgarystampede.com/) - the world's largest outdoor rodeo! This year, the Stampede is celebrating 100 years of chuckwagon racing at the Cowboys Rangeland Derby! The world’s first Chuckwagon Race was staged at the Calgary Stampede in 1923. A true throwback to the wild west, the event was inspired by the tradition of cowboys breaking camp and racing home. And while some of the rules have since changed, the rush has never left. YAHOO!
DEUCE: In curling, a deuce is when a team scores two points in a single end, giving them a strong advantage on the scoreboard. The new [Rock League](https://www.rockleague.com/) kicks off in Toronto from April 6-12, featuring an exciting new format and players from across Canada and around the world. With the slogan “Curling Unleashed,” competitors will be sliding, sweeping, and chasing deuces in a week of fast-paced, international curling action.
DINER: [The Chickenburger](https://chickenburger.com/) in Bedford, Nova Scotia, has been part of Canada’s diner history since 1940 and is reputed to be the country’s oldest drive-in restaurant. Known for its chickenburgers, cheeseburgers and shakes, it preserves the look and feel of a classic 1950s diner, complete with a working jukebox. More than 86 years after opening, the landmark remains a throwback to the golden age of diner culture.
DIRTY: Did you know that the Dirty Thirties was the nickname given to the 1930s in Canada? [The Great Depression](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/great-depression) brought widespread unemployment and hardship, while drought and dust storms created devastating conditions across the Prairies. The challenges of this era transformed Canada and helped shape the social programs that support Canadians today.
DISCO: Disco fever hit Canada in the 1970s, lighting up dance floors across the country. Montreal became one of North America’s disco capitals with iconic clubs like the Lime Light, where dancers grooved under glittering lights and DJs shaped the scene. Today, disco still thrives with clubs and parties, while Canadian acts like the band Lime and ongoing celebrations keep the rhythm alive coast to coast.
DOMES: Canada is home to some famous domes, including Calgary's unmistakeable Saddledome, the SkyDome in Toronto, the Montreal Biodome, and BC's Snow Dome peak which is a "[hydrological apex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_divide)" (a single point where three different watersheds meet).
DONUT: Canada has the most donut shops and consumes the most donuts per capita of any other country in the world - around 1 billion annually! The donut-eating capital of Canada is Lloydminster, Alberta/Saskatchewan. National Donut Day was last Friday, June 3rd - we hope you celebrated with your favourite donut! In Canada, the preferred spelling is “doughnut”, but most dictionaries list “donut” as an acceptable variant. We wanted to include it in the game since the doughnut/donut is considered by some as Canada's unofficial national sugary snack! 🍩🍁
DOUBLE: Few coffee orders are more Canadian than a double-double. Popularized by Tim Hortons, it means two creams and two sugars, and has become part of the country's everyday vocabulary. The phrase was even added to the Canadian Oxford Dictionary in 2004.
DRAKE: The Village of Andrew, Alberta is home to the [world's largest mallard duck](https://www.travelalberta.com/listings/worlds-largest-mallard-duck-andrew-5641)! The statue honours the area's wetlands and mallard nesting grounds. It features a male mallard duck (also known as a drake) with a wingspan of 23 feet, weighing 1 tonne and standing seven metres tall. This drake is not quite as famous as Canadian rapper and singer, Drake, who also starred as Jimmy Brooks in the teen drama series Degrassi: The Next Generation.
DRAWN: In Canada, traditional horse-drawn carioles were a common winter sight in the 19th and early 20th centuries. These elegant, narrow sleds, pulled by a single horse, carried families and goods across snowy landscapes, especially in Quebec and Ontario. Today, carioles are celebrated as a charming symbol of Canadian winter heritage and horse-drawn history.
DREAM: In many Indigenous cultures across Canada, dreams are seen as powerful sources of guidance and healing.
