The dreamcatcher, which originated with the Anishinaabe people, is a handmade web traditionally hung above a bed to catch bad dreams while allowing good ones to pass through. Crafted from natural materials like willow and sinew, each part holds deep meaning – symbolizing protection, connection, and the cycle of life. Today, dreamcatchers remain a meaningful symbol of Indigenous identity and the enduring strength of traditions across the land.
DRESS: Red Dress Day, also known as the National Day of Awareness for Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls and Two-Spirit People, is observed annually on May 5th. The day honours and brings awareness to the thousands of Indigenous women, girls and two-spirit people who have been subject to disproportionate violence in Canada. Red Dress Day was inspired by Métis artist Jaime Black’s REDress Project installation, in which she hung empty, red dresses to represent the missing and murdered women. Red dresses have become symbolic of the crisis as a result of her installation.
DRIED: Pemmican is a nutrient-rich food made from dried meat, tallow, and sometimes dried berries. Traditionally prepared by Indigenous Peoples in parts of North America, it has long been valued for its long shelf life and high energy content, making it an essential food for survival, particularly during long journeys across Canada's vast landscapes. Pemmican can be eaten raw or used in prepared meals, and it remains part of Indigenous cuisine today. The word pemmican comes from the Cree word 'pimikan,' meaning 'manufactured grease.'
DRIFT: Along Canada’s coastlines, driftwood is carried by waves, tides, and currents before washing ashore in ever-changing shapes. It has long been used in coastal Indigenous communities for practical purposes such as carving, building, and fuel, and continues to hold cultural and creative significance. Today, it is also widely used in Canadian driftwood art, where artists transform weathered pieces into sculptures, furniture, and natural décor that reflect the beauty of the shoreline.
DRILL: The [Royal Military College of Canada](https://www.rmc-cmr.ca/) is well known for the quality and diversity of its ceremonial drill. Reaching this high standard can only be gained through the hard work and dedication of each cadet. Cadets are expected to reach and maintain a high standard of personal drill with the service rifle, colours, and the sword.
DRINK: One of Canada’s most iconic drinks, the Caesar, was invented in Calgary in 1969 by bartender Walter Chell to celebrate the opening of an Italian restaurant at the Calgary Inn. Inspired by spaghetti alle vongole, he mixed vodka, Clamato juice, Worcestershire sauce and hot sauce, and the Caesar was born. Canadians are estimated to drink more than 400 million Caesars each year, making it one of the country’s most popular cocktails.
DRONE: On a vast swath of southern Alberta prairie, near the tiny village of Foremost, unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) have unrivalled freedom to roam. The Foremost UAS Test Range offers more than 700 square nautical miles of restricted airspace, making it uniquely positioned to advance Canada’s drone technology development. This gives small and medium-sized firms plenty of space to test new drone technologies. It is one of only two places approved by Transport Canada to conduct beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) testing.
DRUID: Modern druidry has taken root in Canada, where groups gather to celebrate the changing seasons, honour nature, and explore Celtic-inspired spiritual traditions. From coastal ceremonies in Atlantic Canada to forest gatherings in British Columbia, Canadian druids blend ancient symbolism with local landscapes, reminding us how deeply connected many Canadians feel to the land around them.
DRUMS: Drumming has always been, and continues to be, an important part of First Nations ceremonies, traditions and cultural practices. Drums are often considered sacred amongst Indigenous peoples, representing the heartbeat of people, animals and Mother Earth herself. Drums range in size from small enough for a child to hold, to large enough to seat several drummers around at a ceremony or powwow.
DRYER: The word dryer is forever tied to Sidney Crosby's rise to hockey greatness. Growing up in Cole Harbour, Nova Scotia, Crosby spent hours shooting pucks in the basement of his childhood home, and the family clothes dryer bore the marks of many slapshots sent its way. This makeshift training ground played a part in shaping Crosby into the NHL legend he became. In fact, the battered dryer was even featured in an exhibit at the [Nova Scotia Sport Hall of Fame](https://nsshf.com/), a testament to the role it played in his journey. Now, as he leads Team Canada as captain in the 4 Nations Face-Off, Crosby continues to inspire the next generation of hockey stars.
DUCKS: With roughly 22 different species of duck found in Canada, the most common is the Mallard. Saskatchewan is renowned for having some of the most abundant and productive waterfowl habitat in North America. Check out [Ducks Unlimited Canada](https://www.ducks.ca/) and how they are working to conserve, restore and manage Canadian wetlands.
DUNES: The world's smallest desert can be found in the Yukon! In truth, the moniker is used in good fun as the Carcross Desert isn't a desert at all. The beautiful 2.5 square kilometre patch of land is a series of sand dunes left over from a glacial lake thousands of years ago. The tiny area is kept dry year-round thanks to the surrounding mountains. In contrast, the Athabasca Sand Dunes in Saskatchewan is the largest active sand surface in Canada at 1925 km² and one of the world's most northerly major sand dunes.
EAGER: Canada’s official national animal since 1975, the [beaver](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/official-symbols-canada.html#a3) is famous for its tireless work ethic and ability to shape Canada’s landscapes. Known for building dams that create important wetland habitats, this busy animal inspired the phrase “eager beaver,” a nickname for someone who is enthusiastic and hardworking. A fitting tribute to one of Canada’s most iconic creatures!
EAGLE: Although the bald eagle is the national bird of the United States, the town of Squamish, British Columbia is the bald eagle capital of the world! Thousands of bald eagles converge between December and March to feed on spawning salmon in the Squamish River. In Indigenous culture, it is believed that all things possess inherent power and wisdom, and the eagle is a powerful spiritual symbol signifying a connection with the Creator. The eagle is seen as a messenger of the Creator who imparts wisdom and medicine, so its feathers are sacred gifts to be used reverently in ceremonies, to honour people, show respect, or to purify and pray for blessings.
EARLY: Natural Resources Canada has developed a national [Earthquake Early Warning](https://www.earthquakescanada.nrcan.gc.ca/eew-asp/system-en.php) (EEW) system designed to provide early detection and warning in areas of moderate to high earthquake hazard and with concentrations of population and infrastructure. In Canada, this earthquake risk is concentrated in western British Columbia, eastern Ontario, and southern Quebec. The EEW system began operation in BC in the spring of 2024 and will begin in Quebec and Ontario in early 2025.
EARTH: Happy Earth Day! 🌎 Every year on April 22, [Earth Day](https://earthday.ca/) marks the anniversary of the birth of the modern environmental movement in 1970. In 1990, the creation of the organization in France and in Canada goes hand in hand with the internationalization of the Earth Day movement. Earth Day in 1990 became a global celebration, with participation by an estimated 200 million people in at least 136 countries. Over the years, Earth Day has become the largest participatory environmental movement on the planet.
EASEL: Altona, Manitoba is home to the [world's largest painting on an easel](https://altona.ca/p/big-easel)! Artist and art educator, Cameron Cross, developed the vision of a giant steel easel displaying the likeness of Vincent Van Gogh's 'Sunflowers' painting. This landmark stands 76'6" high and is on a 3-legged steel easel. It is a symbol of international fine art and celebrates Altona’s reputation as the Sunflower Capital of Canada.
EATER: The Smoke Eaters (aka Smokies) have existed as both junior and senior hockey teams in Canada since the 1920s. The senior Smoke Eaters won two Allan Cup championships, 1938 and 1962, and two Ice Hockey World Championships playing for Canada in 1939 and 1961. The senior Smokies were the last independent ice hockey club to represent Canada in international competition before the Canada men's national ice hockey team was established in 1963. The current Trail Smoke Eaters are a junior A ice hockey team from Trail, British Columbia, that are part of the British Columbia Hockey League. Learn more about the Smoke Eaters in [Craig Baird's Canadian History Ehx podcast episode](https://canadaehx.com/2022/01/11/the-trail-smoke-eaters-2/)!
EAVES: In Canada, the term "eavestroughs" is commonly used to refer to the rain gutters attached to the eaves of a roof! While "gutters" is the more common term elsewhere, Canadians prefer "eavestroughs" to describe these important drainage systems that help manage rainfall and protect buildings from water damage. This uniquely Canadian term reflects the country's distinctive linguistic features and regional vocabulary!
EDICT: An edict is a formal announcement or decree that establishes a law or order. Often associated with monarchies, edicts have been used throughout history to communicate official orders, mandates, and laws. In Canada, royal edicts played a key role in shaping governance and establishing provinces under the Crown. The Quebec Act of 1774, an edict from King George III, protected French civil law and religious rights, helping to preserve Quebec's distinct identity. Even today, Canada remains a constitutional monarchy, with royal proclamations continuing to mark significant national events.
EERIE: As Halloween draws near, Canada is home to some truly eerie locations that promise spine-chilling experiences! From the haunted Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel in Alberta, known for its ghostly bride roaming the halls, to the Ottawa Jail Hostel, where visitors report unsettling encounters, the country offers numerous sites steeped in supernatural lore. These places not only showcase Canada's rich history but also the spooky tales that come alive during the Halloween season. So, if you're in the mood for some thrills this October, consider exploring one of these eerie spots!
EGRET: Egrets are a beautiful sight in Canada, particularly the Great Egret, which can be spotted in southern parts of the country during the warmer months! These elegant birds, known for their striking white plumage and graceful flight, are most commonly found in wetlands, marshes, and along riverbanks. The Great Egret was once a rare visitor in Canada but has been increasingly seen in provinces like Ontario and Quebec, much to the delight of birdwatchers and nature enthusiasts. This species has been identified as a priority for conservation and/or stewardship in one or more Bird Conservation Region Strategies in Canada.
EIGHT: Canada has a proud tradition in rowing, especially in the men's and women's eight events. The coxed eight boat class (8 rowers with one oar each and a coxswain to steer) has been Canada's most successful rowing event with notable triumphs on the world stage. The Canadian men's and women's eight teams have collectively won a total of six Olympic medals: two golds and four silvers.
EJECT: The ejection seat, invented in Britain during the 1940s by Sir James Martin of Martin-Baker Aircraft, has saved thousands of pilots’ lives. Canada was among the early adopters, equipping its jets with this life-saving technology. Today, Royal Canadian Air Force pilots flying CF-18 Hornets rely on rocket-powered ejection systems that can launch them clear of danger in under two seconds – a dramatic but vital safeguard in Canadian aviation.
ELBOW: "Elbows Up" is a phrase that means to protect yourself or fight back, and it recently gained attention as Canada flexed its muscle in the ongoing trade dispute with the United States. Just like in hockey, where players use their elbows to shield themselves or push back against opponents, Canada has been using its economic power and strategic policies to stand firm and defend its interests. Whether it's in the rink or the world of international trade, "elbows up" is all about resilience and standing your ground!
ELDER: Elders are respected individuals who play key roles in Indigenous communities. They are important knowledge keepers, and they also help to ensure cultural continuity.
ELECT: Canada is a representative democracy. During an election, all Canadian citizens who are at least 18 years old on election day can vote in their electoral district.
EMAIL: Long before smartphones became everyday tools, BlackBerry was changing the way the world communicated. Created by Waterloo, Ontario-based company Research In Motion (RIM), BlackBerry devices became famous for putting email in the hands of millions, making “push email” a must-have feature for business users around the globe.
EMBER: [Girl Guides of Canada](https://www.girlguides.ca/) (GGC) announced a new branch name for girls ages 7 and 8 in 2023, replacing the name Brownies with Embers. GGC implemented the name change after hearing from current and former members that the previous name caused harm and was a barrier to belonging for racialized girls and women. With the new Embers name, the hope is that even more girls will see Guiding as a space where they can just be themselves.
ENVOY: Canada has a proud history of diplomacy and peacekeeping, often playing the role of envoy on the world stage. Canadians have been involved in key international missions as ambassadors, peacekeepers, and negotiators, striving to promote peace and collaboration globally. In fact, Canadian Lester B. Pearson, who served as an envoy in the United Nations, is credited with establishing the modern concept of peacekeeping and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1957 for his efforts. Through its envoys, Canada has built a legacy of promoting unity, peace, and goodwill around the world - a true reflection of Canadian values.
EPOCH: In the world of Artificial Intelligence (AI), "epoch" is a term used to describe one cycle through a full dataset during the training of a machine learning model. Canada is a major player in AI, and Dr. Geoffrey Hinton, often called the "godfather of AI," has been a pivotal figure. In October 2024, Dr. Hinton won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his groundbreaking contributions to neural networks and deep learning, helping to shape the modern AI era. His research has played a major role in advancing the field, with lasting effects on everything from healthcare to natural language processing.
EVENT: The Big Event was a professional wrestling spectacle held at Toronto’s Exhibition Stadium on August 28, 1986. Produced by the World Wrestling Federation (WWF), it drew a massive crowd of over 70,000 fans, making it one of the largest wrestling events in Canadian history. This closed-circuit broadcast helped cement Toronto as a major stop on the wrestling map and showcased how Canadians have long embraced live sporting and entertainment events on a grand scale.
EXPAT: Canada is home to a vibrant expat community, with people from around the world making it their home temporarily for work, study, or lifestyle. At the same time, there are over 3 million Canadians living abroad, with popular destinations like the United States, the UK, and Australia. Whether in Canada or overseas, expats play an important role in connecting cultures and expanding global networks.
EXTRA: The phrase “Extra! Extra! Read all about it!” was once shouted on Canadian streets to announce breaking news and special editions of newspapers. Long before digital headlines, these extras kept Canadians informed about major events and the latest news. It all began with the Halifax Gazette, first published on March 23, 1752, by printer John Bushell - the start of printing and publishing in what would become Canada.
FABLE: Fables of the Green Forest introduced Canadian kids in the 1980s and 1990s to woodland adventures on [TVOntario](https://www.tvo.org/) (TVO). Each episode unfolded like a classic fable, with animal characters learning simple lessons about friendship, courage, and life in the forest. It remains a nostalgic example of how storytelling on TVO helped shape early childhood viewing in Canada.
FACES: [Faces Magazine](https://facesmag.ca/) is Ottawa’s premier lifestyle publication, showcasing the faces behind the city's businesses, sports, and entertainment scene. Faces highlights the best of Ottawa with a uniquely Canadian flair. From restaurants to community leaders, it’s all about connecting people and celebrating what makes the capital great!
FACTS: Did you know that the beloved game Trivial Pursuit was invented by Canadians? Scott Abbott, a sports editor, and Chris Haney, a photo editor, came up with the idea in 1979 while playing Scrabble. The game, which challenges players on their knowledge of a wide range of trivia facts, has since become a global sensation and an iconic part of Canadian pop culture.
FAITH: Religion in Canada encompasses a wide range of beliefs and customs. The constitution of Canada refers to God and the monarch carries the title of Defender of the Faith, however Canada has no official church and the government is officially committed to religious pluralism. Freedom of religion in Canada is a constitutionally protected right, allowing individuals to assemble and worship without limitation or interference.
FALLS: About 28 million litres of water travel down Niagara Falls every second.
FALSE: Pacific Central Station is a railway station in Vancouver, British Columbia, which acts as the western terminus of Via Rail's cross-country service. The station is located in the False Creek area of Vancouver and is a handsome illustration of Beaux-Arts architectural principles, retaining both the exterior features and interior detailing typical of the style. Designed by the Canadian Northern Railway to serve as the western terminus of its transcontinental route, it was originally named False Creek Station and was designated a heritage railway station in 1991.
FARCE: The Royal Canadian Air Farce was a comedy troupe that was active from 1973 to 2019. It is best known for their various Canadian Broadcasting Corporation series, first on CBC Radio and later on CBC Television. Although their weekly radio series ended in 1997 and their television series ended in 2008, the troupe produced annual New Year's Eve specials on CBC Television until 2019.
FARMS: In 2020, roughly 1 out of every 9 Canadian jobs was in the agriculture and agri-food sector.
FENCE: Canadian fencing dates back to 1816 when Maitre Girard opened the first fencing school in Montréal. The first Canadian Championships were held in 1902. The [Canadian Fencing Federation](https://fencing.ca/) was incorporated in 1971 with a mandate is to establish, develop and support fencing in Canada and to represent Canada on the international scene.
FERNS: Found throughout Canada, fiddlehead ferns are the tightly coiled tips of early spring ferns with a tender texture and mildly nutty flavour. They are only available for a short window of time during the spring and are considered a seasonal delicacy in many parts of Canada.
FETAL: Montreal born Leon Katz was a pioneering biomedical engineer whose work significantly improved patient care and safety throughout Canada. Katz invented, innovated and hand-crafted a wide range of medical devices: Canada's first fetal heart monitor, a scanner-printer to detect radioactive iodine uptake in the thyroid gland, infant incubators, and a high-speed contrast injector for angiography. Notably, using his own original heart-lung bypass machine, he was the perfusionist for Canada’s first successful open heart surgery, and for thousands of subsequent operations.
FIFTY: On June 16, 2025, Canadian ultramarathoner and mental health advocate Sachin "Sach" Latti began running 50 km a day for 75 days across Canada, from Victoria, B.C. to St. John’s, Newfoundland. Known as Canada’s Longest Run for Mental Health, his mission aims to raise $1 million for mental health initiatives. Along the way, Sach is connecting with Canadians from all walks of life, sparking open conversations about mental health and inspiring others to take action. You can follow Sach's journey at [sachinmotion.ca](https://sachinmotion.ca/) and support his cross-Canada run with a donation to the [Sach In Motion Fund](https://form.123formbuilder.com/6647897/sach-in-motion-donation-form). Every step matters. Every donation helps.
FILMS: The film industry in Canada has grown so much over the years that it has been referred to as Hollywood North. Toronto is the home to the [Toronto International Film Festival](https://tiff.net/), which is considered by many in the film industry to be second only to Cannes in terms of influence. James Cameron, born in Kapuskasing, Ontario, is the writer and director of the two highest-grossing movies of all time, Avatar (2009) and Titanic (1997). The two films have combined to gross nearly $500 million dollars. Save the date: April 19, 2023 is [National Canadian Film Day](https://canfilmday.ca/)!
FIRES: Fires have been a natural part of Canada’s landscapes for thousands of years, shaping forests, grasslands, and wildlife habitats. Indigenous peoples have long used controlled burns to renew the land and support healthy ecosystems. Today, wildfire season, which peaks from spring through late summer, remains an important part of life in Canada. Modern wildfire management combines skilled crews, advanced technology, and careful planning to protect communities and the environment while respecting fire’s natural role in the ecosystem.
FJORD: Fjords in Canada are long, narrow inlets characterized by steep sides, created in a valley carved by glacial activity. Canada is home to many of these impressive natural features, including the many islands that make up the Arctic Archipelago in northern Canada, the Saguenay Fjord National Park in Quebec, Newfoundland's iconic Western Brook Pond Fjord located in Gros Morne National Park, and all along the west coast in British Columbia which is one of the longest fjord coastlines in the world!
FLAGS: Today is National Flag of Canada Day! Flag Day is observed annually on February 15 to commemorate the inauguration of the flag of Canada on that date in 1965. Check out this [Heritage Minutes video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ikY7bMDVQTg) about the many designs proposed for consideration for Canada's flag. Read more about the National Flag of Canada on [The Canadian Encyclopedia](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/national-flag-of-canada).
FLAIR: [National Ribbon Skirt Day](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/N-16.2/FullText.html) on January 4 honours Indigenous women and the ribbon skirt – a centuries-old spiritual symbol of womanhood, identity, and resilience. The skirt represents a deep connection to Mother Earth, culture, and the passing of knowledge across generations. With their flowing designs and vibrant ribbons, these garments embody both tradition and flair, inviting all Canadians to learn, reflect, and celebrate the richness of Indigenous cultures. The day was inspired by the experience of Isabella Kulak, an Indigenous girl in Saskatchewan who was shamed for wearing a ribbon skirt to school.
FLAME: The Centennial Flame is a monument on Parliament Hill commemorating the 100th anniversary of the Canadian Confederation. It was first lit in January 1967 and burns atop a fountain that has a bronze shield with the coat of arms of a province or territory on each side.
FLASH: Today is National Lighthouse Day! Canada is home to more than 750 lighthouses, and every lighthouse emits a distinctive series of flashes known as its "characteristic." These flash sequences allow ship captains to time intervals between flashes so that they can identify lighthouses, using a publication called the List of Lights.
FLEET: The [Royal Canadian Navy](https://www.canada.ca/en/navy.html)'s (RCN) fleet is made up of numerous classes of ships, submarines and other support vessels, as well as specialized units that allow Canada to maintain one of the most active blue-water navies in the world. The Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) aircraft fleet ranges from huge transport aircraft to helicopters to fighters to patrol aircraft and more. They are used to carry out a multitude of roles at home and abroad, in peace and in conflict, all in support of the RCAF's mission of providing relevant, responsive and effective air power to meet the defence challenges of today and into the future. November 5 to 11 is [Veterans' Week](https://www.veterans.gc.ca/eng/remembrance/commemorative-events/veterans-week), an opportunity for Canadians to honour the extraordinary efforts and sacrifices of our veterans. Thank you for your service!
FLIES: Canada’s summers are famous for many things, including the arrival of blackflies, one of the country’s most notorious outdoor pests. Found near rivers, forests, and lakes across the country, these tiny biting insects have earned a legendary reputation among campers, hikers, and outdoor enthusiasts. The National Film Board of Canada even celebrated their infamous status in the 1991 animated short [Blackfly](https://www.nfb.ca/film/blackfly/), a humorous ode to one of Canada’s tiniest summer annoyances.
FLIRT: [Flirt Drinks](https://flirtdrinks.com/) is a Canadian company founded in Quebec's Outaouais region by two lifelong friends determined to reduce food waste. Their Flirt sparkling lemonades are made with rescued fruit that might otherwise be discarded, turning a simple idea into a refreshing made-in-Canada success story. Cheers to a Canadian company finding a fresh way to make every piece of fruit count!
FLOAT: Did you know that Canada has its own version of the Dead Sea? The waters of Little Manitou Lake near Saskatoon are roughly five times saltier than the ocean - and approximately half as salty as the Dead Sea in Israel and Jordan. Fed by underground springs, the lake is so high in sodium, magnesium and potassium salts that swimmers are able to lie back and float with zero effort whatsoever.
FLOUR: What makes iconic Canadian glacial lakes like Moraine Lake and Lake Louise so blue? Rock flour or glacier flour of course! The small particles of rock flour find their way to the lake via melting streams. Glacial flour being so light, is suspended in the water. This murky appearance is referred to as glacial milk. The more of this glacial milk mixture there is, the more turquoise the glacial lake appears!
FLUSH: Dundurn Castle in Hamilton, Ontario was once home to Sir Allan Napier MacNab, railway magnate, lawyer and Premier of the United Canadas (1854-1856) and his family. The 40-room villa was built in the 1830s and featured the latest conveniences of gas lighting and running water. Sir Allan’s washroom even featured an indoor flushing toilet with running water, which was one of the first in Upper Canada.
FOGGY: Newfoundland, Canada is widely considered one of the foggiest places on Earth. On average, Newfoundland experiences over 200 foggy days every year.
FORGE: [Hamilton Forge FC](https://forgefc.canpl.ca/) is a Canadian professional soccer club based in Hamilton, Ontario, that competes in the [Canadian Premier League](https://canpl.ca/), the top tier of Canadian soccer. Forge FC joined the CPL in 2019 as one of the league's seven inaugural teams. The team name represents Hamilton's industrious roots and aligns with its nickname "Steeltown."
FORKS: The Forks, located in Winnipeg at the junction of the Red and Assiniboine rivers, has been a meeting place for over 6,000 years. Indigenous peoples traded at The Forks, followed by European fur traders, Scottish settlers, railway pioneers and tens of thousands of immigrants. The Forks was designated a National Historic Site of Canada in 1974 due to its status as a cultural landscape. The Canadian Museum for Human Rights is located on Indigenous ancestral lands just adjacent to The Forks.
FORTS: Parks Canada administers a range of historic forts and fortified places across the country. Forts were the focal points of many important developments in Canada's history. As bases for defence, crossroads of trade, and centres of growing communities, they have been gathering places for generations. The [Fortress of Louisbourg National Historic Site](https://parks.canada.ca/lhn-nhs/ns/louisbourg) is the largest reconstructed 18th-century French fortified town in North America.
FOXES: Four species of foxes live in Canada: arctic, swift, grey, and red being the most common. The grey fox is one of only 2 members of the dog family that can climb trees.
FOYER: The [House of Commons foyer](https://www.ourcommons.ca/heritage/en/parliamentary-buildings/past/house-of-commons-foyer) is the Centre Block's primary meeting place. It has vaulted ceilings, marble floors and dramatic lighting. Many Canadians recognize the foyer from media scrums where journalists ask members of Parliament questions after question period and after debates in the House of Commons. The foyer's lower level contains sculptures that depict themes of art, history and philosophy. In the upper level, the stonework shows the coat of arms of each Canadian province. The foyer also contains framed portraits of Canada's prime ministers, contributing to the foyer's dignified character.
FREED: On April 17, Canada marks the anniversary of the [Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms](https://www.justice.gc.ca/eng/csj-sjc/rfc-dlc/ccrf-ccdl/), a key part of our Constitution that protects the freedoms and rights of all Canadians. The Charter guarantees basic rights, such as freedom of thought, expression, and peaceful assembly, while ensuring equality for all citizens. It's a reminder that freedoms like these are fundamental to our democracy and way of life.
FRIES: Canadians consumed over 240,000 metric tonnes of frozen fries in 2019.
FRONT: Front Page Challenge was a Canadian panel game about current events and history. Created by comedy writer/performer John Aylesworth (of the comedy team of Frank Peppiatt and John Aylesworth) and produced and aired by CBC Television, the series ran from 1957 to 1995. Famous guests on the show included Gordie Howe, Pierre Trudeau, Malcolm X, and Rick Hansen. When Front Page Challenge left the air in 1995, it was the longest continually running non-news program in Canadian television history.
FULLY: The Tragically Hip, often referred to simply as the Hip, were a Canadian rock band formed in Kingston, Ontario in 1984, consisting of vocalist Gord Downie, guitarist Paul Langlois, guitarist Rob Baker, bassist Gord Sinclair, and drummer Johnny Fay. They have received numerous Canadian music awards, including 17 Juno Awards. Their album "Fully Completely" is widely considered the Hip's breakthrough record, and songs like "Wheat Kings" and "Courage" became Canadian anthems. The Hip played their final concert together in Kingston on August 20, 2016. Frontman Gord Downie passed away on October 17, 2017 after a battle with brain cancer.
FUNGI: Canada's forests are home to a wide variety of fungi, including mushrooms, molds, and lichens, playing important roles in decomposition, nutrient cycling, and ecosystem health. With its vast forests, wetlands, and diverse ecosystems, Canada provides the perfect habitat for fungi to thrive. In fact, Canada is home to over 10,000 species of fungi! A fun tribute to these fascinating organisms can be found in Vilna, Alberta, at Mushroom Park, where you'll find the [World's Largest Mushrooms](https://www.vilna.ca/community-profile/things-to-see-do/world-s-largest-mushroom) – a giant sculpture celebrating the area's rich fungal heritage.
GAMER: Canada has earned a place on the global esports map thanks to some legendary gamers. Kingston’s Sasha “Scarlett” Hostyn became one of the world’s top StarCraft II players, while Vancouver’s Artour “Arteezy” Babaev and Kurtis “Aui_2000” Ling are stars in Dota 2. And in Counter-Strike, Russel “Twistzz” Van Dulken from Toronto is a Major champion and one of the most decorated Canadian players ever. From strategy to sharpshooting, Canadian gamers continue to shine on the world stage.
GAMES: The Canada Games is a multi-sport event held every two years, alternating between the Canada Winter Games and the Canada Summer Games. They represent the highest level of national competition for Canadian athletes. The [Niagara 2022 Canada Summer Games](https://www.canadagames.ca/previous-games/niagara-2022) will take place Aug 6-21, 2022!
GASES: Happy [Earth Day](https://earthday.ca/)! Did you know that Canada's veteran satellite, [SCISAT](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/satellites/scisat/), has been orbiting Earth 15 times a day for over 21 years? It's the only satellite in the world that can monitor all the regulated gases covered by the Montreal Protocol – an international agreement to protect the ozone layer. SCISAT helps scientists around the globe track the impact of over 70 gases in our atmosphere, playing a vital role in efforts to reduce harmful emissions and combat climate change.
GAVEL: Did you know that despite what movies and television shows might suggest, the iconic courtroom gavel is largely absent from Canada's justice system and Parliament? Following British tradition, Canadian judges, including those of the Supreme Court of Canada, do not use gavels, and neither does the Speaker of the House of Commons. Instead, order is maintained through voice, procedure, and long-standing tradition rather than a symbolic tap of wood found in many legislatures elsewhere.
GEESE: Although Canada has no official bird, the Canada Goose has long been a part of the national identity. Canada Geese are well known for flying in a distinctive V-shaped formation, their loud "honk" and their unmistakable looks.
GENIE: The Genie Awards were given out annually by the [Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television](https://www.academy.ca/) to recognize the best of Canadian cinema from 1980–2012. The Genie Awards succeeded the Canadian Film Awards (1949-1978), and were merged with the Gemini Awards in 2013 to form the Canadian Screen Awards. The 11th annual Canadian Screen Awards were held at Meridian Hall in Toronto from April 11-14 to honour achievements in Canadian film, television and digital media production. Highlights of the awards ceremony air on CBC and CBC Gem tonight on the final day of Canadian Screen Week 2023!
GENRE: The [Juno Awards](https://junoawards.ca/) celebrate the diversity of Canadian music across multiple genres, from pop and rock to country, hip-hop, jazz, and beyond! Since their inception in 1970, the Junos have evolved to reflect Canada's rich musical landscape, adding new genre categories over the years to spotlight emerging talent. Whether it's indie, electronic, or traditional Indigenous music, the Junos showcase the best of Canada's sound! Tonight, the Junos return to Vancouver, British Columbia, marking the city's fifth time hosting Canada's biggest night in music!
GHOST: BOO! Ghost stories are always much creepier when they hit close to home! From gothic hotels to gruesome battlefields, Canada is home to numerous spooky sites from coast to coast! Some of the most haunted places in Canada include: the Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel, the Hockey Hall of Fame and Keg Mansion in Toronto, the Fairmont Château Laurier and Jail Hostel in Ottawa, the Tranquille Sanatorium in Kamloops, the Fairmont Empress Hotel in Victoria, and the Plains of Abraham in Quebec City. Are you brave enough to visit them?
GIANT: The Sibley Peninsula just outside of Thunder Bay, Ontario is home to The Sleeping Giant, a series of cliffs which resemble a giant lying on its back. The formation is part of Sleeping Giant Provincial Park and it was voted number one on a list of The Seven Wonders of Canada, and 2007 competition sponsored by CBC. Another famous Canadian giant was "The Friendly Giant", a children's television program that aired on CBC from 1958-1985 with over 3,000 episodes!
GIZMO: Canada has a proud history of tech innovation, with groundbreaking gizmos like the Canadarm, the BlackBerry smartphone, and the IMAX theatre system. Inventions like these have shaped industries around the world showing that Canadian tech has made a global impact. The Canadarm helped astronauts build the International Space Station, BlackBerry revolutionized mobile communication, and IMAX brought breathtaking visuals to theatres globally. Canada's knack for creating world-changing gizmos shows that tech innovation is truly in our DNA!
GLAZE: Pottery has been produced by Europeans in Canada since the mid-17th century (and by the Indigenous peoples long before). Glaze is used to give the pottery a glassy coating, for decoration, and to preserve the pottery over time. Today is National Donut Day! To celebrate, [Tim Hortons](https://www.timhortons.ca/) brought back two classic glazed donuts - the Walnut Crunch and the Cherry Stick! We hope you celebrate today with your favourite donut! Our favourite is the Canadian Maple! 🍩🍁
GLIDE: Air Canada Flight 143, commonly known as the [Gimli Glider](https://gimliglider.org/), was a Canadian scheduled domestic passenger flight between Montreal and Edmonton that ran out of fuel on Saturday, July 23, 1983. The flight crew successfully glided the Boeing 767 to an emergency landing at a former Royal Canadian Air Force base in Gimli, Manitoba, which had been converted to a racetrack, Gimli Motorsports Park. It resulted in no serious injuries to passengers or persons on the ground, and only minor damage to the aircraft. This unusual aviation incident earned the aircraft the nickname "Gimli Glider."
GLOBE: The Globe and Mail newspaper originated from two competing newspapers, “The Globe” and “The Mail and Empire”.
GNOME: If you happen to be walking through the [Parc écologique Godefroy](https://tourismebecancour.com/profiter/sports-et-plein-air/parc-de-gnomes-du-parc-ecologique-godefroy) in Bécancour, Quebec, you might stumble upon a little village complete with tiny houses with working doors and windows, and no shortage of gnomes going about their business. The display, and the handiwork, is straight out of the imagination of Michel Marchand. He built all the little gnome houses himself and crafted the tiny characters who inhabit "Gnome Park" inside the Quebec eco-park. Come walk the paths and discover the magical world of gnomes!
GOALS: Canadian soccer great Christine Sinclair is the world's all-time leading International goalscorer with 190 goals - the most any player, men's or women's, has ever tallied at the international level. The all-time leading goal scorer and most-capped player of the Canadian national team, Sinclair is also its captain. She announced her retirement from international soccer on Oct 20, 2023. #ThankYouSinc
GORGE: Canada is home to some incredible gorges & canyons. One of the best-known canyons in Ontario is the Niagara Gorge, which starts at the base of Niagara Falls, and it ends 11 km downriver, near the town of Queenston, where the famous falls originated some 14,000 years ago. Other notable gorges/canyons in Canada include: Elora Gorge (Ontario's Grand Canyon!), Eau Claire Gorge (Ontario), Grand Falls Gorge (New Brunswick), Coaticook Gorge (Quebec), Ouimet Canyon (Thunder Bay, Ontario), Maligne Canyon (Alberta), Nahanni Canyons (Northwest Territories), Canyon Sainte-Anne (Quebec City, Quebec), and Horseshoe Canyon (Alberta).
GRACE: Merry Christmas from Canuckle! Grace is often part of Canadian holiday traditions, as many families pause on Christmas Day to say a blessing before a meal. Whether it’s a few words of thanks around the table or a quiet reflection on the year, taking a moment for grace reminds Canadians of the importance of gratitude, togetherness, and the little joys that make the season bright.
GRADE: September in Canada means back to school! Students head into a new grade, ready for fresh notebooks, sharpened pencils, and new adventures in learning. Grades mark more than just progress – they’re milestones filled with growth, challenges, and proud moments. In Quebec, high school finishes at Grade 11, after which students move on to CEGEP to continue their studies. No matter where they are in the country, every grade is a step forward in the journey of learning.
GRADS: The Edmonton Grads were a powerhouse women's basketball team. The Edmonton Commercial Graduates Basketball Club, better known as “The Grads,” started as a high school girls basketball team and became a sports dynasty. World Champions for 17 years, the Grads dominated regionally, nationally, and internationally for 25 years beginning in 1915. Their record of 502 wins and only 20 losses is unmatched in all of sport. Dr. James Naismith called them "the finest team to ever step out onto a floor." Check out the [Heritage Minutes video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qxJcXsFxyLI) celebrating the Edmonton Grads.
GRAFT: In the Okanagan Valley, renowned for its orchards and vineyards, grafting is a vital horticultural technique. Scion grafting involves joining a young shoot (the scion) from a prized fruit tree onto the rootstock of another, combining strengths to grow healthier, more productive plants. This method helps Okanagan growers cultivate delicious apples, cherries, and grapes suited to the region’s unique climate, supporting one of Canada’s most important fruit-growing areas.
GRAIL: For hockey fans across Canada, the Stanley Cup is often referred to as the 'Holy Grail' of hockey. The Stanley Cup, awarded annually to the champion of the National Hockey League (NHL), holds a special place in Canadian sports culture as the ultimate prize in professional hockey. With its rich history dating back to 1893, the Stanley Cup has become one of the most iconic trophies in sports, symbolizing excellence, perseverance, and the pursuit of victory. The Edmonton Oilers are the only Canadian team left with a chance to hoist hockey's holy grail this year, and they are truly Canada's team with 16 Canadian-born players in their 20-man lineup.
GRAIN: The grain sector is a key driver of Canada's economic growth, exporting 26.4 million tonnes of wheat in 2020-21 and over $25 billion in exports sales.
GRAMS: When Canada switched to the metric system in the 1970s, grams replaced ounces as the standard way to measure small weights. Today, you’ll spot grams on everything from nutrition labels to coffee bags – a daily reminder of Canada’s move toward metric and its blend of precision and practicality!
GRAND: Montreal is home to the [Formula 1 Canadian Grand Prix](https://www.gpcanada.ca/), the biggest sporting event in all of Canada! 338,000 fans were in attendance at Circuit Gilles Villeneuve over the 2022 Canadian Grand Prix weekend.
GRANT: The Government of Canada offers funding through grants and contribution (Gs&Cs) programs that help support a variety of jobs, research, training and financial assistance across the country. A grant can provide funding to individuals, nonprofits, community organizations and small businesses to support upcoming projects, programs and initiatives. For many Canadians, the ability to access, stay safe and succeed on the internet is still out of reach. To help close this gap, CIRA is launching its 2024 grants program to support not-for-profits, Indigenous communities, researchers and registered charities across the country that are working to bridge that digital divide. [Learn more about CIRA's Net Good Grants program](https://www.cira.ca/en/grants?utm_source=canuckle)!
GRASS: In Indigenous culture, braided sweet grass is believed to attract good spirits, energies, and influences. Sweet grass, with its sweet aroma reminding people of the love, kindness, and gentleness provided by Mother Earth, is known to have a calming effect and is often used during talking circles and healings. Sweet grass is often used during smudging to call in the good Spirit.
GRAZE: Canada is home to over 800,000 sheep, grazing across pastures in provinces like Ontario, Alberta, and Quebec - together accounting for over 70% of the national flock. These flocks support sustainable farming, help maintain healthy grasslands, and are an important part of Canada’s agricultural heritage. Today, there are about 8,400 sheep farms across the country.
GREAT: Although it is unknown who coined the term “Great White North” in reference to Canada, the nickname has been in use for many decades. “Great” because it’s the second largest country in the world. “White” because of the amount of Arctic frozen tundra and snow within the country. Finally, “North” because not only does Canada take up most of the northern half of North America, it also stretches nearly to the North Pole! Canada is also home to the Great Lakes, the largest group of freshwater lakes on Earth, as well as Great Bear Lake and Great Slave Lake in the Northwest Territories.
GRILL: Happy Father's Day from Canuckle! Every year, on the third Sunday in June, families across the country fire up their grills to honour dads with a feast of barbecued delights. From juicy steaks and burgers to fresh fish and vegetables, the grill becomes the centerpiece of many Canadian Father's Day celebrations. It's a time for family gatherings, backyard fun, and enjoying the great outdoors. Whether it's a classic barbecue or a gourmet grilling experience, Father's Day in Canada is a perfect occasion to fire up the grill and enjoy some quality time with loved ones.
GRIPS: In the sport of wrestling, grips are crucial for securing holds and executing techniques. [Canadian wrestlers](https://wrestling.ca/) have excelled in both freestyle and Greco-Roman wrestling, showcasing their mastery of various grips and maneuvers. One notable Canadian wrestler is [Erica Wiebe](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/erica-wiebe/), who won gold in women's freestyle wrestling at the 2016 Rio Olympics. Her incredible performance highlighted the importance of strong grips and technique in achieving success on the mat. Wiebe's victory was a proud moment for Canada, emphasizing the country's strength in wrestling on the world stage and following the Olympic successes of [Tonya Verbeek](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/tonya-verbeek/), [Carol Huynh](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/carol-huynh/), and [Daniel Igali](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/daniel-igali/).
GRIZZLY: [Grizzly bears](https://naturecanada.ca/discover-nature/endangered-species/grizzly-bear/) are one of Canada’s most iconic wildlife species, found mainly in the western provinces and territories. These powerful mammals can be recognized by the distinctive hump on their shoulders and their long claws, which help them dig for roots, insects, and food. Canada’s grizzlies are an important part of the ecosystem, and conservation efforts continue to protect their habitat for future generations.
GROVE: Wander through Vancouver Island's [Cathedral Grove in MacMillan Provincial Park](https://bcparks.ca/macmillan-park/) and you'll experience the unforgettable sight of some the oldest and tallest trees in Canada. The park's name will make perfect sense when you see sunlight filtering through the soaring 80-metre-high canopy. Plan to spend a few hours wandering Cathedral Grove's trail system and gazing up at 800-year-old giant Douglas Fir, Grand Firs, Western Hemlocks, and Western Red Cedar trees.
GUARD: The Ceremonial Guard is an ad hoc military unit in the Canadian Armed Forces that performs the Changing the Guard ceremony on Parliament Hill and posts sentries at Rideau Hall. We stand on guard for thee!
GUEST: Twenty-five years ago, nearly 6,600 passengers became unexpected guests in Newfoundland after 38 planes were diverted following the 9/11 attacks. Local residents in Gander and surrounding communities welcomed the “come from aways” into their homes and communities, providing food, shelter, friendship and remarkable Newfoundland hospitality. Their story inspired the hit musical [Come From Away](https://comefromaway.com/).
GUILD: A guild is an association of artisans and merchants who oversee the practice of their craft/trade in a particular territory. Some notable guilds in Canada include the Canadian Merchant Service Guild, Canadian Media Guild, Writers Guild, Directors Guild, Playwrights Guild, Screen Composers Guild, and various Quilters, Spinners & Weavers Guilds!
GULCH: A gulch is a deep V-shaped valley formed by erosion. It may contain a small stream or dry creek bed and is usually larger in size than a gully. In eastern Canada, a gulch can also refer to a narrow deep cove (Newfoundland) or a narrow saltwater channel (Nova Scotia). Gulches can be found all across the country!
GUSTO: [Gusto TV](https://gustotv.com/) is a Canadian food and lifestyle channel that serves up delicious programming with a dash of flair! From sizzling cooking competitions to heartwarming travel-meets-food adventures, Gusto is all about flavour, culture, and creativity. Whether you're watching chefs whip up gourmet dishes or exploring global cuisines from a Canadian lens, every show is packed with - you guessed it - gusto!
HAIRY: It’s the end of Movember, and things got a little hairy across Canada this past month! From handlebar to horseshoe, moustaches of every style helped raise awareness and funds for men’s health, supporting research and programs for prostate cancer, testicular cancer, mental health, and suicide prevention. Canuckle co-creators [Mark and Jeff proudly joined the cause](https://ca.movember.com/mospace/15437932) – growing their own Mo’s to spark conversation and support this important movement. Thanks to all the hairy heroes across the country who helped make a difference this Movember!
HAUNT: [Halloween Haunt](https://www.canadaswonderland.com/events/haunt) is on right now at Canada’s Wonderland in Toronto! Halloween Haunt turns the theme park into a scream park filled with Halloween attractions that offer unforgettable thrills and unspeakable horror. From rides, to scare zones, to monsters, it's Canada's biggest haunted wonderland! So, whether you’re seeking heart-pounding coaster thrills or spine-tingling scares, Canada’s Wonderland Halloween Haunt has it all.
HAWKS: The [Golden Hawks](https://cahf.ca/royal-canadian-air-force-golden-hawks/) were a Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) aerobatic flying team established in 1959 to celebrate the 35th anniversary of the RCAF and the "Golden" 50th anniversary of Canadian flight, which began with the AEA Silver Dart in 1909.
HAZEL: Canada is home to several species of hazel trees and shrubs. The beaked hazelnut, native to British Columbia, produces edible nuts that have been enjoyed by Indigenous peoples for centuries. Witch hazel is valued for its natural astringent properties and fragrant yellow flowers that bloom late in autumn. Its branches can simultaneously bear fruit, flowers, and buds, making it a remarkable part of Canada’s forest flora.
HEATS: In Olympic racing events, heats are the preliminary rounds that decide who advances to the finals. From short-track speed skating to snowboarding and skiing, Canadian athletes push hard in every heat, giving fans a front-row view of the skill, speed, and determination that define Team Canada at the Games.
HELIX: [Helix](https://www.planethelix.com/) is a Canadian hard rock and heavy metal band from Kitchener, Ontario. They formed in 1974, and are best known for their 1984 single "Rock You". Helix have toured with bands such as Kiss, Aerosmith, Rush, Mötley Crüe, Alice Cooper, Whitesnake, Heart, and Motörhead among others.
HERON: Great blue herons are Canada's most widespread heron and are found from the Maritimes to British Columbia. As the largest heron in North America, the great blue heron stands about one metre tall.
HERTZ: Measured in hertz, radio waves power the sounds and signals that surround us – and Canadian inventor Reginald Fessenden helped make it all possible. Born in Quebec, Fessenden was a true pioneer of wireless communication. In 1906, he made history by broadcasting the first voice and music over radio waves, sending “O Holy Night” across the air. His groundbreaking work paved the way for radio, television, and the technology that connects us today. He also laid the groundwork for AM radio, sonar, and even early radar – innovations that still echo through modern communication.
HIDES: On May 15, we mark [Moose Hide Campaign Day](https://moosehidecampaign.ca/), a national day of action for the Indigenous-led grassroots movement to engage men and boys in ending violence towards women and children. The Moose Hide Campaign began with a small patch of moose hide, worn as a symbol of commitment to safety and healing. Today, millions across Canada wear these hides to stand up against gender-based violence. To support them in igniting powerful change, please consider [donating to the Moose Hide Campaign](https://moosehidecampaign.ca/donate/) today.
HIGHWAY: The Trans-Canada Highway is one of the longest national highways in the world, stretching more than 7,800 kilometres from Victoria, British Columbia, to St. John’s, Newfoundland and Labrador. Officially opened in 1962, it connects communities across all 10 provinces and has become an iconic route for exploring Canada’s diverse landscapes, historic towns, and natural wonders from coast to coast.
HIKES: National Parks Day is the perfect time to lace up your boots and explore some of Canada’s incredible hikes. Trek the rugged peaks of Banff and Jasper in Alberta, discover the fjords and unique geology of Gros Morne in Newfoundland, wander ancient forests in Fundy National Park, or take in coastal views at Pacific Rim National Park Reserve in British Columbia. Each park offers unforgettable adventures and stunning landscapes – grab your boots and hit the trail!
HILLS: On Vimy Ridge Day, we remember the bravery of Canadian soldiers who fought in one of the most pivotal battles of World War I. The rugged hills of Vimy Ridge posed a massive challenge, as soldiers had to climb and fight through difficult terrain to capture the position from enemy forces. The victory at Vimy in 1917 marked a defining moment in Canadian history, solidifying Canada's reputation on the world stage. Today, the [Vimy Memorial](https://www.veterans.gc.ca/en/remembrance/memorials/vimy) stands proudly on those very hills, honouring the sacrifices of those who fought there.
HIPPO: The [house hippo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TijcoS8qHIE) is the subject of a Canadian television public service announcement (PSA) produced by Concerned Children's Advertisers in 1999. The fake infomercial about the fictional critters was created in order to raise awareness about the importance of media literacy. It was produced in the style of [Hinterland Who's Who](https://www.hww.ca/), the Canadian educational series that ran in the 1960s and 1970s. Two decades later, Ottawa-based not-for-profit [MediaSmarts](https://mediasmarts.ca/) brought back the house hippo in a [new commerical](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5R_tOSRynZU) as part of a media literacy campaign called [Break the Fake](https://mediasmarts.ca/break-fake). Real or not, the house hippo will always be a nostalgic piece of Canadiana.
HIVES: Beekeeping is buzzing across Canada, with more than 800,000 honeybee hives managed nationwide. These hives not only produce millions of kilograms of honey each year, but also play a vital role in pollinating crops from blueberries in Nova Scotia to canola in the Prairies. In Ottawa, [Gees Bees Honey Company](https://www.geesbees.ca/) has created a buzz by bringing beekeeping into the city, setting up hives in urban spaces and teaching people about the importance of pollinators. Whether in city backyards or rural farms, Canada’s hives help keep our food system sweet and thriving.
HOLLY: Holly, a symbol of holiday cheer, adds a beautiful touch to Canadian winter decor with its glossy green leaves and bright red berries. Though not native to Canada, English and American holly thrive in British Columbia, especially around Vancouver Island and the Lower Mainland, where the mild climate supports their growth. In Newfoundland and Labrador, there's even a native type called Mountain holly, adding a uniquely Canadian twist to this festive plant. From wreaths to garlands, holly's vibrant colours bring warmth to Canadian homes and holiday traditions coast to coast.
HOMER: Today marks the start of the Major League Baseball Postseason! [Sam Bat](https://canada.sambat.com/), officially The Original Maple Bat Corporation, is a Canadian company based in the town of Carleton Place, Ontario that manufactures baseball bats. It was the first company to supply baseball bats manufactured from maple wood to professional baseball players. Loved by baseball players at all levels worldwide, the legendary Sam Bat was used by Barry Bonds to to break the world record for both most homers in a season and a career. The records continued with Miguel Cabrera using a Sam Bat to win the Triple Crown in 2012, and Giancarlo Stanton using a Sam Bat to win the 2016 Home Run Derby.
HOMES: The word HOMES is a handy mnemonic many Canadians use to remember the names of the Great Lakes: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, and Superior. Together, these five vast freshwater lakes hold about 21% of the world’s surface fresh water and border both Canada and the United States. From boating and fishing to providing drinking water, the Great Lakes are an essential part of life and nature in Canada.
HONEY: Canadian honey is recognized around the world for its high quality. Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta produce 80% of Canada's honey crop. Canada is the world's sixth largest producer of honey. The average honey yield per hive in Canada is twice the world's average due to our long and warm summer days and a vast supply of nectar producing crops!
HORNS: The [Great Horned Owl](https://www.hww.ca/en/wildlife/birds/great-horned-owl.html) is one of Canada’s commonest large birds of prey. This nocturnal predator ranges through all urban and rural wooded areas of Canada. The majestic owl is named after its iconic “horns” that are actually bunches of feathers and is the provincial bird of Alberta. Voted upon in 1977 by children in the province, the Great Horned Owl represents Alberta’s impressive biodiversity!
HORSE: On April 30, 2002, a bill was passed into law by the Canadian Government making the Canadian horse an official symbol of Canada. The Canadian horse is known for its great strength and endurance, resilience, intelligence and good temper.
HOSER: Hoser is a slang word for a Canadian of limited intelligence.
HOSTS: Canada has been the birthplace of many beloved television hosts who have entertained audiences both nationally and internationally. One notable example is [Alex Trebek](https://standuptocancer.org/the-alex-trebek-fund/), best known for hosting the iconic game show 'Jeopardy!' for over three decades. Other famous Canadian hosts include Howie Mandel, Monty Hall, Rick Mercer, George Stromboulopoulos, Ron MacLean, Gerry Dee, Jillian Harris, Jesse Palmer, Jessi Cruickshank, Jon Montgomery, Marilyn Denis, Ben Mulroney, Dini Petty, Bryan Baeumler, and Drew and Jonathan Scott. So, whether it's game shows, talk shows, or variety shows, Canada has been home to some of the most memorable hosts in television history!
HOTEL: There are many iconic hotels in Canada known for their history, their cultural significance, and their incredible architecture, including the Banff Springs Hotel, Château Frontenac, Château Laurier, Château Lake Louise, and the Empress Hotel, but there is only one hotel in Canada that is made entirely of snow and ice. The "[Hôtel de Glace](https://www.valcartier.com/en/lodging/hotel-de-glace-ice-hotel/)" (Ice Hotel) in Saint-Gabriel-de-Valcartier, Quebec is the oldest ice hotel in North America. Located just a short drive from Quebec City, this architectural marvel is a wonder to behold. Guests can explore the grand hall, an ice slide, a chapel, and a bar, where all furniture is made of ice and drinks are served in ice glasses.
HOUSE: The House of Commons of Canada is a democratically elected body whose members are known as members of Parliament (MPs). It is the lower house of the Parliament of Canada (the Senate is the upper house) and provides a link between Canadians and their Parliament. Many laws in Canada first begin as bills in the House of Commons.
HOVER: One of the first regularly scheduled hovercraft ferries in the world operated out of Vancouver - but it didn't last long. In 1969, the Pacific Hovercraft route went from Vancouver to Nanaimo twice daily, zipping across the Strait of Georgia at up to 60 km/h (in calm weather) and making the crossing in under an hour. While there were plans to expand the service with more trips, the company petered out before the end of '69 and went into receivership in 1971. While it didn't last long, it made waves as the first scheduled hovercraft ferry service in North America at the time.
HUMID: Canada may be known for cold winters, but summer can get seriously humid. On June 20, 1953, [Windsor, Ontario](https://www.citywindsor.ca/) recorded a humidex of 52.1°C, with an actual temperature of 37°C. For more than 50 years, it stood as Canada’s highest recorded humidex until Carman, Manitoba, reached 52.6°C on July 25, 2007, surpassing the longstanding Windsor mark.
HUNTS: [National Hunting, Trapping, and Fishing Heritage Day](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/annualstatutes/2014_26/FullText.html) is celebrated on September 21, 2024, across Canada! This special day recognizes the long-standing traditions of hunting, trapping, and fishing, which have been integral to Canada’s cultural and economic history, especially for Indigenous communities and early settlers. Whether hunting for sport or sustenance, these activities remain a significant part of life in many parts of the country.
HURRY: In Canada, "hurry hard" is curling’s battle cry, as team members sweep harder and faster. Hurry Hard is such an iconic phrase that it was the title for Canadian curling legend [Russ Howard's memoir](https://www.amazon.ca/Hurry-Hard-Written-Publisher-Hardcover/dp/B005M4URAC), it was the name of a curling comedy show put on by the [Playgoers of Lethbridge](https://www.playgoerslethbridge.ca/), and it was enshrined as the name of an [amber lager beer](https://hurryhard.com/) by Toronto's Triple Bogey Brewing Company. Tune in to the [2024 World Women's Curling Championship](https://www.curling.ca/2024worldwomen/) this week in Sydney, Nova Scotia where you'll be sure to hear a few "Hurry Hard" calls from Rachel Homan who is wearing the maple leaf as Team Canada!
HYDRO: Waterpower is Canada's most abundant source of clean and renewable electricity, providing more than 60% of Canada's total electricity today. Canada is the fourth largest generator of hydroelectricity in the world.
HYPER: [Hyper Canada](https://www.virtualhyper.net/) is a digital arts and tech conference, hosting panels on interactive arts, game development, virtual reality, and artificial intelligence. It's a one-of-a-kind conference in Winnipeg, bringing immersive tech enthusiasts, digital creators, and visionaries together to explore the creative, commercial and technical possibilities of new emerging immersive digital worlds. This year, Hyper Lite takes place on November 19, 2024!
ICING: Happy National Donut Day! Canada is so sweet, it has two National Donut Days each year: the summer edition in June and another sweet treat on November 5th. Donuts, often topped with delicious layers of icing, are a beloved snack enjoyed coast to coast. Whether at a local bakery or shared with family and friends, these sugary delights help mark the day. So, on this second National Donut Day, don't forget to indulge in your favourite iced donut. Cheers to celebrating Canada's donut love, twice a year!
INGOT: Gold is often cast into an ingot, a solid bar that makes the precious metal easier to store, transport and process. Canada has a long history of gold mining and ranked as the world’s fourth-largest gold producer in 2024, with Canadian mines producing nearly 200 tonnes. Ontario and Quebec accounted for 68% of the country’s gold production, making gold Canada’s most valuable mined commodity.
INLAY: Inlay artwork is a decorative technique that embeds one material within another to create patterns or designs. Indigenous artists in Canada have long used inlay to add meaning and beauty to their work, incorporating materials like shell, bone, stone, or metal into wood and other surfaces. The technique appears in carvings, tools, ceremonial objects, and jewelry, with patterns that often reflect stories, symbols, and connections to the land.
INLET: The west coast of Canada is one of the major fjord coastlines of the world, hosting about 150 inlets. The remote and rugged coastline of British Columbia is indented with stunning inlets that cut deep into the Coast Mountains of the BC mainland north of Vancouver. Inlets can be found across the country from coast to coast to coast!
INTER: [Inter Toronto FC](https://www.cplsoccer.com/intertoronto) traces its roots back to the Canadian Premier League’s inaugural 2019 season, when the club (then York9 FC) played in the league’s very first match and scored the first goal in CPL history. As Toronto and Vancouver host FIFA World Cup 2026 matches, Inter Toronto FC remains part of the Canadian soccer story, helping grow the sport at home as the world's biggest tournament comes to Canada.
IVORY: International Inuit Day on November 7 celebrates the rich cultural heritage of Inuit communities across Canada's Arctic, including their incredible craftsmanship. Among their many innovations, Inuit carvers have long used natural materials like ivory to craft intricate art pieces and practical tools. Traditional Inuit snow goggles (Inuktitut: ilgaak or iggaak), often made from ivory or bone, were designed with narrow slits to protect against the bright Arctic sun reflecting off the snow - an innovative design to prevent snow blindness.
JACKS: Lumberjacks hold a legendary place in Canadian history, pivotal to the booming timber industry of the 19th and early 20th centuries. Among the most celebrated was Joseph "Jos" Montferrand, a French-Canadian logger and strongman from Quebec. Montferrand earned folk hero status for his remarkable strength and his fearless defence of fellow workers, and was the inspiration for the legendary Ottawa Valley figure Big Joe Mufferaw. Today, the enduring image of the plaid-clad lumberjack with an axe is a proud symbol of Canada’s rugged and resilient heritage.
JAILS: There are multiple communities in Ontario (including Tweed, Coboconk, Creemore, Providence Bay, Port Dalhousie, and Rodney) which lay claim to be the previous home of Canada's smallest jail. However, the absolute distinction belongs to the jail house in Rodney, Ontario, which measures just 4.5 m by 5.4 m. Built in 1890, Ye Olde Jail is the world's smallest jail! The building still bares its original steel cell doors, stove, and yellow brick exterior.
JELLY: The colourful rows of houses in downtown St. John's are often referred to as Jelly Bean Row. The vibrantly coloured Victorian row houses help give the city its distinctive character. According to folklore, the houses got their distinctive colours so returning fishermen could easily find their houses at night through the thick fog.
JEWEL: Looking for the biggest jewel in Canada? The town of Black Diamond, Alberta, is home to the world's largest black diamond! This striking monument was unveiled during the town's centennial Jubilee in 2007, paying homage to its namesake and rich coal mining history. Standing 1.22 metres wide and crafted from painted aluminum, the diamond is more than just a dazzling sight - it symbolizes the resilience and ingenuity of the community that once thrived on coal mining. On January 1, 2023, Black Diamond took on a new chapter in its history by amalgamating with its neighbour, Turner Valley, to form the town of Diamond Valley. Today, Diamond Valley is celebrated not only for its jewel, but also for its vibrant arts scene and stunning foothills views, making it a true gem of Alberta!
JIFFY: Jiffy, Canada's #1 home maintenance app, has been revolutionizing how Canadians tackle their home maintenance since its launch in Toronto in 2015. The app connects homeowners with vetted local service professionals across over 20 categories, such as plumbing, electrical work, and painting. Its name reflects its core promise: connecting users with reliable pros in a jiffy! Since its inception, Jiffy has completed over 450,000 jobs and expanded to cities like Ottawa and Calgary. This homegrown innovation has made managing home repairs easier from coast to coast!
JOLLY: Toronto mother Susan Olivia Poole was an Indigenous Canadian inventor who invented the Jolly Jumper after her first child was born in 1910. In 1948 they were produced for the retail market, and by 1957, the Jolly Jumper was patented.
JUDGE: The Supreme Court of Canada consists of nine judges, including the Chief Justice of Canada, who are appointed by the Governor in Council. The current Chief Justice is Richard Wagner, who succeeded the longest-serving Chief Justice in Canadian history and the first woman to hold the position - Beverley McLachlin.
JUMBO: [Jumbo Video](https://jumbovideomicroplay.com/) is a Canadian brand of franchised video stores that operated in Canada until 2018. The company was founded in May, 1987 and at one point claimed to be the third-largest player in the Canadian video rental industry. It was well known for offering free popcorn to customers, regardless of whether they rented videos. There is actually one remaining Jumbo Video Microplay store still open in London, Ontario. Check it out for the nostalgia and stay for the popcorn!
JUMPS: In Canada, [trampolining](https://olympic.ca/sports/trampoline/) isn't just a hobby – it's a celebrated sport that takes leaps and bounds to new heights! Canadian athletes have excelled in this dynamic sport, with trampoline gymnastics becoming an Olympic event in 2000. Canadian trampoline gymnast [Rosie MacLennan](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/rosie-maclennan/) won back-to-back gold medals in 2012 and 2016, making her the only trampolinist to defend her Olympic title successfully.
KARMA: Karma is the idea that what you put into the world comes back to you – a philosophy that inspired [Farming Karma](https://www.farmingkarma.ca/), a family-run Canadian beverage company based in Kelowna, British Columbia. Founded by Karma and Kuku Gill, longtime Okanagan orchardists, the brand grew out of decades of BC fruit farming and a desire to turn homegrown apples and cherries into better-for-you sodas. Today, Farming Karma products are made with real fruit from the family’s orchards and enjoyed across Canada, carrying a simple message at its core: good fruit, good people, and good karma.
KINGS: Today is [Commonwealth Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/important-commemorative-days/commonwealth-day.html)! The 56 member countries of the Commonwealth, including Canada, celebrate Commonwealth Day every year on the second Monday in March. It is a day of observance by more than 2 billion citizens of their common bonds and the contribution of the Commonwealth to the creation of a harmonious global environment. Canada has been a monarchy for centuries - first under the kings of France in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, then under the British Crown in the 18th and 19th centuries, and now as a kingdom in her own right.
KIOSK: If you’ve flown internationally into Canada, you’ve likely used a CBSA Primary Inspection Kiosk! Operated by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA), which oversees border management and security, these kiosks have streamlined the arrival process since their introduction in 2017. Travellers can scan their passports, snap a quick photo, and complete their customs declarations digitally. Found in major airports across Canada, they help reduce wait times and enhance efficiency while maintaining Canada’s high standards for border security.
KNEEL: The kneel jump is a traditional Inuit game that tests explosive strength and agility. Starting from a kneeling position, athletes launch themselves forward, aiming to land as far as possible on their feet – without using their hands for support. Practised across the Arctic, the kneel jump builds skills once vital for hunting on unpredictable ice and snow. Today, it remains a celebrated event at the Arctic Winter Games, showcasing athleticism and cultural pride.
KNIFE: The city of [Yellowknife](https://www.yellowknife.ca/) is the capital of the Northwest Territories and the territory's only city. The city gets its name from the copper tools historically made and traded by the local [Dene First Nation](https://ykdene.com/). The city and Yellowknife Bay were named after the Yellowknives, a Dene band who lived on the islands of Great Slave's East Arm and travelled as far north as the Arctic coast to obtain copper for knives and other implements. They, in turn, acquired their name from the copper-bladed knives they carried.
KNOLL: Knolls are found throughout Canada, and the term generally refers to small, rounded hills or mounds that often create scenic viewpoints or unique natural features in the landscape. Knolls are a common geographical feature, especially in hilly or mountainous regions, and are present in various places across the country. High Knoll in Minnekhada Regional Park near Coquitlam, British Columbia, is a popular hiking destination with impressive views. Additionally, knoll-like formations appear in areas across Alberta and Ontario, adding character to the natural landscape and offering vantage points in parks and along hiking trails. Knolls can also be found in more northern areas of Canada where glacial activity historically shaped the terrain, leaving behind knolls, drumlins, and other geological features.
KUDOS: On Canadian Armed Forces Day, Canadians offer kudos to the women and men of the Canadian Armed Forces, past and present, for their courage, selflessness, and service to Canada at home and abroad. Observed on the first Sunday in June, the day recognizes members of the Royal Canadian Navy, Canadian Army, and Royal Canadian Air Force, along with the families who support them in their commitment to stand on guard for Canada. It is a time to reflect, remember, and say thank you.
LABEL: More than ever, Canadians are looking to the label to guide their choices. Amid rising trade tensions and growing national pride, more shoppers are seeking out goods labelled “Made in Canada” and “Product of Canada.” A recent survey found that 84% of Canadians check labels to see where items are made, and 77% say they’ll choose Canadian – even if it costs more. That little label is a symbol of pride, connecting Canadians to the people and places behind every product.
LAKES: Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined! Almost 9% of Canada's total surface area is covered by freshwater.
LAMPS: Thomas Leopold "Carbide" Willson (March 14, 1860 – December 20, 1915) was a Canadian inventor. He was born on a farm near Princeton, Canada West, in 1860 and went to school in Hamilton, Ontario. By the age of 21, he had designed and patented the first electric arc lamps used in Hamilton. Willson's accidental discovery of calcium carbide in 1892 led to widespread use of carbide lamps in early cars and motorcycles and as headlamps for miners.
LANCE: One of the most prominent symbols of Canada is the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) "Mountie," wearing their red serge uniform and brown Stetson. Put many of these Mounties on black horses, have them perform intricate formations in front of a crowd, and you have another of Canada's most recognizable icons: the [RCMP Musical Ride](https://rcmp.ca/en/corporate-information/musical-ride). The riders carry lances, while the Officer in Charge carries a sword. "The Charge" is one of the final and the most powerful manoeuvres performed by the RCMP Musical Ride. The finely trained horses are lined up and held in position by their riders until the rider lowers the lance and bellows "Charge!" and the horses and riders thunder forward in battle cry of times past.
LANES: Did you know that 5-pin bowling was invented in 1909 by Canadian Thomas F. Ryan in Toronto? Bowling alleys have a rich history in Canada. Hamilton's [Skyway Bowl](https://www.skywaybowl.com/) is home to City 10-pin - the oldest bowling league on the planet that has been rolling for over 120 years! Since opening in 1930, [Commodore Lanes & Billiards](https://www.commodorelanes.ca/) in Vancouver is one of Canada's oldest surviving recreation centres. [Steelheads and Strikes](https://www.steelheadsandstrikes.com/) in Arnprior is the oldest, continually operating bowling alley in the country, with the original lanes dating back to the 1930 as well. If you can spare some time to play, go hit the lanes and give bowling a try...it may be right up your alley!
LAPEL: On November 11, Canadians commemorate Remembrance Day by wearing a red poppy on their lapels to honour military personnel who served and sacrificed in conflicts. The poppy is worn on the left side, close to the heart, symbolizing respect and remembrance. Inspired by the iconic World War I poem "In Flanders Fields" by Lieutenant Colonel John McCrae, this tradition of wearing poppies began in 1921, and the phrase "lest we forget" serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of remembering those who served Canada. This simple yet significant act of wearing a poppy reminds us all of the courage and sacrifice of past generations and honours their memory with deep reverence.
LATCH: Practised by many Indigenous nations along the Northwest Coast of Canada, the potlatch is a ceremonial gathering rooted in generosity, storytelling, music, and the sharing of wealth. Traditionally held to mark major life events like births, weddings, name-giving, and mourning, potlatches are also occasions to reaffirm community ties, pass down ancestral knowledge, and honour cultural laws. Though banned by the Canadian government from 1884 to 1951, potlatches endured and were carried forward with strength and spirit. Today, they continue as powerful expressions of identity, resilience, and cultural pride.
LATTE: September 29th was National Coffee Day! Did you know that lattes are one of the most popular coffee beverages in Canada? In fact, Canadians drink over 1.5 billion cups of coffee annually, with lattes being a go-to choice at many coffee shops. Approximately 7 in 10 Canadians drink coffee daily, making it the most popular beverage in Canada. Whether you prefer it hot or iced, the latte has firmly secured its place in Canada's coffee culture, keeping Canadians caffeinated coast to coast!
LAYER: Nanaimo Bars are a Canadian dessert staple originating in Nanaimo, a city on Vancouver Island in British Columbia. It consists of three layers: a graham wafer crumb and shredded coconut base, a custard-flavoured butter icing filling, and a chocolate ganache topping.
