The Nanaimo bar was popularized nationwide after being highlighted as a classic Canadian dessert at Expo 86. In 2006, the Nanaimo bar was declared Canada’s favourite confection by a reader’s poll in the National Post.
LEAFS: One of the NHL's founding teams, the Toronto Maple Leafs have won 13 Stanley Cups, the most recent being in 1967.
LEARN: October 5 is World Teachers’ Day, a time to celebrate the educators who inspire students to learn and grow. Across Canada, more than 500,000 teachers bring creativity, dedication, and heart into their classrooms each day. Their efforts are a big reason why Canada is recognized for its strong public education system, consistently ranking among the best in the world. Thank you to all the teachers who make a difference every day!
LEDGE: [Balancing Rock](https://www.novascotia.com/see-do/attractions/balancing-rock/2582) in Nova Scotia is a famous volcanic rock balanced precariously on a ledge above the waves of St. Mary's Bay. Called "Nature's Time Post", the Balancing Rock is a narrow vertical column of basalt, balanced on its tip that appears to defy gravity. It is estimated to weigh over 20 tonnes and stands 9 metres (20 feet) tall. It's the most photographed of Long Island's striking basalt formations.
LEGIT: Totally Legit Productions is a Canadian entertainment company known for creating live theatre experiences filled with music, comedy, and storytelling. Their popular production [Oh Canada Eh?! Dinner Musical](https://www.ohcanadaeh.com/) celebrates all things Canadiana with a lively mix of familiar songs, humour, and traditions, bringing audiences together for a fun-filled celebration of what makes Canada special.
LEMON: One of the greatest mysteries of the Canadian Rockies is the legend of the so-called “Lost Lemon Mine.” The Lost Lemon Mine is a legendary gold deposit reputedly somewhere between the Crowsnest Pass and the Highwood River in southwestern Alberta, discovered about 1870 by prospectors Frank Lemon and "Blackjack." Thousands have since searched for the fabulous lode; many have died mysteriously. Check out Craig Baird's [Canadian History Ehx podcast](https://canadaehx.com/2023/06/02/the-lost-lemon-mine/) to learn more!
LEVEL: The High Level Bridge in Lethbridge, Alberta is the longest, highest trestle bridge in the world. It is 1.6 km long and is 96 metres high and was completed in 1909. This Canadian Pacific Railway rail line has stood the test of time and is still used today with numerous trains crossing the bridge throughout the day.
LIGHT: With the world's longest coastline and more than half the earth's area covered in lakes, Canada is home to more than 750 lighthouses. Lighthouses across Canada have long symbolized strength, safety and safe harbour. The first lighthouse in Canada was built in Louisbourg on Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia, in 1734. Did you know that every lighthouse has a distinctive flash pattern?
LILAC: Lilacs are a spring flower and you can find these in gardens across Canada, but the small village of Franktown, Ontario, part of the township of Beckwith, is special as it is known as the Lilac Capital of Ontario. This Lanark County township near Ottawa is famous for its country road called Lilac Lane bordered by beautiful, fragrant lilac bushes, and is home to an annual Lilac Festival every May. If you love gardens, add the Franktown Lilac Festival to your travel list.
LIMIT: Did you know that in Canada, even your change has a limit? Under the [Currency Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/c-52/page-1.html), there are caps on how much you can use in coins for one purchase: up to $25 in loonies, $40 in toonies, $10 in dimes, $10 in quarters, and just $5 in nickels. These limits exist to stop “coin overload” at the counter – so while a store can accept more, they don’t have to once those limits are reached. So next time, leave the big bag of loonies and toonies at home!
LINGO: Before Canuckle brought daily word fun to Canadians, there was Lingo – the classic word game show that combined luck, logic, and quick thinking! Produced in Vancouver and originally airing in the late 1980s, Lingo featured contestants guessing five-letter words to fill a bingo-style grid, with each correct guess bringing them closer to a winning line. A Canadian version later aired in the late 1990s, hosted by Paul Houde, introducing a new generation to the fun of wordplay. Decades later, Canadians are still hooked on guessing words – proving that a love for lingo never goes out of style!
LIONS: The [Canadian Football League](https://www.cfl.ca/) season is underway! The [BC Lions](https://www.bclions.com/) are a professional Canadian football team based in Vancouver, British Columbia. The Lions played their first season in 1954, and have played every season since, making them the oldest professional sports franchise in British Columbia. They have appeared in the league's Grey Cup championship game 10 times, winning six, with their most recent championship occurring in 2011. The team is named for the Lions, a pair of mountain peaks overlooking the team's home city of Vancouver.
LITRE: Canada officially uses the metric system of measurement, and litre is the standard spelling of the metric unit for liquid volume. Canadians purchase gasoline in litres, and also buy milk by the litre (in bags in parts of Ontario, Quebec, and the Maritimes!).
LOGIC: Happy Star Trek Day! In the Star Trek universe, Vulcans are an extraterrestrial humanoid species known as logical beings who have removed emotions from their daily lives. The official Star Trek Capital of Canada is Vulcan, Alberta. The town even has a prominent display of a Starship Enterprise statue. Live long and prosper! 🖖
LOONS: Loons have beautiful, crimson red eyes, but this is only during mating season.
LOOSE: In Calgary, Alberta, you’ll find a legendary spot for improv comedy called the [Loose Moose Theatre](https://www.loosemoose.com/), a Canadian institution since 1977! Famous for its hilarious, off-the-cuff performances, Loose Moose has launched the careers of many comedians and actors, and it remains a beloved venue for improv lovers. If you ever feel like laughing 'til you’re loose from your seat, this is the place to be. Plus, it’s all proudly Canadian - combining creativity, humour, and a bit of wild fun, just like the theatre’s name suggests!
LOTTO: Canada's [Pollard Banknote](https://www.pollardbanknote.com/), headquartered in Winnipeg, plays a major role in the world of lotteries! This Canadian company has been a leader in producing instant lotto tickets for decades, supplying games to lottery corporations around the world. Pollard Banknote is responsible for printing roughly 85 per cent of the scratch-and-win lottery tickets sold in Canada. It's also the second-largest printer of those products in the world! From scratch-off tickets to digital lottery options, Pollard Banknote brings a bit of Canadian creativity and security to lotto experiences far and wide. From coast to coast, chances are, the next scratch ticket you buy has a bit of Canadian innovation behind it.
LOVED: Happy Canada Day from Canuckle! In a recent report by The Reputation Institute, Canada was named the most loved country in the world! The yearly report ranks the reputations of developed nations across the world on the basis of a variety of environmental, political, and economic factors, and Canada has consistently ranked at the top of the list when it comes to global perceptions of countries. Known for its stunning natural landscapes, diverse culture, and welcoming people, Canada has captured the hearts of people around the world.
LUCKY: Whenever Canada needs a bit of good fortune at the Olympic Games, you can count on a lucky loonie to come through. The tradition was started in 2002 at the Salt Lake City Olympics when Canadian icemaker Trent Evans snuck a loonie underneath centre ice when needing a marker for the faceoff dot. Evans left the loonie there as a good luck charm for the Canadians, and it worked beautifully, with Canada winning gold in both men's and women's hockey for the first time.
LUMEN: [Winterlude](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/winterlude.html) is underway in Ottawa and Gatineau, and this year's festivities feature [Lumen Eira](https://limbicmedia.ca/projects/lumen-eira-night-walk/) - a mesmorizing illumination experience animating Confederation Park. This dazzling display blends light and sound, transforming the park into a winter wonderland after dark. Trees glow and pulse with colours synchronized to custom soundscapes, inspired by nature and imagination. Let the interplay of light, sound, and winter's magic draw you into a world where reality is suspended, and imagination takes centre stage!
LUNAR: Happy Lunar New Year! The Lunar New Year is an event celebrated by millions of people across the world on the first new moon of their calendar. It marks the beginning of the new year based on the lunar calendar or lunisolar calendar. It is one of the largest celebrations for Canada's Chinese population, and it is also celebrated by Canadians from Vietnam, Korea and Southeast Asia, among others.
LUNCH: The [Cuban Lunch](https://cubanlunch.ca/) bar was a chocolate bar originally produced in Winnipeg by the Paulin Chambers Company factory for over 100 years. In 1991, the factory closed and production of the iconic Canadian treat ceased. A couple from Camrose, Alberta revived the popular peanut-and-chocolate candy in 2018. Crystal Regehr Westergard, along with her husband Bert, started the comeback venture as a way to cheer up her 85-year-old mother by bringing her favourite candy to her nursing home. The term "Cuban lunch" came into use before WWI, during the Spanish-American War. A Cuban Lunch was a soldier's rectangular chocolate ration, and the slang term held on in common use.
MAGMA: Did you know that Canada is home to several active and dormant volcanoes, where magma from deep within the Earth's crust occasionally makes its presence known? While Canada is not typically associated with volcanic activity, the country does have a number of volcanic regions, particularly in British Columbia and Yukon. Even though you may not see flowing lava or erupting volcanoes in Canada, the presence of magma beneath the surface is a fascinating reminder of the Earth's ever-changing landscape.
MAIZE: Did you know that maize, or corn, is one of Canada's most important crops? It thrives particularly in Ontario and Quebec, where it’s often used for animal feed, as well as human consumption in products like corn syrup and popcorn. As Halloween approaches, corn becomes a festive staple, with many Canadians decorating their homes with corn husks and using maize to create seasonal decorations like cornucopias or even haunted corn mazes. These maize mazes offer a fun way for families to celebrate the spooky season while appreciating the agricultural heritage of Canada.
MAJOR: In the Canadian military, the role of Pipe Major holds significant importance. A Pipe Major is responsible for leading and coordinating the regimental bagpipe band, which plays a crucial role in ceremonial events and military parades. The Pipe Major is a respected and revered figure in the Canadian military, embodying the spirit and heritage of the regiment through the stirring melodies of the bagpipes.
MAKER: David Thompson was a legendary map maker, earning him the title "the Stargazer" or "Koo-Koo-Sint" among some Indigenous peoples. An Anglo-Canadian fur trader, explorer, and surveyor, Thompson travelled an astonishing 90,000 kilometres across North America during his career, meticulously mapping 4.9 million square kilometres of the continent. His unparalleled work in cartography has led many to call him the "greatest practical land geographer that the world has produced." These maps not only shaped the understanding of North America's vast landscapes but also reflected his collaboration with Indigenous communities, whose knowledge greatly influenced his work.
MALLS: Canada is home to some of the world's most famous shopping malls, and the malls here offer more than just shopping! The [West Edmonton Mall](https://www.wem.ca/) in Alberta, once the largest mall on Earth, features an indoor amusement park, waterpark, and even an aquarium. Toronto's Eaton Centre and Montreal's Complexe Les Ailes are also iconic hubs for fashion, food, and culture. Whether you're hunting deals or just exploring, Canadian malls are destinations full of fun and surprises!
MANGA: Manga, the Japanese style of comics and graphic novels, has a growing fanbase across Canada. Readers enjoy a wide range of genres, from action-packed adventures to heartwarming slice-of-life stories. Canadian artists are creating their own manga-inspired works, and conventions like Anime North and Ottawa Comiccon celebrate this art form, showing how Canada embraces global storytelling and visual creativity. Michael Nicoll Yahgulanaas, a Haida artist, has blended Indigenous storytelling with manga aesthetics, creating works like Red: A Haida Manga.
MANIC: Quebec is home to [Manic‑5](https://www.hydroquebec.com/facility-tours/tours-general-public/daniel-johnson-manic-5-cote-nord.html), the world’s largest multiple‑arch‑and‑buttress dam, spanning the Manicouagan River. Since its completion in 1970, it has generated hydroelectric power for Quebec and beyond, making it a cornerstone of the province’s clean energy system. Now known as the Daniel‑Johnson Dam, the steady hum of this engineering marvel is a reminder of the massive, reliable infrastructure that keeps Canada running.
MANOR: [Escape Manor](https://www.escapemanor.com/) is known for its interactive and immersive escape rooms in Ottawa, but on September 10, 2017, they organized the world's largest scavenger hunt consisting of 2,732 people! Participants took part in the scavenger hunt in celebration of Canada's 150th anniversary and attempted to complete as many of the 150 tasks as they could throughout the city of Ottawa. Canada now holds the Guinness World Record for the largest scavenger hunt thanks to Escape Manor!
MAPLE: The maple leaf is one of the most recognizable symbols of Canada and is featured on the national flag.
MARCH: Happy First Day of March! In 2023, the long-held Changing of the Guard ceremony in Ottawa was replaced with a new tradition called Canada on the March. Joined by the Canadian Guard's band, the Ceremonial Guards march from Cartier Drill Hall to Parliament Hill. The ceremony is among Ottawa's most recognized military traditions, and is a summer attraction which has welcomed thousands of visitors to Parliament Hill for more than 55 years.
MASON: June 26th was coined National Canoe Day by [The Canadian Canoe Museum](https://canoemuseum.ca/) following a CBC campaign that, in 2007, declared the canoe one of the Seven Wonders of Canada. The canoe has long been an important symbol of Canada’s Indigenous peoples and their cultures. Used as the principal means of water transportation, Indigenous peoples have been making dugout and birchbark canoes for centuries. Bill Mason was a Canadian naturalist, author, artist, filmmaker, and conservationist, noted primarily for his popular canoeing books, films, and art as well as his documentaries on wolves. Mason once said: "I have always believed that the Canadian wooden canoe is one of the greatest achievements of mankind. There is nothing that is so aesthetically pleasing and yet so functional and versatile as the canoe. It is as much a part of our land as the rocks and trees and lakes and rivers." Bill Mason’s 16 foot red Prospector canoe is on display at The Canadian Canoe Museum in Peterborough, Ontario.
MAZES: The [Hanes Corn Maze](https://www.thetinyshopbakery.ca/hanes-corn-maze) in Dundas, Ontario is Canada’s largest corn maze! The maze is carved into 20 acres of corn stalks! In addition to all the corn mazes across the country, Canada also has the world record for the largest temporary corn/crop maze ever made! Built in October 2022, Luc Pelletier created a corn maze that was 266,106m² (65.8 acres) in size at their premises in La Pocatière, Quebec. "[Le Grand labyrinthe Kamouraska](https://www.kamouraska.com/grand-labyrinthe-kamouraska/)" was the size of over 160 hockey rinks!
MEDAL: Feb 18 marks the start of the [2023 Canada Winter Games](https://www.canadagames.ca/previous-games/pei-2023) in Prince Edward Island! Over 2,500 young athletes will be competing for hard-earned medals. Canadian athletes have won numerous medals on the world stage, and Canada has won at least one medal at every Olympics in which it has competed. Canada has won 551 Olympic medals in total (326 Summer, 225 Winter). Go Canada Go!
MEDIA: Today is Bell Let's Talk Day - a campaign started by Bell Canada/Bell Media in an effort to raise awareness and combat stigma surrounding mental illness in Canada. Bell Let's Talk has a vision of a Canada where everyone can get the mental health support they need. On January 25 and every day throughout the year, we can all take meaningful action to create positive change.
MELON: The Montreal melon, also known as the Montreal market muskmelon or the Montreal nutmeg melon, is a variety of melon recently rediscovered and cultivated in Montreal, Quebec. It was originally widely grown between the St. Lawrence River and Mount Royal, on the Montreal Plain. In its prime from the late 19th century until World War II, it was one of the most popular varieties of melon on the east coast of North America.
METRE: Canada officially uses the metric system of measurement, and metre is the standard spelling of the metric unit for length.
METRO: Metro systems help move millions of Canadians every day, with rapid transit networks operating in cities like Toronto, Montréal, Vancouver, and Edmonton. [Canada’s first true metro](https://www.stm.info/en/info/networks/metro) opened in Montréal in 1966, designed with rubber-tired trains to allow for quieter rides and steeper grades. Even during heavy snowfall, these systems are built to keep commuters moving and cities connected year-round.
MEZZO: In celebration of World Opera Day on October 25th, let's shine a spotlight on some of Canada's incredible mezzo-soprano talents! Mezzo-sopranos sing in the vocal range between soprano and contralto, often playing some of the most dynamic characters in opera. Wallis Giunta, an award-winning Canadian mezzo-soprano, has wowed audiences internationally with her performances. Another iconic Canadian mezzo is Catherine Robbin, whose illustrious career has been celebrated around the world. Canada's opera scene continues to thrive, with these talented voices leading the way on the global stage. Learn more about the Canadian Opera Company at [coc.ca](https://www.coc.ca/).
MILES: Before Canada adopted the metric system in the 1970s, distances were measured in miles - a reminder of which still lingers in some old road signs and stories! One stunning place that shares the name is Miles Canyon near Whitehorse, Yukon. Once a major hazard for Klondike Gold Rush stampeders navigating the Yukon River, this dramatic canyon features striking basalt cliffs formed by ancient lava flows and stunning emerald-green waters rushing beneath.
MINER: Happy National Mining Week! Canada has a rich history of mining, with numerous communities across the country built on the back of the mining industry. One such community is [Estevan, Saskatchewan](https://estevan.ca/), known for its coal mining heritage and the iconic character 'Lignite Louie.' Lignite Louie, a fictional character created by the local mining industry, symbolizes the hardworking spirit and resilience of the miners who toiled underground to extract lignite coal, a type of low-grade coal found in the region. Estevan's coal mines played a vital role in powering Saskatchewan's economy and providing employment opportunities for generations of miners and their families. The next time you hear about a miner in Canada, remember the hardworking men and women who helped build the nation's mining industry and shaped the communities we know today.
MITTS: Celebrated annually on November 21st, National Red Mitten Day encourages Canadians to display their patriotism in support of Canadian athletes! Red mittens represent the pride, generosity, and excellence of every Canadian.
MODEL: [Little Canada](https://little-canada.ca/) is an incredible attraction in Toronto that features highly detailed 1:87 scale models of Canadian cities and landmarks! The brainchild of Dutch-Canadian Jean-Louis Brenninkmeijer, this miniature wonderland inspired by his love of model trains showcases the beauty and diversity of Canada in a unique and captivating way. The skilled model makers at Little Canada have meticulously recreated iconic Canadian sites such as Niagara Falls, the Parliament Buildings in Ottawa, and the Toronto skyline, down to the smallest detail. Visitors can marvel at the intricate craftsmanship and feel a sense of national pride as they explore these miniaturized versions of beloved Canadian locations. Little Canada offers a magical journey through the country, celebrating its rich heritage and stunning landscapes in a truly extraordinary way.
MODEM: Canadian inventor and electrical engineer, Dr. Brent Townshend, created a core concept in 1996 that served as the basis for what is known as the 56K bit/sec modem, a groundbreaking technology at the time that allowed for data transfer between two computers at high speeds over standard analog dial-up phone line connections. 56K doesn't seem like much these days, but back in the mid-90s, it was a big step forward in Internet technology!
MOGUL: Canadian moguls skiers have won an impressive 9 Olympic medals over the years! Medallists include Jean-Luc Brassard, Jennifer Heil, Alexandre Bilodeau, sisters Justine & Chloé Dufour-Lapointe, and Mikaël Kingsbury. Bilodeau won a gold medal in the men's moguls at the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver, becoming the first Canadian to win a gold medal at an Olympic Games held in Canada.
MOIST: [Moist](https://moistonline.com/) is a Canadian rock band that formed in 1992. They released three studio albums in the 1990s, becoming a staple of Canadian rock music. The band, led by frontman David Usher, became a staple of the Canadian alternative rock scene in the 1990s. Moist has been nominated for ten Juno Awards, winning two, including Best New Group at the 1995 Juno Awards.
MONEY: People from around the world refer to Canadian Money as "rainbow money" or "Monopoly money" thanks to its bright colours and unique artwork.
MOREL: Morel mushrooms are among Canada’s most coveted wild edibles, appearing each spring in forests across the country. With their distinctive honeycomb caps, they look like tiny natural sponges and are prized by both chefs and foragers. One of Canada’s best-known foraging patterns is their response to fire: morels often fruit abundantly in the year following a forest burn, taking advantage of nutrient-rich soil. In western Canada, commercial harvesters and foragers closely track these conditions, and Alberta alone produces thousands of kilograms of harvested morels in strong years.
MOTOR: Happy Father's Day from Canuckle! The 2023 Formula 1 Canadian Grand Prix is on today in Montréal! The F1 Canadian Grand Prix (F1 Grand Prix du Canada) is an annual motor racing event that has been held in Montréal since 1978. Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve, the track on which the motor race is run, is located on Île Notre-Dame at Parc Jean-Drapeau, right in the heart of the majestic Saint Lawrence River. The event is synonymous with festivities and the start of Montréal's summer season. Start your engines!
MOUNT: Canada is home to some impressive mountain peaks, but Mount Logan tops them all at 5956m high. It is part of the St. Elias Mountains in the Kluane National Park and Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Canada's Yukon Territory is home to 8 of Canada's tallest mountains, including Mount Logan.
MOUSE: Toopy and Binoo is an animated series based on the popular French Canadian book series created by Dominique Jolin that features Toopy the mouse and his best friend Binoo the cat. A total of 175 episodes were produced overall. The show has been broadcast in over 179 countries and dubbed into 30 languages, and a film adaptation was released on August 11, 2023 in theatres across Canada.
MOVIE: If you take in a movie over the holidays, you can thank Montreal-born Léo-Ernest Ouimet for the magic of the movie theatre. In 1906, he opened his first movie house, the Ouimetoscope, on Saint Catherine Street. In 1907, Ouimet expanded the Ouimetoscope to house the first luxury projection room in North America, making it the world's first and largest cinema theatre to open exclusively for movies!
MOWER: In Enderby, British Columbia, you’ll find the world’s largest non-motorized lawnmower – an enormous 7-metre tall replica of a classic reel mower. Built by Herb Higginbottom between 2007 and 2009, it’s an exact scale-up of the smaller mower displayed beside it. Today, the giant mower stands proudly on a patch of astroturf next to Herb’s Deep Creek Tool Museum, celebrating both ingenuity and a bit of Canadian lawn-loving humour.
MUDDY: The [Big Muddy Badlands](https://greatsouthwest.ca/big-muddy/) in southwestern Saskatchewan are a breathtaking mix of rugged beauty and rich history. Nestled within the Big Muddy Valley, this unique landscape features striking cliffs, hoodoos, and winding trails shaped by millennia of erosion. At the heart of the region lies Big Muddy Lake, a shallow, picturesque body of water that complements the area's stark, otherworldly charm. This hidden gem offers visitors a chance to explore Saskatchewan’s dramatic geography and learn about the deep cultural significance of the land to Indigenous peoples. It's a truly muddy marvel waiting to be discovered!
MUMMY: As spooky season is upon us, let's talk about a famous "mummy" of sorts in Dawson City, Yukon! The legendary Sourtoe Cocktail involves a mummified human toe, which is dropped into a drink. Participants who are brave enough take a sip with the preserved toe touching their lips, all in the spirit of a tradition that dates back to the 1970s. While it’s not your typical Halloween mummy, it’s certainly a Canadian story that’s both eerie and fascinating!
MURAL: [The world's tallest mural](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/calgary/graffiti-calgary-daim-peter-oliver-beltline-bump-alberta-1.6509542) can be found in downtown Calgary, Alberta! It was completed in the summer of 2022 by internationally renowned graffiti artist Mirko Reisser (known as DAIM) and stands 95 metres high on the side of a building across the train tracks from the Calgary Tower. It took 130 litres of paint primer, 207 litres of base coat paint and 543 cans of spray paint.
NAMES: In 1995, Brent Peterson & Margot Newton, an expectant Toronto couple, combed through thousands of baby names trying to agree on just one. Their debate inspired them to invent [Namesake](https://www.namesakegame.com/), a homegrown Canadian board game where players pair up famous people who share the same first name. Thirty years later, Namesake has been reborn as a free daily web puzzle. Try it for yourself at [namesakegame.com](https://www.namesakegame.com/)!
NEVER: Never Cry Wolf by Canadian author Farley Mowat is a landmark work of Canadian nature writing that follows his time studying Arctic wolves in the North. First published in 1963, the book challenged widespread fears about wolves and helped shift public perception toward understanding and conservation. Blending observation, storytelling, and humour, it remains one of Canada’s most influential wilderness narratives.
NICKEL: Canada has a long history with nickel, so much so that our five-cent coin earned its name from the metal! The town of Sudbury, Ontario became one of the world’s leading sources of nickel after a massive deposit was discovered in the late 1800s—thanks to a meteor strike over 1.8 billion years ago! To celebrate this mining heritage, Sudbury is home to the [Big Nickel](https://www.sciencenorth.ca/dynamic-earth), a 9-metre-tall replica of a 1951 Canadian nickel. It’s one of Canada’s most iconic roadside attractions!
NIGHT: Hockey Night in Canada (HNIC) is a weekly Saturday night broadcast of NHL games. It has been a staple in Canadian homes since the first radio broadcast in 1931. HNIC began airing on Saturday nights on CBC Television in 1952. It is Canada’s longest-running television program and the Guinness World Record holder as the longest-running TV sports program. Instant replay even made its world debut on a 1955 Hockey Night in Canada broadcast.
NINJA: The [Canadian Ninja League](https://www.canadianninjaleague.org/) is a competition that features obstacle courses inspired by the popular television show American Ninja Warrior(™). Across Canada, Ninja gyms host regional competitions through-out the year where participants compete in various stages of challenging obstacles to demonstrate their speed, strength, and agility. The [Canadian Ninja League National Finals](https://www.canadianninjaleague.org/2023-national-finals) are in Edmonton Nov 24-26, 2023!
NINTH: Did you know that the border between Canada and the United States along the 49th parallel is the longest undefended international boundary in the world? Stretching over 8,891 kilometres, the 49th parallel serves as the dividing line between the two countries for much of their shared border. The bi-national International Boundary Commission deals with matters relating to marking and maintaining the boundary, and the International Joint Commission deals with issues concerning boundary waters.
NITRO: In the iconic [Heritage Minute about the Canadian Pacific Railway](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EE3ISzalVuo), titled 'Nitro,' a young Chinese railway worker bravely risks his life to set a dangerous nitroglycerine charge, helping carve a path through the rugged Canadian Rockies in the 1880s. His actions are a powerful symbol of the perilous work undertaken by thousands of Chinese labourers who played a vital role in building Canada's first transcontinental railway. Between 1880 and 1885, over 15,000 Chinese workers toiled under hazardous conditions, constructing some of the most challenging sections of the railway in British Columbia.
NOBLE: Today, Canada marks the Coronation of its new monarch, His Majesty King Charles III, beginning a new chapter in our country's history. In recognition of the RCMP's 150th anniversary and the Coronation, the King was officially presented with RCMP Musical Ride horse "Noble". The King has shared a personal connection to the RCMP as their Honorary Commissioner since 2012, and on Friday he was officially appointed Commissioner-in-Chief of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
NOISE: Happy National Acadian Day! Tintamarre is an Acadian tradition of marching through one's community making noise with improvised instruments and other noisemakers. The term originates from the Acadian French word meaning "clangour" or "din" meaning noise. The practice is intended to demonstrate the vitality and solidarity of Acadian society, and to express their pride in their Acadian heritage.
NOSED: The Eastern hog-nosed snake is a fascinating creature that gets its name from the distinct upturned scale on the tip of its snout. While Canada doesn't have cobras, this unique snake can mimic one by flattening its head into a dramatic, cobra-like hood to ward off threats. Found in Southern Ontario, south of the Canadian Shield, the Eastern hog-nosed snake is a master of disguise and one of Canada's most intriguing reptiles.
NOVEL: Canadian authors have given the world some outstanding must read novels, including "The Handmaid's Tale" by Margaret Atwood, "The Book of Negroes" by Lawrence Hill, "Indian Horse" by Richard Wagamese, "Anne of Green Gables" by Lucy Maud Montgomery, "Life of Pi" by Yann Martel, and "Five Little Indians" by Michelle Good, just to name a few. Canadian literature has certainly made its mark!
NUTTY: [Scott-Bathgate Limited](https://scottbathgate.com/) is a Canadian-based direct-selling manufacturer, distributor, and importer of confectionery, specialty grocery, and other foodstuffs. It is known for its Nutty Club brand of candy, syrup and nut products, as well as its Food Club line of condiments and food colouring. Headquartered in Winnipeg, Manitoba, the company services Canada from British Columbia to Ontario. Scott-Bathgate recently announced in a news release that its operations are winding down, with a late January 2024 end date.
NYMPH: In Canada’s cold freshwater ecosystems, including trout streams in the Rockies, many insects such as mayflies and dragonflies spend the early part of their lives as aquatic nymphs. These underwater stages can last from months to years as they develop in rivers and lakes. Mayfly nymphs are especially important in the food chain, serving as a key food source for native trout and other freshwater fish across Canada.
OASIS: Near Osoyoos in British Columbia, a patch of wetlands, ponds, and lush vegetation creates a true oasis in the sun-soaked Okanagan. This rare ecosystem supports a variety of plants and wildlife, including species found nowhere else in the country. Migrating birds stop here, pollinators thrive, and the vibrant greenery provides a striking contrast to the surrounding arid landscape. Visitors to this desert oasis can see nature flourishing in unexpected places – a reminder that even in dry regions, life finds a way.
OMEGA: Canada is one of the world’s leading [flaxseed](https://www.flaxcouncil.ca/about-flax/food) producers, with much of the crop grown across the Prairies. Flaxseed is one of the richest plant-based sources of omega-3 fatty acids, particularly alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), an essential fatty acid that plays an important role in maintaining good health. These tiny seeds pack a powerful nutritional punch!
OPERA: World Opera Day is celebrated each year October 25th. It raises awareness for the positive impact and value of opera for society. Throughout the 20th century, great operatic singers have populated Canada’s cultural landscape - from Raoul Jobin, Portia White, Maureen Forrester and Jon Vickers to Gerald Finley, Rihab Chaieb, Rebecca Cuddy and Measha Brueggergosman. Over the years, opera singers from Canada have made Canadians proud on stages around the world! Learn more about the Canadian Opera Company at [coc.ca](https://www.coc.ca/).
OPTIC: Fibre-optic cables carry data as pulses of light, letting information travel vast distances at incredible speeds. In Canada, optic-based networks expand internet access to rural, remote, and northern communities, connecting them to essential services. As more fibre reaches farther corners of the country, optical technology continues to play a quiet but powerful role in helping Canadians stay connected, no matter where they live.
ORBIT: The Manitoba government launched the Orbit program in 1965, which saw unique fibreglass sphere trashcans placed along the province's highways in an effort to reduce the amount of litter. The program lasted roughly till the 1990s across Manitoba highways.
ORDER: The Order of Canada is how our country honours people who make extraordinary contributions to the nation.
ORGAN: Canadian Joseph Casavant was a world-renowned organ maker. In 1840, he produced his first church organ in his shop at Saint-Hyacinthe. When he retired in 1866, Casavant organs were in demand throughout eastern Canada. Under the direction of his sons, Claver and Samuel, the firm Casavant Frères acquired an international reputation as builders of fine instruments. Casavant Frères continues to build internationally recognized pipe organs for churches, concert halls, religious communities and teaching institutions.
OUTER: The vastness of outer space is now a little more Canadian! As the [Artemis II](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/missions/artemis-ii/mission.asp) crew completes its historic lunar flyby mission, Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen is aboard the Orion spacecraft, travelling over 400,000 kilometres from Earth. Hansen is the first Canadian to journey this far into outer space, taking part in humanity’s first trip around the Moon in over half a century.
OWNED: Across Canada, many beloved businesses are family owned and operated, with traditions and know-how passed down through generations. From corner stores and hardware shops to local cafés and diners, these family-run enterprises are deeply rooted in the communities they serve. Built on trust, pride, and a personal touch, they continue to play a vital role in Canada’s economy and daily life.
OWNER: Happy [Canadian Innovation Week](https://canadianinnovationspace.ca/about/)! Business owners are the backbone of the Canadian economy, with small and medium-sized enterprises making up a whopping 99.8% of all businesses in the country. From local coffee shop owners to cutting-edge tech start-ups, these entrepreneurs drive growth and spark innovation across the nation. With their strong entrepreneurial spirit, Canadian business owners are fuelling progress, creating jobs, and helping communities thrive from coast to coast to coast.
OXIDE: [Canada's mining industry](https://natural-resources.canada.ca/our-natural-resources/minerals-mining/mining-data-statistics-and-analysis/minerals-and-the-economy/20529) plays a crucial role in the global supply of metal oxides, which are key components in producing everything from batteries to electronics. Iron oxide, for example, is an essential ingredient in the steel production process, and Canada is a leading producer of iron ore, particularly from the mines of Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador. These oxides are not just by-products but vital resources that drive innovation and manufacturing around the world. Canada’s vast mineral wealth ensures its place at the forefront of industrial development, contributing to technology and infrastructure on a global scale.
OZONE: September 16 is [World Ozone Day](https://www.un.org/en/observances/ozone-day)! Canada is known for its commitment to environmental conservation, including efforts to protect the ozone layer through initiatives such as the [Montreal Protocol](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/corporate/international-affairs/partnerships-organizations/ozone-layer-depletion-montreal-convention.html). The Montreal Protocol has succeeded in halting the damage to the ozone layer and is helping the world in the battle against climate change. In Canada and around the world, the Montreal Protocol regulates the production and consumption of numerous substances that deplete the ozone layer, the Earth’s atmospheric shield that prevents UV radiation from harming humans and other forms of life. It is considered one of the most successful, global environmental agreements of all time.
PAGES: In Canada’s House of Commons, pages are post-secondary students selected from across the country through the [Page Program](https://www.ourcommons.ca/about/pageprogram/index-e.html) to support the daily work of Parliament. Dressed in traditional uniforms, they assist Members of Parliament by delivering documents, carrying messages, and helping proceedings run smoothly during debates and Question Period. The role is highly competitive and offers a unique behind-the-scenes look at Canada’s democratic process.
PAINT: Norman Breakey from Toronto created the first paint roller in 1939. Unfortunately, he didn't patent the innovation and knock-offs quickly emerged. He may not get the credit he deserves, but Norman's invention has aided generations of painters. Next time you are painting a wall or ceiling, take a moment to remember Canadian Norman Breakey!
PAIRS: Canadian pair skaters Deanna Stellato-Dudek and Maxime Deschamps made history at the 2024 World Figure Skating Championships in Montreal by clinching the gold medal in the pairs event. Their exceptional performance captivated audiences and judges alike, earning them top marks and solidifying their status as world champions. Notably, Stellato-Dudek, at 40, became the oldest woman to win a figure skating world title in any discipline, breaking a record set over a century ago. Their victory marked the first world title for a Canadian pair since 2016, highlighting their remarkable skill, grace, and athleticism on the ice.
PANDA: The Panda Game is an annual Canadian football game between the two OUA football teams in Ottawa, Ontario: the University of Ottawa Gee-Gees and Carleton University Ravens. It is the most significant rivalry in Canadian university football and is a long-running tradition which has ignited school spirit since 1955. Its name is derived from Pedro the Panda, the trophy presented to the winner each year. The 2023 edition of the Panda Game marked the 54th game in the storied series, with uOttawa holding an all-time record of 37-17.
PAPAL: The word papal refers to the pope, the leader of the Catholic Church. Following the recent passing of Pope Francis, many Canadians are reflecting on his 2022 papal visit to Canada – a "pilgrimage of penance" during which he delivered a historic apology for the Catholic Church's role in residential schools. His words at Maskwacîs, Alberta marked a significant moment in the ongoing journey of truth and reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples.
PAPER: Charles Fenerty was a Canadian inventor who invented the wood pulp process for papermaking, which was first adapted into the production of newsprint and later the modern paper we use today. Fenerty was born in Sackville, Nova Scotia and was also a well-known poet of his time, publishing more than 35 (known) poems.
PARKS: There’s a whopping 48 National Parks and over one thousand Provincial and Territorial parks in the Great White North!
PARRY: In fencing, a parry is a defensive move used to block an opponent’s attack – an essential skill in a sport where speed and precision are everything. In Canada, fencing has been gaining momentum on the world stage, highlighted by [Eleanor Harvey](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/eleanor-harvey/)'s historic bronze medal in women’s foil at the Paris 2024 Olympics, marking the country’s first-ever Olympic podium in the sport.
PASTE: In 1884, Canadian chemist and pharmacist Marcellus Gilmore Edson received a patent for the manufacture of a peanut paste, which he named “peanut-candy.” Edson's patent for peanut-candy has been recognized as a forerunner to the commercially available peanut butter or spread.
PATCH: The [2023 Tim Hortons Brier](https://www.curling.ca/2023brier/) starts today in London, Ontario and runs from Mar 3-12. What makes the Brier different from other sporting events is the intimate nature of the competition and the lack of barriers between fans and curlers. Nothing represents this better than the ‘Brier Patch,’ which has been a staple of the event since 1982. At the Brier Patch, there’s live music, games, food and drink and a chance to mingle and have lots of fun. Whatever the form, the Patch has always been a place where good times are had and lifetime memories are made.
PATIO: Happy Victoria Day! Today is a federal Canadian public holiday celebrated annually on the last Monday preceding May 25 to honour Queen Victoria. The holiday has been observed in Canada since at least 1845, originally on Victoria's natural birthday, May 24. Today also marks the unofficial start to the summer season in Canada, and along with the warmer weather comes patio season! However you celebrate this long weekend, we hope you get to enjoy some beautiful weather on a patio and support local businesses!
PEARL: The northern pearl dace is a small freshwater fish found across Canada’s lakes, streams, and beaver ponds. A member of the minnow family, it thrives in cool, clear waters from the Atlantic to the Great Lakes. Often spotted in sandy or peaty waters, this hardy little fish adds a shimmer of silver to the Canadian wild!
PECAN: Pecans bring a rich, nutty flavour to Canadian holiday baking, starring in festive favourites like pecan pies, spiced cookies, and butter tarts. A staple on Christmas tables, these versatile nuts add warmth, crunch, and a touch of sweet tradition to seasonal celebrations across the country.
PEEPS: Canada’s tiniest sandpipers are affectionately called “peeps,” just like the fluffy chicks we associate with Easter. The Least Sandpiper flits through wetlands each spring in small, energetic flocks. These tiny birds have bright yellow legs and can weigh less than a golf ball, making them one of North America’s lightest shorebirds.
PEONY: Peonies are a beloved flower in Canadian gardens, known for their vibrant blooms and resilience to our northern climate. The [Canadian Peony Society](https://peony.ca/), established in 1998, is dedicated to the cultivation and appreciation of these beautiful flowers. Peonies are often seen as a symbol of prosperity and good fortune in many cultures, and their lush blossoms make them a popular choice for Canadian gardens. With over 30 species of peonies found worldwide, they thrive in Canada's diverse climates from coast to coast!
PETAL: It's tulip time in Ottawa! Every May, over a million tulip petals pop open across the capital for the [Canadian Tulip Festival](https://tulipfestival.ca/) - a blooming beautiful tradition that started with a royal thank-you. Back in 1945, the Dutch royal family sent 100,000 tulip bulbs to Canada to show their gratitude for sheltering Princess Juliana and her daughters during World War II. To ensure Princess Margriet was born a Dutch citizen, the maternity ward at the Ottawa Civic Hospital was temporarily declared international territory. That act of kindness planted the seeds of a friendship that still blossoms today - one tulip petal at a time!
PHONE: In 1876, Scottish-born inventor Alexander Graham Bell patented the first practical telephone, a concept that he conceived in Brantford, Ontario.
PHOTO: Yousuf Karsh was a Canadian photographer known for his portraits of notable individuals. He has been described as one of the greatest portrait photographers of the 20th century. Read more about Karsh at karsh.org.
PIANO: Canada has a storied piano making past, and was home to more than 100 piano manufacturing companies during the peak era of the industry. Piano building in Canada began in the early 19th century and grew into a major, thriving industry between 1890 and 1925. Many Canadians have become noted pianists. Glenn Gould is a bona fide Canadian icon who became one of the most famous and celebrated classical pianists of the 20th century, while Oscar Peterson has had an equally influential role in jazz piano and is considered one of the greatest jazz pianists of all time. Other notable Canadian pianists include Angela Hewitt, Chantal Kreviazuk, Diana Krall, Marc-André Hamelin, Anton Kuerti, Charles Richard-Hamelin, and Jan Lisiecki.
PIECE: Towering over the Guinness-certified World’s Largest Chess Set in Medicine Hat, Alberta between the library and the Court of King’s Bench is what could be the [World’s Largest Chess Piece](https://chatnewstoday.ca/2021/11/10/checkmate-royal-addition-to-downtown-medicine-hat-could-be-a-record-setter/). Installed in 2021, the king piece stands 20 feet, 11 inches (6.37m) tall and is 9 feet, 3 inches (2.81m) at the base. The current record-holding piece is in St. Louis, standing 20 feet (6.09m) tall and 9 feet, 2 inches (2.79m) at the base. The Medicine Hat Chess Club will be in contact with Guinness World Records to see if there’s a new king in town.
PIERS: Canada’s coastlines are dotted with iconic piers that connect communities to the water. In British Columbia, White Rock is home to [Canada’s longest pier](https://www.whiterockcity.ca/401/Pier-Promenade), stretching an impressive 470 metres into Semiahmoo Bay and offering stunning ocean views year-round. On the opposite coast, Halifax’s [Pier 21](https://pier21.ca/) stands as a National Historic Site and once welcomed nearly one million immigrants to Canada between 1928 and 1971. Together, these piers reflect the country’s deep maritime heritage from sea to sea.
PIKES: The Glacier Pikes are twin-peaked lava domes rising to about 2,145 metres in Garibaldi Provincial Park, British Columbia. Perched at the southern end of the Sentinel Glacier Neve, they offer stunning views and rugged scrambling for adventurers. First summited in 1911 by members of the British Columbia Mountaineering Club, the Pikes stand as a dramatic landmark in the Coast Mountains.
PINCH: Happy St. Patrick's Day from O'Canuckle! According to fun folklore, you get pinched on St. Patrick's Day for not wearing green because green makes you invisible to leprechauns. Leprechauns are mischievous creatures, and according to legend, they like to pinch people. Canada's first St. Patrick's Day parade was held in Montreal in 1824. Ever since, parades and festivals of Irish culture have been held annually on March 17th in cities across Canada.
PINES: Merry Christmas from Canuckle! The Scotch pine reigns as the top Christmas tree in Canada. Scotch pines hardly shed any of their long needles, and their strong, curved branches also hold ornaments well. Canada exported over 2.4 million fresh Christmas trees to countries all over the world in 2021! Pines are the also the arboreal emblem of the provinces of Alberta (Lodgepole pine) and Ontario (Eastern white pine).
PINOT: Pinot grapes have found a home in Canada’s wine regions, including British Columbia’s Okanagan Valley and Ontario’s Niagara Peninsula. Varieties like Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris have helped Canadian winemakers showcase the country’s unique climates and growing conditions.
PINTS: On October 9th, Canadians across the country raise their glasses to celebrate [Canadian Beer Day](https://canadianbeerday.ca/), a day dedicated to the craft, culture, and community that beer fosters from coast to coast. With over 85% of the beer consumed in Canada brewed locally, our pints tell a story of connection, pride, and homegrown flavour. Whether you're enjoying a cold one at a local brewery or sharing a laugh over a pint with friends, Canadian beer brings us together. Cheers to community and great Canadian beer!
PIPES: Canada has a long tradition of bagpipe music, especially in communities with strong Scottish roots. Pipe bands are a familiar sight at parades, ceremonies, and Highland games across the country. The [Glengarry Highland Games](https://www.glengarryhighlandgames.com/) in Maxville, Ontario, are one of the largest gatherings of their kind in North America, hosting competitions in piping, drumming, Highland dancing, and heavy athletics. From coast to coast, Canadian pipers help keep this centuries-old musical tradition alive and thriving.
PITCH: As the 2022 FIFA Men's World Cup wraps up in Qatar, we are reflecting on the time that the Canada Men's National Soccer team spent on the pitch proudly representing our country. After Canada's 36-year-long wait to return to the men's FIFA World Cup, they inspired fans from coast to coast to coast with their performance. The Canada Women's National Soccer team's success on the pitch includes 3 straight Olympic medals, including gold in 2020! They'll be competing in the [2023 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://www.fifa.com/fifaplus/en/tournaments/womens/womensworldcup/australia-new-zealand2023) in Australia and New Zealand so get ready to cheer them on! #WeCAN
PIVOT: Burdett, Alberta is home to the first pivot irrigation system in Canada. The first water drive pivot irrigation system was introduced to Canada by Donald and Wyman Campbell, who moved to the area from Nebraska during 1962. The system was in operation by May 1962 and was used continuously for 25 years.
PLACE: Located in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada Place is Canada's busiest harbour. Canada Place is the main cruise ship terminal for the region. To mark Expo 86, Canada Place was officially opened as the Canada Pavilion by HRH Prince Charles, Diana, Princess of Wales and former Prime Minister Brian Mulroney. The land that Canada Place is built upon was known as Pier B-C and served as the western terminus for Canadian Pacific Railway's transcontinental railroad.
PLAID: The official tartan for Canada as a whole is known as the Maple leaf tartan.
PLANE: Aviation is an integral part of the Canadian economy. In 2018, the air transport industry, including airlines, and its supply chain, supported over $50 billion of GDP in Canada.
PLANK: Plank houses were structures built by various Indigenous peoples on the Northwest Coast of Canada to shelter extended families. Plank houses still exist in some communities and are used mainly for community and ceremonial purposes.
PLANT: The [Bruce Nuclear Generating Station](https://www.brucepower.com/) is a nuclear power plant located on the eastern shore of Lake Huron in Ontario. With eight CANDU pressurized heavy-water reactors, it is the largest operating nuclear power plant in the world! The plant is the largest employer in Bruce County, with over 4000 workers.
PLATE: [The King's Plate](https://woodbine.com/events/kings-plate/) is Canada’s oldest and most prestigious Thoroughbred horse race. Formerly known as The Queen's Plate, North America's longest continuously run stakes race is once again known as The King's Plate. This year's race takes place on August 20, 2023 at [Woodbine Racetrack](https://woodbine.com/) in Etobicoke, Ontario.
PLAYS: Today marks the start of the Stratford Festival's 2024 season! The [Stratford Festival](https://www.stratfordfestival.ca/), located in Stratford, Ontario, is North America's largest classical repertory theatre company. Each season, numerous productions take to the stage, with special emphasis on the plays of Shakespeare. The 2024 Stratford Festival lineup includes 12 plays and runs from April to October.
PLUME: The members of the [Ceremonial Guard](https://www.canada.ca/en/army/corporate/4-canadian-division/ceremonial-guard.html) are instantly recognizable in their distinctive scarlet tunics and bearskin caps. Although they come from many units across Canada, members of the Guard continue to uphold the traditions of two of Canada’s finest regiments - the Governor General’s Foot Guards (GGFG) of Ottawa, and the Canadian Grenadier Guards (CGG) of Montreal. They are easily discernable by the coloured plume in the bearskin hat: red for Foot Guards and white for Grenadier Guards. All of the bearskin hats worn by the Ceremonial Guard are more than 20 years old and are well-maintained from the thorough care they have received over the decades.
POINT: Point Pelee is the southernmost point of mainland Canada, and is an important rest stop for migrating birds. [Point Pelee National Park](https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/on/pelee) is Canada's second smallest but most ecologically diverse national park, and is home to more than 390 bird species and 70 species of trees, some of which are species at risk.
POKER: Canada has produced some elite poker players over the last few decades, and Toronto-born [Daniel Negreanu](https://danielnegreanu.com/) is at the top of the list! Negreanu (aka "Kid Poker") has won 6 World Series of Poker (WSOP) bracelets and two World Poker Tour (WPT) championship titles. Other famous and successful Canadian poker players include Guy Laliberté (of Cirque du Soleil fame), Evelyn Ng, Jonathan Duhamel, Sam Greenwood, Timothy Adams, Daniel Dvoress, Mike McDonald, Sorel Mizzi, Michael Watson, and Peter Jetten.
POLAR: Canada is home to about 16,000 polar bears, which is approximately two-thirds of the world's total estimated population.
POLIO: Happy World Polio Day! Canadian researchers at Toronto’s Connaught Laboratories played a key role in developing the polio vaccine. In the late 1940s, Raymond Parker, Joseph Morgan, and Helen Morton created Medium 199, the world’s first synthetic nutrient formula for growing cells. In 1951, Arthur Franklin used Medium 199 to grow the poliovirus, giving Dr. Jonas Salk the tools to develop the first polio vaccine. Their work helped make safe testing possible and led to polio’s eradication in Canada by the 1970s. By 1994, the World Health Organization declared the Americas polio-free, a milestone made possible by decades of vaccination efforts and Canadian ingenuity.
POLKA: Polka Dot Door was a Canadian children's television series which was produced by the Ontario Education Communications Authority (later known as TVOntario) from 1971 to 1993. One of the most well-known elements of the series was the "Polkaroo", a mythical character whose name combines the words "polka dot" and "kangaroo". In 2010, the Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television gave Polka Dot Door a Masterworks award, calling it a "groundbreaking children's educational series" that "changed the nature of children's television programming" and "impacted countless young Canadians and raised the international profile of the Canadian television industry."
POPPY: From the last Friday in October to Remembrance Day, millions of Canadians wear a poppy as a visual pledge to never forget those who sacrificed for our freedom.
PORTS: Canada is home to numerous ports, but the Port of Vancouver is Canada's largest port, and is the most diversified port in North America.
POSSE: The Las Vegas Posse were a [Canadian Football League](https://www.cfl.ca/) (CFL) team, that played at the Sam Boyd Silver Bowl in Las Vegas, Nevada, United States, in the league's 1994 season as part of the CFL's American expansion. The team folded after only one season, proving that whatever happens in Vegas doesn't always stay in Vegas.
POSTS: Founded in 1670, the Hudson’s Bay Company built hundreds of [trading posts](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/hbc-trading-posts-in-canada) across what is now Canada, often along rivers and lakes that served as important transportation routes. These remote outposts became centres of trade and communication, exchanging European goods for furs with Indigenous peoples and helping shape the growth of communities across the country.
POUCH: [Pouch Cove](https://pouchcove.ca/), Newfoundland & Labrador, is a friendly town on the northern tip of the Avalon Peninsula, neighbouring Torbay, Flatrock, and Bauline. Known as the place “first to see the sun” in North America, it’s also a gateway to the East Coast Trail, with rugged hikes like the Biscan Cove and Stiles Cove paths offering breathtaking ocean views.
POUND: Lobster season has officially started in Canada in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. Canada currently supplies more than half of the world’s supply of “hard-shelled” Atlantic Lobster, considered one of the world’s premier seafood. A lobster pound is where live lobsters are held until they are harvested and sold, like at [Halls Harbour Lobster Pound](https://hallsharbourlobster.com/) in Nova Scotia and [Lobster on the Wharf](https://www.lobsteronthewharf.com/) in PEI, known as MacKinnon's Lobster Pound to locals.
POWER: Globally, Canada is a major energy producer. It is a top ten producer of oil, natural gas, hydroelectric power, uranium, nuclear power, biofuels and wind. Over 60% of Canada's electricity is generated by waterpower, and nuclear energy accounts for about 15% of the total Canadian electricity supply, generated at power plants in Ontario and New Brunswick.
PRIDE: Since 2016, the month of June has been declared Pride Month in Canada to celebrate the LGBTQ2+ community.
PRIME: The Prime Minister (PM) is the head of the federal government in Canada. It is the most powerful position in Canadian politics. While the Queen may be Canada's head of state, and the Governor General the Queen's representative, it's the Prime Minister who is known as the nation's head of government.
PRINT: Happy Labour Day! Labour Day has been marked as a statutory public holiday in Canada on the first Monday in September since 1894. However, the origins of Labour Day in Canada can be traced back to numerous local demonstrations and celebrations in earlier decades. Such events assumed political significance in 1872, when an April labour demonstration in Toronto, in support of the printers of the Toronto Typographical Union on strike for a nine-hour day, led directly to the enactment of the Trade Unions Act, a law that confirmed the legality of unions. The Printers' Strike of 1872, part of the Nine Hour Movement, was a key moment in Canadian labour history and marked the start of a shorter workday.
PRIOR: [Arnprior](https://www.arnprior.ca/) is a charming Ottawa Valley town known affectionately as “The Prior.” Founded in the 1820s and named after a village in Scotland, it grew into a major centre for Ontario’s lumber industry thanks to its location at the meeting of the Madawaska and Ottawa Rivers. Today, it’s known for its historic downtown, waterfront, and the towering white pines of [Gillies Grove](https://parks.canada.ca/culture/designation/lieu-site/gillies).
PRIZE: The [Giller Prize](https://scotiabankgillerprize.ca/) is the most prestigious literary prize in Canada, recognizing excellence in Canadian fiction. The prize was established in 1994 by Toronto businessman Jack Rabinovitch in honour of his late wife Doris Giller, a former literary editor at the Toronto Star.
PROOF: Dr. Henri J. Breault, a career paediatrician from Windsor, Ontario, Canada famously invented the childproof safety cap. Breault is known for spearheading a national campaign to prevent accidental childhood poisonings. He advocated for the development of childproof containers with the Palm-N-Turn, a safety cap that drastically reduced child deaths due to poisoning in Canada and around the world.
PROUD: There is little doubt that Canada is one of the best places to live in the world, and there is a lot to be proud of in this amazing country! A few of the things that make us proud to call the Great White North home: universal health care, a rich ethnic diversity & inclusive culture, gorgeous scenery & landscapes, extraordinary wildlife, delicious food like poutine, butter tarts and maple syrup, real beer, and of course Canada's game, hockey! We feel a deep sense of pride towards this beautiful land and its inhabitants, and can proudly wear the maple leaf wherever we go. True north strong and free! 🍁
PROWL: Canada is home to some of the world’s most stealthy prowlers! Majestic creatures like cougars, wolves, and lynx can be spotted in forests and mountains across the country, often moving silently as they hunt for food. The elusive cougar, for example, roams areas from British Columbia to the Maritimes, mostly at dusk and dawn when they're hardest to spot. Next time you're hiking through Canadian wilderness, remember you may not see them - but some of Canada’s wild hunters could be on the prowl!
PUFFS: In October 2022, Cheetos unveiled a giant Cheetos statue in Cheadle, Alberta. The monument, which is almost 5.2 metres tall (17 feet), shows a thumb and two fingers holding a Cheetos Puffs snack in the air. The fingers are covered in the Cheetos orange dust – which Cheetos says is officially called 'Cheetle.' The Cheetle Hand Statue was only in Cheadle for a short time, but it made its orange mark and received worldwide attention!
PULLS: From horse pulls to truck pulls, the [Massey Fair](https://masseyfair.ca/) celebrates the strength, skill and agricultural traditions that have brought the community together for generations. What began as a small local fair showcasing farm equipment, produce and livestock has grown into one of the largest agricultural fairs in Northern Ontario, historically welcoming around 15,000 visitors. The 120th anniversary fair runs August 28-30 in Massey, Ontario.
PUPIL: The ophthalmoscope, a small hand-held telescope for looking through the pupil of the eye, allows doctors to see inside the eye and to examine the retina and optic nerve, which are extensions of the brain. In 1864, Toronto doctors pioneered retinal photography by connecting an ophthalmoscope to a camera to photograph the retina of a cat, a first step in photographing the inside of the living human eye and a technique that today is essential all over the world in evaluating and treating patients with eye diseases.
PUPPY: The mudpuppy is Canada's largest salamander species. Found in southern Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec, this unique creature spends its entire life underwater. Its feathery, dark red external gills are a striking feature and an adaptation to its aquatic lifestyle. Mudpuppies live at the bottoms of freshwater lakes, ponds, rivers, and streams, where they quietly play a vital role in their ecosystems by feeding on insects, small fish, and other invertebrates. These fascinating creatures are an important and unique part of Canada's natural biodiversity!
QUACK: Canada is a haven for duck lovers! Our country hosts over 11 duck species, and our vast network of wetlands, lakes, and marshes make it a prime stopover in the Mississippi and Atlantic Flyways, two major North American migration routes. Every spring and fall, you can witness flocks of mallards, wood ducks, and teal filling the skies and making quite the racket with their quacks.
QUAKE: Seismologists locate more than 4000 earthquakes every year in Canada and the surrounding areas. Thankfully most of these earthquakes are smaller than magnitude 3 and are not felt. Government of Canada monitoring and research on earthquakes is undertaken by Natural Resources Canada’s Earth Sciences Sector. For more information on earthquakes visit the Geological Survey of Canada, NRCan website: earthquakescanada.ca
QUEST: At the top of the world in the Yukon and Alaska wilderness of northwestern North America, the [Yukon Quest](https://www.yukonquest.com/) 1,000 Mile International Sled Dog Race, an epic winter sports event takes place every year on the first Saturday of February. Covering 1,000 miles (1,600 km) between Whitehorse, Yukon and Fairbanks, Alaska during the depths of winter, the Yukon Quest is known for excellence in canine care and fostering the traditions of northern travel by dog sled. It has been run every year since 1984 over rough, sometimes hazardous terrain. The Yukon Quest Trail follows historical Gold Rush and mail delivery dog sled routes from the turn of the 20th Century.
QUICK: At the Paris 2024 Olympics, Canada’s men’s 4x100m relay team proved they were the quickest on the planet, storming to gold in 37.50 seconds. Their victory secured Canada’s first relay title since 1996, when the lightning-quick Donovan Bailey won the individual 100m gold in world-record time and anchored the relay team to victory. From Bailey’s historic era to Andre De Grasse’s spectacular final leg in Paris, Canadian athletes have always known how to move quickly.
QUIET: The Quiet Revolution ("Révolution tranquille" in French) refers to a significant period of socio-political and socio-cultural transformation in French Canada, particularly in Quebec, following the election of 1960. This vivid yet paradoxical description of the period was first used by an anonymous writer in The Globe and Mail. The Quiet Revolution is a major reference point used by successive Québec governments in power since the Liberal defeat in 1966.
QUILT: Quilts were extremely important to the early settlers of Canada, since they had no good way of heating or insulating their homes, especially at night. The first quilts arrived in Canada with immigrants to "New France" in the early 1600s. Today, the [Canadian Quilters' Association](https://canadianquilter.com/) celebrates quilting and Canadian quilters across the country.
QUIRK: CBC Radio's [Quirks & Quarks](https://www.cbc.ca/radio/quirks) is a Canadian science news program that covers the quirks of the expanding universe to the quarks within a single atom...and everything in between. It has been airing since October 8, 1975, and is consistently rated among the most popular CBC programs. Bob McDonald has been the host of the weekly radio show since 1992, succeeding former hosts David Mowbray, Jay Ingram, and David Suzuki, the show's original host.
QUOTA: Fishing quotas play an important role in managing Canada’s marine resources. In 1992, the federal government placed a major moratorium on the Atlantic cod fishery after decades of overfishing led to the collapse of cod stocks, dramatically impacting communities across Newfoundland and Labrador. Since then, strict quotas and management measures have been used to help protect remaining fish populations and support the long-term sustainability of Canada’s fisheries.
RABBI: Canada’s Jewish community has long been shaped by remarkable rabbis. In 1846, Rabbi Abraham de Sola became the first to settle permanently here, leading Montreal’s Spanish and Portuguese Synagogue and even preaching before Queen Victoria. In Ottawa, Rabbi Reuven Bulka built on that legacy – founding Kindness Week, now a national celebration of compassion passed into law in 2021. Today, rabbis across Canada continue to serve as spiritual leaders, educators, and advocates, helping to enrich the diverse fabric of Canadian life.
RACER: On April 1st, 2024, ultramarathon racer Ryan Keeping started running across Canada to raise funds and awareness for the Heart & Stroke Foundation. Inspired by his hero, Terry Fox, Ryan is running 75km a day for 99 days to cover the distance of 7,386km from St. John's, Newfoundland to Victoria, British Columbia. You can follow Ryan's journey at [ryankeeping.com](https://ryankeeping.com/) and support his cross-Canada run with a donation on his [GoFundMe page](https://www.gofundme.com/f/ryans-crosscanada-run). Canuckle will be donating proceeds from today's puzzle to Ryan's campaign. Let's help him Flip The Switch!
RADAR: Perched in the heart of Huron at the junction of Highways 4 and 8 is the iconic radar antenna that has forever identified Clinton, Ontario as '[the Home of Radar](https://www.stopsalongtheway.ca/clinton-monument)' in Canada. The antenna is part of the AN/FPS-20 long range radar system and is a relic of the Cold War. It was originally donated by the Canadian Forces Base Clinton in 1967 in honour of the Canadian Centennial as a monument to the country and the people trained at the base. The base was Canada's first radar school, opening in August 1941, and the site trained nearly 9,000 students by the end of World War II: more than 6,500 Canadians and over 2,300 Americans.
RAINBOW: The rainbow flag is a powerful symbol of LGBTQ+ pride and diversity worldwide. In Canada, Pride Month is celebrated every June with colourful parades and festivals from coast to coast, highlighting the country’s commitment to inclusion, equality, and the ongoing fight for LGBTQ+ rights. The rainbow’s vibrant colours remind us all to embrace love and respect for everyone!
RAINY: It is no secret that it rains a great deal in British Columbia. In fact, many of Canada's rainiest places are located in the province. Located on Vancouver Island, Hucuktlis Lake (pronounced "who chook-tlis"), formerly Henderson Lake, receives more rainfall throughout the year than any other place in North America. The soggy spot receives 7296 mm of precipitation annually. What's more, the area holds the record for the most rainfall in a year ever: a jaw-dropping 9,307 mm fell in 1997!
RAISE: Yesterday would have been Terry Fox's 65th birthday! Terry Fox is one of the most prominent figures in all of Canada. In 1977, 18-year-old Terry Fox was diagnosed with bone cancer and gave up his right leg to prevent the spread of the disease. The Canadian Cancer Society helped sponsor his run across Canada to raise funds and awareness for cancer research. The Marathon of Hope raised $24.2 million for cancer research and Terry became an inspiration to millions of people worldwide. To date, the [Terry Fox Foundation](https://terryfox.org/) has raised over 600 million dollars for cancer research.
RALLY: May 17 marks the [International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia, and Transphobia](https://may17.org/). Canada has a rich history of rallies and protests, where citizens come together to advocate for change and raise awareness about important social and political issues. The 'We Demand' rally, which took place on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Ontario on August 28, 1971, was the first large-scale LGBTQ2+ rally in Canadian history. The rally marked a pivotal moment in Canada's LGBTQ2+ rights movement. Today, rallies and protests remain an important part of Canada's democratic process, providing a platform for citizens to voice their concerns and hold their government accountable.
RAMEN: Did you know that ramen has found a special place in Canada’s diverse culinary landscape? While traditionally a Japanese dish, ramen shops have popped up across Canadian cities, from Vancouver to Toronto, with many chefs adding local twists. The first dedicated ramen shop in Canada opened in Vancouver in 1996, and since then, the dish has been embraced coast to coast. Whether it’s the cold winters that call for a warm, comforting bowl or the multicultural nature of the country, Canadians have welcomed ramen as part of their rich food scene!
RANGE: Canada is home to some incredible mountain ranges, including the famous Rocky Mountains. The Canadian Rockies house over 50 high mountains whose elevation exceeds the 11,000 ft (3,350 m) mark. The highest peak of this range of mountains is Mount Robson, which stands at 12,972 ft (3,954 m) above mean sea level.
REACH: A reach is a geographical term for a section of a river. Molly's Reach was a fictional restaurant in the real community of Gibsons, British Columbia, during the nineteen years the iconic Canadian television series "The Beachcombers" was set there. The Beachcombers was the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's longest running series.
READS: [Canada Reads](https://www.cbc.ca/books/canadareads) is an annual "battle of the books" competition organized and broadcast by Canada's public broadcaster, the CBC. During Canada Reads, five Canadian personalities champion five different books, with each advocate extolling the merits of one of the titles. The Canada Reads 2023 winner was ["Ducks: Two Years in the Oil Sands"](https://www.cbc.ca/books/ducks-by-kate-beaton-1.6559688) by author Kate Beaton, championed by Jeopardy super-champion Mattea Roach.
READY: Ready or Not is a Canadian teen drama television series that aired for five seasons and 65 episodes from 1993 to 1997. The show centred on two teenage girls in the suburbs of Toronto, best friends Amanda Zimm and Elizabeth "Busy" Ramone, following their life's struggles as well as showcasing the different households they grew up in. In 1996, Ready or Not won a Gemini Award for best youth series.
REALM: Canada is unique among countries in that it borders three marine realms: the Arctic, Temperate Northern Atlantic, and Temperate Northern Pacific. These realms can be further subdivided into three marine biomes and fifteen marine ecoregions based upon biological distinctiveness.
REELS: Today is [National Canadian Film Day](https://canfilmday.ca/)! Canada has a rich film history full of memorable stories and incredible talent - both in front of and behind the camera. Before digital editing, movies were physically cut and spliced on film reels, which became a lasting symbol of the film industry. Today, Canadian filmmakers continue to spin powerful stories on screens big and small. So grab some popcorn and press play on a Canadian classic to celebrate the creativity and talent of Canadian filmmakers!
REEVE: In Canada, a reeve is the head of a rural or small-town municipal council, similar to a mayor. The role dates back to the early days of local governance when reeves presided over townships to oversee taxes, infrastructure, and community concerns. While fewer communities use the term today, reeves remain an important part of rural governance in some provinces, connecting modern leadership to Canada's history. Of course, the most famous of all the reeves in Canada is actor Keanu Reeves - but he enforces justice in a very different way!
REGAL: Tomorrow is Commonwealth Day! It is the annual celebration of the Commonwealth of Nations. We join our Commonwealth partners around the world to celebrate the shared values and the strong bonds of cooperation and friendship that bind us together. The Governor General of Canada is the federal viceregal representative of the Canadian monarch, currently King Charles III.
REIGN: The reign of Canada's new monarch, King Charles III, began when Queen Elizabeth II died on September 8. Queen Elizabeth II was Canada's monarch for over 70 years, making her the longest reigning monarch in Commonwealth history.
RELAY: Canada has a proud history of excelling in relay events across multiple sports at the Olympics. Our swimmers have made waves with medal-winning performances, like the women's 4x100m freestyle relay team winning bronze and the women's 4x100m medley relay team winning silver at Tokyo 2020. On the ice, our speed skating teams have brought home numerous medals in the relay events, with the men's 5000m relay team claiming gold at PyeongChang 2018. On the track, Canada's 4x100m men's relay team sprinted to gold in Atlanta 1996, a historic moment anchored by the legendary [Donovan Bailey](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/donovan-bailey/). These successes showcase Canada's strength, teamwork, and spirit in relay competitions on the world stage!
RELIC: Robert Allan Clothier was a Canadian stage and television actor most famous for his role as Relic on the CBC television series, The Beachcombers. He portrayed Bruno Gerussi's rival beachcomber, Relic - a curmudgeonly, conniving man of Welsh descent who lived on a house boat and used his jetboat to outrun and challenge Nick's claims to logs. After landing this memorable role, Clothier became a household face among viewers, as the show originally aired from 1972 to 1990, one of the longest running Canadian television dramas of all time.
RENEW: The National Trust is a registered charity that leads and inspires action to save and renew historic places. Their [Next Great Save](https://nextgreatsave.nationaltrustcanada.ca/2024) competition empowers communities to save heritage places and advance projects that protect, adapt, renew, or improve heritage places for the future. The Next Great Save competition highlights the impact of saving and renewing these places, and getting people from coast-to-coast-to-coast involved in the process.
RESET: For many Canadians, spring brings more than warmer weather – it’s the season for a full household reset. From washing windows and airing out rooms to clearing garages and tackling winter clutter, spring cleaning has long been a tradition across Canada. After months spent indoors during the colder seasons, many families use this time of year to refresh their homes, routines, and outlook for the months ahead.
REVEL: Each March 17, communities across Canada revel in the spirit of St. Patrick’s Day! From lively parades to seas of green, people across the country join in celebrating Irish heritage. In fact, Canada is home to one of the largest Irish diasporas outside Ireland, with millions of Canadians tracing at least some of their roots to the Emerald Isle.
RHINO: Did you know Canada once had a political party called the [Rhinoceros Party of Canada](https://www.partyrhino.ca/)? Founded in 1963, it became famous for its satirical and humorous platform. The party proposed outrageous policies like repealing the law of gravity and banning lousy Canadian winters.
