While they never gained significant political power, the party remains a quirky part of Canadian political history, known for mocking traditional politics and using humour to encourage people to think about the system in a new way.
RIDGE: The Battle of Vimy Ridge, during the First World War, is Canada's most celebrated military victory – an often mythologized symbol of the birth of Canadian national pride and awareness.
RIGHT: The [Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms](https://www.justice.gc.ca/eng/csj-sjc/rfc-dlc/ccrf-ccdl/) protects a number of rights and freedoms, including freedom of expression and the right to equality. It forms part of our Constitution – the highest law in all of Canada – and is one of our country’s greatest accomplishments. Every year on April 17th, we celebrate the anniversary of the Charter which was signed in 1982.
RINGS: Curling is played on a rink or sheet of ice that has 3 concentric rings and the button which make up the house or target. "Roar of the Rings" was the name of the Canadian Olympic Curling Trials, and "[Rocks & Rings](https://rocksandrings.com/)" is a Curling Canada program designed to introduce the sport of curling to children. The [2023 Scotties Tournament of Hearts](https://www.curling.ca/2023scotties/) is currently underway in Kamloops, BC and the members of the winning team receive gold rings in the four-heart design of the Tournament of Hearts logo. The winner will represent Canada at the World Women's Curling Championship!
RIVER: Annually, Canada’s Rivers discharge 7% of the world’s renewable water supply at a flow rate per second more than four times that of Niagara Falls.
ROAST: Happy [Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/celebrate-canada/saint-jean-baptiste-day.html)! On June 24, Francophones across the country show their pride on the National Day of Quebec by celebrating their language and their traditions. Canada boasts a rich culinary tradition of hearty roasts, including the iconic Quebecois dish known as Bouilli! Similar to the French pot-au-feu, Bouilli, which translates to 'boiled' in English, is a traditional Quebecois pot roast or stew made with beef and an assortment of root vegetables such as carrots, potatoes, and turnips. This comforting and flavourful dish is typically slow-cooked until the beef is tender and infused with the rich flavors of the vegetables and aromatic spices. Bouilli has deep roots in Quebecois cuisine and is often enjoyed as a warm and satisfying meal during the cold winter months.
ROBIN: The return of the robin is a sure sign of Spring in Canada! American Robins begin to arrive at their breeding grounds in southern areas of Canada in March each year. Few birds are as familiar to the Canadian public as the robin. Its plumage is easily recognizable, and it is one of the first birds to sing in the morning and one of the last to be heard at night.
ROCKS: Canada is home to some stunning rock formations, including New Brunswick's Hopewell Rocks, Ontario's Flowerpot Rocks, the Hoodoos found in Alberta's Badlands, Balancing Rock in Nova Scotia, and Rocher Percé (Pierced Rock) in Quebec.
ROCKY: The Rocky Mountains, also known as the Rockies, are the largest mountain system in North America!
ROLLS: On the East Coast of Canada, fresh lobster rolls are the epitome of local comfort food. With succulent chunks of fresh lobster meat, nestled in a buttery toasted bun, this iconic dish is a true delicacy that evokes the charm and flavour of the Atlantic shoreline. The classic East Coast lobster roll is a culinary masterpiece that captures the essence of coastal living.
ROOMS: [The Rooms](https://www.therooms.ca/) is Newfoundland and Labrador’s largest public cultural space and home to its most extensive collection of artifacts, art and archival records. Part sanctuary, part showcase, part classroom and part playground, it’s both a destination and a journey. A place for people, The Rooms is a portal to the many stories the province of Newfoundland and Labrador has to tell.
ROOST: In Canada, chickens don’t just roost on farms - they help support a multi-billion-dollar industry! The country's poultry sector thrives under supply management, a system that balances production with demand to keep grocery shelves stocked with fresh, high-quality chicken. This approach supports thousands of jobs while maintaining strict food safety and animal welfare standards. From coast to coast, [Canadian chicken farmers](https://www.chickenfarmers.ca/) ensure there's always a perfect perch for poultry!
ROOTS: Roots Canada opened its first store in 1973 selling footwear, and started using the beaver logo in 1985 with the launch of their athletic brand.
ROSES: The Farine Five Roses sign is a feature of the Montreal skyline, first erected above the Ogilvie flour mill in 1948. The unmistakeable symbol is over 75 years old, making it older than the Canadian flag. Its shining neon lights, which overlook the Lachine Canal, call out to Montreal drivers and pedestrians and remind them that they are, in fact, home.
ROUGE: In the Canadian Football League (CFL), a rouge is a one-point score that is awarded for certain plays that involve the ball being kicked into the end zone. The rouge is uniquely Canadian!
ROUGH: The Canadian Football League (CFL) once had two teams with nearly identical names: the Ottawa Rough Riders and the Saskatchewan Roughriders. This led to some confusion among fans and broadcasters, especially during games between the two teams. In 1996, the Ottawa team folded, leaving Saskatchewan as the sole "Roughriders" in the CFL. The Ottawa franchise returned in 2002 as the Ottawa Renegades, and later became the Ottawa Redblacks in 2014. Despite the name changes, the legacy of the "Rough Riders" and "Roughriders" remains a unique chapter in Canadian football history.
ROUND: On National Donut Day, Canadians celebrate the sweet, round treat found in bakeries and coffee shops across the country. From classic glazed rings to filled and frosted varieties, donuts are a popular indulgence enjoyed with coffee or hot chocolate. Canada is also among the highest donut-consuming countries in the world, with Canadians enjoying roughly a billion donuts each year. Their familiar round shape is part of what makes them so iconic and instantly recognizable.
ROUSE: "The Rouse" is a bugle call most often associated with the military in Commonwealth countries. It is commonly played following "Last Post" at military services. "The Rouse" was traditionally played following "Reveille", which was a bugle call played in the morning to wake soldiers up.
ROWAN: The rowan tree, also known as mountain ash, is one of Canada’s most widespread native trees, found from Newfoundland to British Columbia. In autumn, its bright red berry clusters become an important food source for migrating birds such as cedar waxwings, robins, and pine grosbeaks. In Atlantic Canada, Scottish settlers often planted rowans near their homes, carrying with them a Highland tradition that believed the trees brought protection and good fortune. The berries have also been used in Maritime kitchens for generations, turned into jams, jellies, and even rowan wine.
ROWDY: Roderick George Toombs, better known as "Rowdy" Roddy Piper, was a Canadian professional wrestler and actor. Piper was best known to international audiences for his work with the World Wrestling Federation (now WWE) and World Championship Wrestling between 1984 and 2000. Although he was Canadian, Piper was billed as coming from Glasgow and was known for his signature kilt and bagpipe entrance music. In 2005, Piper was inducted into the WWE Hall of Fame by Ric Flair, who dubbed him "the most gifted entertainer in the history of professional wrestling".
ROYAL: Canada is one of the oldest continuing monarchies in the world. The title “Royal” is a sign of honour and distinction, and the granting of this distinction is a prerogative of the Sovereign. In Canada, we have the Royal Canadian Navy, the Royal Canadian Air Force, the Royal Canadian Regiment in the Canadian Army, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Royal Canadian Legion, the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada, and the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada. In Canada's legislative process, a bill can only become law once it has received royal assent.
RUGBY: Buoyed by its inclusion in the 2016 Olympic Games, Rugby is one of the fastest growing team sports in Canada, particularly in youth and women.
RUSTY: Rusty was the cheerful puppet rooster on The Friendly Giant, a classic Canadian children’s television show that aired from 1958 to 1985. Voiced and puppeteered by Canadian Rod Coneybeare, Rusty lived in a book bag that hung on the castle wall, delighting generations of viewers and becoming a symbol of warmth, friendship, and fun in households across Canada.
SAFER: On May 17, we mark [International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia](https://may17.org/), a global day dedicated to raising awareness of discrimination and promoting dignity, inclusion, and respect for 2SLGBTQIA+ communities. Across Canada, ongoing efforts in schools, workplaces, and public spaces focus on building safer environments where people can live openly and authentically, without fear of harassment or exclusion. The goal is simple but vital: safer communities where understanding, education, and respect help reduce harm and support everyone’s right to belong.
SALSA: Toronto’s [Canada Salsa & Bachata Congress](https://www.canadasalsacongress.com/) is Canada’s longest-running salsa event and one of the largest in North America. Held every October, the festival brings together 60 international artists and 70 dance companies, with workshops, performances, competitions and 22 hours of social dancing across three ballrooms. Founded by Jennifer Aucoin, the event has been bringing the rhythm and energy of salsa to Toronto for more than two decades.
SALTY: Known as the "Dead Sea of Canada", the waters of Little Manitou Lake near Saskatoon are roughly five times saltier than the ocean - and approximately half as salty as the Dead Sea in Israel and Jordan. Fed by underground springs, the lake is so high in sodium, magnesium and potassium salts that it's almost impossible for swimmers to sink. Locals and visitors alike swear by Little Manitou Lake's ability to cure skin conditions, arthritis and joint pain, although the science on its healing powers is up for debate.
SAUNA: Sauna culture is picking up steam across Canada! While modern sauna houses and mobile units are rising in popularity for wellness and relaxation, heat-based traditions have deep roots here: Indigenous communities have long used sweat lodges for ceremony, healing and spiritual renewal. Today’s revival of sauna culture reflects both new trends and timeless practices that connect people through warmth, reflection and community.
SCARF: Winter is officially here! The scarf is an essential item of clothing for the winter season in Canada. It's all about layers if you want to be comfortable in the cold weather, and the scarf is one of the best winter accessories for staying warm. The Kokom (Kokum) Scarf or Ukrainian Scarf are a symbol of relations of the Indigenous peoples supporting Ukrainian settlers that arrived to Canada. These scarves were traded among Indigenous and Ukrainian women. There are many similarities between the two cultures and the scarf today resembles unity and respect for each other.
SCENE: Did you know that Canada's improv scene thrives with the [Canadian Improv Games](https://www.improv.ca/)? This annual event celebrates high school improvisational theatre, fostering creativity and teamwork among students nationwide. From April 16 to 19, 2025, the National Arts Centre in Ottawa will host the National Festival and Tournament, where top teams from across the country will take the stage. Competing teams perform a variety of improvised scenes, from hilarious character-driven sketches to heartfelt dramatic moments, all created on the spot. Every performance ends with a resounding 'Scene!' as players wrap up their spontaneous storytelling in front of an energetic audience!
SCION: In Canada, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau is often considered a scion - a descendant of a prominent family. His father, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, was one of Canada's most famous and influential prime ministers, serving for 15 years. Justin followed in his father's footsteps, becoming the second Trudeau to hold the country's highest office. November 4th marked the 9th anniversary of Justin Trudeau being sworn in as Canada's 23rd prime minister.
SCOPE: It's [Canadian Innovation Week](https://canadianinnovationspace.ca/)! Did you know that Canada played a significant role in the development of the James Webb Space Telescope? The [Canadian Space Agency](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/) contributed two important elements, built by Honeywell: the Fine Guidance Sensor (FGS), which allows the telescope to point at and focus on objects of interest, and the Near-Infrared Imager and Slitless Spectrograph (NIRISS), a scientific instrument that helps study many astronomical objects, from exoplanets to distant galaxies. Canada receives a guaranteed share of Webb's observation time, making Canadian scientists some of the first to study data collected by the most advanced space telescope ever built.
SCOUT: For more than 100 years, [Scouts Canada](https://www.scouts.ca/) has brought a world of adventure, outdoor experience, friendship and fun to 17 million Canadian youth. Scouts Canada is the country's leading co-ed youth organization, offering programming for children and youth aged 5-26. Scouts Canada is part of the [World Organization of the Scout Movement WOSM](https://www.scout.org/) which has over 40 million members in 167 National Scout Organizations around the world.
SCREW: In 1907, Canadian Peter L. Robertson invented a square socket-head screw. He produced his screws in his Milton, Ontario, factory starting in 1908. At that time, it was a revolutionary change in the fastener industry. Robertson screws and screwdrivers carry his name to this day.
SEALS: Seals are found in the waters of all three Canadian oceans: harbour in both Pacific and Atlantic; bearded and ringed in the Arctic; harp and hooded in the North Atlantic and parts of the Arctic; and grey in Atlantic Canada.
SEEDS: Canada is the world's largest producer of mustard seed, most of it farmed in the southern prairie regions of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Canada is also the largest producer of flaxseed in the world, representing about 40% of world production.
SEINE: Seine net fishing has been one of the most important methods used on Canada’s Pacific and Atlantic coasts for generations. A seine net encircles a school of fish such as salmon, herring, or mackerel, then closes like a drawstring purse at the bottom. Commonly used by purse seiners in British Columbia during salmon season, the technique has deep roots in both Indigenous and settler fishing traditions and remains a key part of Canada’s coastal fisheries today.
SERVE: For more than 100 years, millions of Canadians have proudly served our country in uniform. While the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) are known to put their lives on the line to support international operations, they also fulfill important roles on home soil. They provide national and regional security, serve on search and rescue missions and respond to natural disasters. On this Remembrance Day, we honour those who made the ultimate sacrifice. Lest we forget.
SEVEN: The Group of Seven was a group of painters from 1920 to 1933, best known for their paintings inspired by the Canadian landscape that initiated the first major Canadian national art movement.
SEWED: On [National Flag of Canada Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/national-flag-canada-day.html), we remember the woman who literally sewed Canada’s identity into history. In 1964, Ottawa civil servant Joan O’Malley stayed late into the night at her Singer sewing machine to sew the first Canadian flag, turning cloth and thread into a symbol that would unite a nation. Every stitch carried pride, purpose, and the promise of a flag that would fly over homes, schools, and Parliament – and, of course, soar above Canadian athletes at the Olympics!
SEWER: [Flin Flon](https://cityofflinflon.ca/), Manitoba is known for its unique above-ground “sewer boxes,” wooden-covered utility structures built because the rocky Canadian Shield made underground installation difficult. In the city’s early development, they also doubled as pedestrian walkways and remain a distinctive part of the local infrastructure today.
SHACK: The end of March means it's time to visit a sugar shack in Canada! Sugar shacks ("cabanes à sucres" in French) are cabins where sap is collected from sugar maple trees and boiled into maple syrup through a technique originally developed by the Indigenous and passed on to the French colonizers of New-France. If you are visiting Canada, don't miss your chance to experience an authentic sugar shack meal, where everything is drowned in maple syrup!
SHAKE: Did you know Canada has an island that literally shakes? Tremble Island, located in British Columbia’s Seymour Inlet, experiences a phenomenon where the ground quivers due to the power of the water currents surrounding it. This inlet has some of the fastest tidal surges in the world, and at peak tides, the force of the water is so intense that it causes the entire island to tremble! Visitors to Tremble Island are in for a unique (and slightly shaky) experience, showcasing the raw power of Canada’s incredible natural landscapes.
SHALE: The Burgess Shale is a fossil-bearing deposit exposed in the Canadian Rockies of British Columbia, Canada. Found in Canada's Yoho National Park, it is one of the most important fossil sites in the world! The rocks here preserve not only the usual hard shells of ancient organisms, but also soft skin and tissue, allowing for stunning impressions of the strange creatures of 500 million years ago!
SHARP: Did you know that one of the most iconic signature moves in professional wrestling, the Sharpshooter, was popularized by Canadian wrestler [Bret 'The Hitman' Hart](https://brethart.com/)? Born and raised in Calgary, Alberta, Bret Hart is one of Canada's most celebrated professional wrestlers, known for his technical prowess and showmanship in the ring. The Sharpshooter, also known as the Scorpion Deathlock, is a submission hold that involves the wrestler locking their opponent's legs and applying pressure to their lower back, causing intense pain and potentially forcing a submission. Bret Hart perfected this devastating move and used it to win numerous championship titles throughout his illustrious career, earning him a place in wrestling history as one of the greatest performers of all time.
SHELF: The [Scotian Shelf](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/scotian-shelf) is a geological formation, part of the Continental shelf, located southwest of Nova Scotia, Canada. It covers an area of 120,000 square kilometres, is 700 kilometres long and has an average depth of 90 metres. The Scotian Shelf contains the ecologically important Scotian Shelf Large Marine Ecosystem (LME) and the Scotian Shelf Waters (SSW).
SHINY: Big Shiny Tunes is a series of rock albums compiled and released by the Canadian music television station MuchMusic, and through MusiquePlus in Quebec, from 1996 to 2009. The best-selling album of the series was Big Shiny Tunes 2, which was certified Diamond in Canada (1,000,000 units). It has been cited as the best-selling album series in Canadian history, with 5 million albums sold in ten years.
SHIPS: The most famous ship in Canadian history, the Bluenose, was both a fishing and racing vessel in the 1920s and 1930s. The Nova Scotia schooner achieved immortality when its image was engraved onto the Canadian dime.
SHIRT: Feb 22 is Anti-Bullying Day, also known as [Pink Shirt Day](https://www.pinkshirtday.ca/), where people wear a pink-coloured shirt to stand against bullying. The initiative was started in Canada in 2007 by two Nova Scotia teenagers when a fellow Grade 9 student in Berwick was being teased and bullied for wearing a pink shirt on the first day of school.
SHOAL: Located in Kingston, Ontario, [Shoal Tower](https://www.pc.gc.ca/apps/dfhd/page_nhs_eng.aspx?id=407) is one of four Martello towers built in the mid-19th century to defend the entrance to Kingston Harbour and the Royal Naval Dockyard. These towers were part of a network of fortifications constructed during the tensions between Canada and the United States, particularly during the War of 1812 and its aftermath. Shoal Tower, constructed on a submerged shoal in Lake Ontario, served as a strategic point of defense against potential enemy attacks from the lake. Today, Shoal Tower stands as a testament to Canada's military history and is open to visitors interested in exploring its historic significance and architectural design.
SHOOT: In the biathlon, athletes must ski fast and shoot with precision, and Canada has excelled in this challenging sport! [Myriam Bédard](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/myriam-bedard/) made history by winning two gold medals at the 1994 Lillehammer Olympics in the 7.5 km and 15 km biathlon events. She also won a bronze medal at the 1992 Albertville Olympics. Bédard's remarkable marksmanship and skiing prowess have made her a Canadian legend in the biathlon world.
SHRUB: The [Arctic Willow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salix_arctica) is a unique dwarf shrub found throughout Canada’s northern tundra. In this harsh environment, it grows close to the ground to shelter from freezing winds, typically reaching only 15-20 cm in height. Yet despite its tiny stature, this resilient shrub can live for over 200 years and provides an important food source for Arctic wildlife, including caribou and muskoxen. A small but mighty example of how life can thrive in Canada’s most extreme landscapes.
SIEGE: The Siege of Québec was a pivotal three-month military campaign during the Seven Years’ War that helped lay the foundation for modern Canada. From June 26 to September 18, 1759, British forces besieged the city before defeating French forces in the [Battle of the Plains of Abraham](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/battle-of-the-plains-of-abraham). The victory led to British control of New France and a realignment of alliances with First Nations.
SIGNS: The [Neon Sign Museum](https://www.edmonton.ca/city_government/edmonton_archives/neon-sign-museum), the first of its kind in Canada, features a collection of functional historic signs that tell a story about Edmonton's neon past. The City of Edmonton has collected 20 neon signs, all of which have been restored and installed on the east wall of the Telus building and the south wall of the Mercer Warehouse building. The signs chosen are iconic and represent the commercial signage from Edmonton's history.
SILOS: Silos are a familiar sight across Canada’s rural landscape, standing tall on farms from coast to coast. These structures are used to store grain or fermented feed (silage), helping farmers preserve crops and keep livestock fed through long Canadian winters. Whether cylindrical towers or long bunker-style builds, silos play a key role in Canada’s agricultural system and food supply.
SINKS: Canada plays an important role in the global climate system through its vast natural carbon sinks, ecosystems that absorb more carbon dioxide than they release. Forests, wetlands, and peatlands across the country store large amounts of carbon, helping to regulate greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. In regions like the boreal forests of the Hudson Bay Lowlands and across northern Canada, these natural sinks are among the largest intact carbon stores on Earth, making them a key part of Canada’s environmental landscape.
SKIES: The Prairie Skies were voted one of [Canada's Seven Wonders](https://www.cbc.ca/sevenwonders/) in a 2007 competition sponsored by CBC Television's The National and CBC Radio One's Sounds Like Canada. Rounding out the list of Canada's Seven Wonders were Niagara Falls, Halifax's Pier 21, The Rockies, Old Quebec, the igloo, and the canoe. The province of Saskatchewan is known as the "Land of Living Skies" and even features the slogan on its provincial license plates.
SKINS: Did you know one of Canada’s most iconic school supplies began with discarded cod skins? In the 1870s, chemist William Nelson LePage of Charlottetown, PEI, developed a new adhesive from fish byproducts, launching the famous LePage mucilage glue. With its soft-tip applicator, it became a classroom staple for generations of Canadian kids. By 1887, over 50 million bottles had been sold, and LePage’s clever advertising helped shape how products were marketed across North America!
SKIPS: In the sport of curling, the skip is the captain of a team. The skip determines strategy, and holds the broom in the house to indicate where a teammate at the other end of the curling sheet should aim the stone. Canada is home to some of the best curling skips in the world, including household names like Jennifer Jones, Kevin Martin, Sandra Schmirler, Russ & Glenn Howard, Colleen Jones, Ernie Richardson, Randy Ferbey, Connie Laliberte, Jeff Stoughton, Rachel Homan, Kevin Koe, Kerri Einarson and Brad Gushue.
SLACK: [Slack](https://slack.com/), the popular cloud-based collaboration tool used by millions worldwide, was co-created by Canadian entrepreneur Stewart Butterfield! Originally from Lund, British Columbia, Butterfield launched Slack in 2013, revolutionizing how teams communicate and work together online. The product name Slack was derived from the phrase "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Today, Slack is an essential tool for businesses and organizations, enabling seamless messaging, file sharing, and project management.
SLANG: Canada has some very unique slang words, sayings and phrases that make the Great White North a little bit different! Do you know how to speak Canadian? [Check out this video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o34VzENNPic) to learn how! Don't be a hoser, eh?
SLATE: In Canada’s early one-room schoolhouses, students didn’t have notebooks or tablets – they used slates! These small, handheld chalkboards were a reusable and affordable way for kids to practise writing and arithmetic. With a slate pencil in hand, students could solve math problems, copy sentences, or spell out their lessons, then simply wipe it clean and start again. Slates were especially common in rural schools, where supplies were scarce and learning had to be practical. It’s a little piece of classroom history that helped shape generations of Canadian students!
SLEET: Sleet is a familiar part of Canadian winters, forming when snowflakes melt into raindrops and then refreeze before hitting the ground. Canada experiences some of the widest temperature swings on Earth, which makes mixed precipitation like sleet especially common in late fall and early spring. In fact, parts of southern Canada can see all four types of precipitation – rain, snow, sleet, and freezing rain – within the same day!
SLIME: You Can't Do That on Television is a Canadian sketch comedy television series that aired on CTV and Nickelodeon from 1979-1990. The show was notable for launching the careers of many performers, including Canadian musician Alanis Morissette. The show is most famous for introducing the network's iconic green slime, which was subsequently featured in game shows in the 90s, and continues to be a highlight of the annual Kids' Choice Awards.
SLOPE: Canada has seen remarkable success on the slopes at the Olympics! Slopestyle is a winter sport in which athletes ski or snowboard down a course including a variety of obstacles including rails, jumps and other terrain park features. At the 2014 Sochi Olympics, Canada had a double podium in women's ski slopestyle with [Dara Howell](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/dara-howell/) winning gold and [Kim Lamarre](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/kim-lamarre/) winning bronze. Slopestyle success continued with [Alex Beaulieu-Marchand](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/alex-beaulieu-marchand/) taking home the bronze in men's ski slopestyle at the PyeongChang 2018 Olympics. In men's snowboard slopestyle, both [Max Parrot](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/max-parrot/) and [Mark McMorris](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/mark-mcmorris/) have won multiple Olympic medals. So, when you think of "slope," remember Canada’s incredible achievements and the talented athletes who navigate these thrilling inclines with finesse!
SLUSH: In Newfoundland and Labrador, it’s not Christmas without slush! This shockingly easy and potent batch cocktail is a holiday must-have in the easterly province and, abandoning all cocktail etiquette, is prepared in a salt beef bucket. Christmas slush is traditionally prepared with amber rum, frozen cans of lemonade and orange juice concentrate, pineapple juice and a whole lot of sugar. Newfoundland Christmas slush encapsulates beloved tradition, a sense of community and holiday hospitality in Newfoundland and Labrador.
SMACK: Did you know that a group of jellyfish is called a "smack"? In Canada, jellyfish can be found along the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic coasts. One of the most notable species is the Lion's Mane jellyfish, which is commonly seen in the colder waters off the coast of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. These jellyfish can have tentacles that extend over 30 metres, making them one of the largest jellyfish species in the world. Encountering a smack of jellyfish is a mesmerizing experience, showcasing the diversity of marine life in Canadian waters.
SMART: Canada is the most educated country globally, with over 56% of adults meeting the OECD criteria of residents aged 25 to 64 who have completed some form of tertiary education.
SMILE: Canadians have lots of reasons to smile! Canada is the 13th happiest country in the world out of 157 countries ranked according to the 2023 World Happiness Report. This week is [Smile Cookie](https://www.timhortons.ca/smile-cookie) week at Tim Hortons! From May 1st through May 7th, 100% of proceeds from every Smile Cookie support charities and community groups across Canada. The Smile Cookie campaign has raised over $92 million across North America since 1996 and last year, restaurant owners raised a record-breaking $15 million! Get your #SmileCookie this week and put a smile on someone's face!
SMOKY: The town of [Smoky Lake](https://smokylake.ca/), proudly known as the Pumpkin Capital of Alberta, celebrates all things pumpkin with its famous Great White North Pumpkin Fair each fall. The highlight of the fair is the impressive Pumpkin Park, home to giant concrete pumpkins that have become a beloved sight for visitors. The pumpkins represent the region's deep agricultural roots and its status as a pumpkin-growing hub. Smoky Lake also serves as a launch point for adventurers heading down the Iron Horse Trail, one of Alberta's most iconic multi-use trails.
SNACK: June 7 is National Donut Day! Donuts are one of Canada's most beloved snack foods and these sweet treats have become a staple of Canadian culture. In fact, Canada has the most donut shops and consumes the most donuts per capita of any other country in the world - around 1 billion annually! Whether you prefer a classic style donut or a more elaborate creation, donuts hold a special place in the hearts (and stomachs) of Canadians from coast to coast.
SNAKE: Canada is home to the largest known congregations of snakes anywhere in the world. In spring and fall, over 50,000 red-sided gartersnakes congregate at hibernation sites in the Narcisse Wildlife Management Area in Manitoba.
SNEER: Remember Cyril Sneer from The Raccoons? That pink-nosed villain with a love for money and a signature scowl was part of a classic Canadian cartoon created by Kevin Gillis and produced by Sheldon Wiseman. Set in the Evergreen Forest, the series followed raccoon friends who often found themselves standing up to Cyril's scheming ways - all while promoting messages of friendship, conservation, and doing the right thing. A true gem of Canadian animation!
SNOWY: On February 10, 1999, Tahtsa Lake, British Columbia got hit with 145 cm (4'9") of snow in ONE day!
SNUFF: Across parts of Canada with deep Scottish roots, you might spot a curious artifact known as a snuff mull. Traditionally crafted from ram’s horn and silver, these ornate containers held finely ground tobacco “snuff” that was passed around at gatherings and celebrations. Today, snuff mulls are cherished as cultural keepsakes, reflecting the Scottish heritage woven into Canadian communities from Nova Scotia to the Prairies and all the way to British Columbia.
SOILS: [Salish Soils](https://salishsoils.com/) is an Indigenous-led company based in Sechelt, British Columbia, focused on converting compostable materials into high-quality soil to nourish the community. They offer the most comprehensive recycling and organic waste disposal solutions on the Sunshine Coast. Salish Soils honours the earth by empowering people and healing lands - collecting, processing, and composting waste resources into nutrient-rich organics.
SOLVE: Yesterday was National Puzzle Day! Each year on January 29th, National Puzzle Day recognizes how exercising our brains with puzzles is just one of its many benefits. It's the perfect day to solve some puzzles and do a little brain exercise! Whether it’s a solving a jigsaw, a word game like [Canuckle](https://www.canucklegame.ca) or a sudoku game like Canoku, puzzles engage our brain in more ways than one. We've even launched a new Brain Health Edition of Canoku - check it out at brainhealth.canoku.ca and give your brain a boost! 🧠💪
SONAR: As part of the British effort to combat German U-boats in 1917, Canadian physicist Robert William Boyle combined transducers made with quartz with amplifiers developed by French researchers to create the world's first high-frequency echolocation device: SONAR. Originally an acronym for SOund Navigation And Ranging, sonar is a technique that uses sound to navigate, communicate with or detect objects on or under the surface of the water. Boyle's work on sonar was built upon the work of another Canadian-born inventor, Reginald Fessenden, who is best known for his pioneering work developing radio technology.
SONNY: “Sonny’s Dream” is a beloved Canadian folk song written by Newfoundland singer-songwriter Ron Hynes. Released in 1976, the song tells the story of a young person dreaming of a better life while staying connected to home. It gained international recognition through recordings by artists such as Mary Black and The Rankin Family.
SOUND: Clayoquot Sound, on the west coast of Vancouver Island in British Columbia, is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve known for its stunning fjords, ancient temperate rainforests, and rich marine life. This protected area is home to whales, sea otters, and bears, and its waterways are popular for kayaking, sailing, and wildlife watching. Clayoquot Sound’s dramatic landscapes and thriving ecosystems make it one of Canada’s most spectacular coastal regions.
SOUPS: Soups have been a beloved part of Canadian cuisine for generations, with one of the most iconic being split pea soup! Split pea soup has deep roots in Canadian culinary tradition, dating back to early settlers and Indigenous communities who relied on this hearty dish for sustenance during long winters. Made from dried split peas, vegetables, and often featuring ham or bacon, split pea soup has become a quintessential comfort food in Canada, cherished for its rich flavours and warming qualities.
SOUTH: The Great White...South? Point Pelee is the southernmost point of mainland Canada, and is located on a foundation of glacial sand, silt and gravel that bites into Lake Erie. The word pelée is French for 'bald'. Point Pelee was the first national park in Canada to be established for conservation. The national park lies on the 42nd Parallel, making it the same latitude as northern California, Barcelona and Rome.
SPACE: Canada's contributions to space exploration include one of Canada’s most celebrated and iconic technological advances: The Canadarm - a remote-controlled robotic arm used to help build and maintain the International Space Station (ISS).
SPARK: Sparks is a [Girl Guides of Canada](https://www.girlguides.ca/) program is for five and six-year-old girls. Sparks were given their own branch in 1988, although they didn’t get their name until 1989. The program aims to spark curiosity, creativity, and confidence in young girls as they embark on their Girl Guides journey. A Spark is a reference to a Celtic Fairy spirit, which would be encountered in natural areas such as forests. The Sparks Promise is to share and be a friend.
SPEAK: Did you know that during the Prohibition era in the 1920s, Canada had its own network of secret bars called speakeasies? These hidden establishments provided Canadians with a place to enjoy alcoholic beverages despite the nationwide ban on alcohol. From Montreal to Vancouver, speakeasies popped up in basements, back rooms, and secret locations, often requiring a special password for entry. Today, the legacy of Canada's speakeasies lives on in the country's vibrant nightlife scene, with modern bars paying homage to this clandestine era through their decor, cocktails, and atmosphere.
SPEED: In Canada's olympic history, its athletes have received a total medal count of 79 in speed skating making it Canada's most successful Olympic sport! Charles Hamelin (short track) and Cindy Klassen (long track) are Canada's most decorated winter olympians with 6 medals each.
SPELT: Spelt is one of the world’s oldest cultivated grains and is still grown on Canadian farms today. This heritage wheat variety is known for its distinctive nutty flavour and is prized by artisan bakers for creating traditional breads, pastas, and other specialty foods. As part of Canada’s rich grain-growing tradition, spelt joins a diverse agricultural industry that makes Canada one of the world’s leading grain exporters.
SPINY: Canada's most unique terrestrial animal is probably not what you might think. A recent study published in the journal The [Canadian Field-Naturalist](https://www.canadianfieldnaturalist.ca/index.php/cfn/article/view/2673) has found the country's most evolutionarily distinct Canadian animal is the spiny softshell turtle! These turtles can be found in Ontario and Quebec, and are one of the largest freshwater turtle species in North America. But unfortunately, they have been listed as one of Canada's rarest species for over 20 years. If we let them disappear from Canada, we would lose almost 180 million years of unique evolutionary history. This shows how important it is to prioritize the conservation of this species and its unique legacy amongst Canadian wildlife.
SPLIT: Split pea soup is an authentic French Canadian dish that is made with yellow peas, ham, and veggies. This traditional pea soup is the ultimate in Quebec-style comfort food. This early settler soup became a staple item on the menu for Quebec's settlers as it was a filling and nutritious meal that helped them survive harsh Canadian winters.
SPORT: Canada's official national sports are ice hockey (winter) and lacrosse (summer).
SPOTS: Spotted Lake (Lake Kliluk) in British Columbia’s Similkameen Valley is made up of hundreds of separate pools that contain some of the world’s highest concentrations of Epsom salts, calcium, sodium sulphates and magnesium sulphates. When the warm summer months roll in, much of the water evaporates, leaving behind concentrations of the minerals that form spots across the lake. The spots can change in size and colour from blue to green to yellow, as minerals within each spot alter with further evaporation. According to Destination Osoyoos, Spotted Lake is a sacred place of healing for the people of the Syilx Okanagan Nation.
SPOUT: The [Spout Path](https://eastcoasttrail.com/choose-a-path/listing/13-spout-path/) is a challenging and rewarding hiking trail in Newfoundland that is part of the East Coast Trail. It features dramatic sea cliffs, sea stacks, a historic lighthouse and five waterfalls. The Spout Path is named for its most interesting feature, a wave-powered geyser that shoots a misty spray several metres into the air at regular intervals.
SQUAD: Cold Squad is a Canadian police television series that premiered on CTV on January 23, 1998, and ran for seven seasons. Known for its gripping stories and compelling characters, Cold Squad follows a team of homicide detectives from the Vancouver Police Department that reopen long-unsolved, or "cold" cases, using present-day forensic technology and psychological profiling to help crack them. Cold Squad was the first prime time national series produced out of Vancouver. With a total of 98 episodes, it became the longest-running prime time drama series on Canadian television and won several Gemini awards, Canada's highest television honours.
SQUID: The Canadian fishing village of Glover's Harbour, Newfoundland (formerly known as Thimble Tickle) claims to be the "Home of the Giant Squid." It earned this distinction in 1878, when a living giant squid was discovered stranded offshore. Now enshrined in the form of a "life-sized" sculpture, the world's largest squid is the subject of an annual festival, and in 2011, the sculpture was featured on a Canadian postage stamp.
STAGE: The [Stratford Festival](https://www.stratfordfestival.ca/) located in Stratford, Ontario is North America's largest classical repertory theatre company. Each season, numerous productions take to the stage, with special emphasis on the plays of Shakespeare. Designed by Tanya Moiseiwitsch in 1953, their flagship Festival Theatre stage was revolutionary because it was the first thrust stage built in the Western theatre since Shakespeare's time. The 2023 Stratford Festival lineup includes 13 plays and runs from April to October.
STALL: The [Richmond Night Market](https://www.richmondnightmarket.com/) in Richmond, BC, is the largest night market in North America, inspired by the vibrant night markets of Asia. Open seasonally from spring to fall, it packs more than 200 food and retail stalls into a bustling outdoor venue and attracts over one million visitors each year. From sizzling street food and sweet treats to games and unique finds, there’s something new waiting at almost every stall.
STAND: Happy Canada Day from Canuckle! Today we stand together to celebrate our country’s strength and spirit. The word stand is at the heart of our national pride - from the famous line ”We stand on guard for thee” in O Canada to the uplifting anthem ”A Place to Stand” written for Expo 67 celebrating Canada’s Centennial. That song’s message of growth and belonging perfectly matches the unity and joy we feel each July 1st as Canadians come together to honour our shared home. Here’s to standing tall, proud, and united - today and every day!
START: In 2025, [Canadian Tire’s Jumpstart program](https://jumpstart.canadiantire.ca/) celebrates 20 years of helping kids across Canada start their journey in sports by removing financial barriers. Since 2005, Jumpstart has provided funding for equipment, registration fees, and transportation so thousands of children can get active, build confidence, and feel part of their communities. Getting a great start in sports helps kids grow stronger – on the field and off.
STATE: Canada's political system is based on that of the United Kingdom. It is a constitutional monarchy, which means that we recognize the Queen or King as the Head of State, while the Prime Minister is the Head of Government. Currently, His Majesty King Charles III is King of Canada and Canada's Head of State. He is the personal embodiment of the Crown in Canada. A state funeral for former Prime Minister Brian Mulroney is being held today in Montreal. Wayne Gretzky will be among the high-profile figures to eulogize the former PM. Mulroney passed away on Feb 29, 2024 at the age of 84. He served as the 18th prime minister of Canada from 1984 to 1993.
STAVE: The NHL Stanley Cup Playoffs began on Saturday, April 18, launching a grueling postseason where every series is a best-of-seven battle. From coast to coast to coast, teams will try to stave off elimination in pursuit of the Stanley Cup, arguably the hardest trophy in sports to win. Canadian fans will be cheering on their teams throughout the chase for hockey’s ultimate prize.
STEAD: [Homesteading](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/homesteading) was a cornerstone of Canada’s western expansion. Settlers were given land to cultivate and build a life, transforming untouched prairies into farms and communities (though this land had long been home to Indigenous Peoples). Through hard work and resilience, thousands of families built homes, broke ground, and established new lives on the Prairies. Their efforts helped shape Canada’s rural landscape and agricultural heritage, leaving a legacy that still thrives today.
STEAK: Alberta has become synonymous with choice cuts of AAA beef, and chowing down on a delicious and tender steak is at the top of most people's list when they first come to the province. Beef produced in Alberta is recognized around the world for its rich taste, even fat distribution and consistent quality.
STEEL: Steel plays an extremely important role in the Canadian economy as a whole: in 2019, the Canadian steel industry contributed $4.2 billion to Canada's GDP. According to the Canadian Steel Producers Association, the Canadian steel industry employs, directly and indirectly, more than 120,000 Canadians.
STEIN: Raise a stein to Kitchener-Waterloo [Oktoberfest](https://www.oktoberfest.ca/), one of the largest Bavarian festivals outside Germany! First held in 1969, the annual celebration honours the region’s strong German-Canadian heritage with traditional food, music, dancing and festivities throughout the community. It’s a fitting tradition for Kitchener, a city once known as Berlin before being renamed in 1916.
STERN: Located in Kaslo, British Columbia, the [S.S. Moyie stern wheeler](https://www.klhs.bc.ca/) is the oldest intact passenger steam vessel of its type in the world. The machinery and the steel frames of its hull were built by the Bertram Engine Works of Toronto, shipped west by rail and assembled in Vancouver. Launched at Nelson on 22 October 1898 by the Canadian Pacific Railway, the S.S. Moyie carried passengers and freight on Kootenay Lake for 59 years. It was retired from service in 1957. Rescued and preserved by the people of Kaslo, the "sweetheart of the lake" recalls the role of sternwheelers in the history of western Canada. 2023 marks the 125th birthday celebration of the S.S. Moyie, which was designated a national historic site of Canada in 1958 and reaffirmed in 1983.
STING: Today marks the start of the [Ontario Hockey League](https://chl.ca/ohl/) (OHL) regular season in Canada! The [Sarnia Sting](https://chl.ca/ohl-sting/) are a junior ice hockey team based in Sarnia, Ontario. They are one of the 20 teams that make up the OHL. The franchise was granted in 1969 as one of the inaugural teams of the Quebec Major Junior Hockey League. At the time, the team was located in Cornwall, Ontario and known as the Cornwall Royals.
STOAT: Stoats, also known as short-tailed weasels or ermines, are widespread across Canada. Found in most regions, they grow a white winter coat for camouflage, slipping through snow and tunnels as fearless hunters of mice, voles, birds, and insects. That same nimble, energetic spirit comes to life in [Tina and Milo](https://www.olympics.com/en/milano-cortina-2026/brand/mascots), the stoat siblings who are mascots for the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics, bringing fun, cheer, and Olympic excitement to athletes and fans alike.
STOMP: Charles Thomas "Stompin' Tom" Connors was an iconic Canadian country and folk singer-songwriter. Focusing his career exclusively on his native Canada, he is credited with writing more than 300 songs and has released four dozen albums, with total sales of nearly four million copies. Connors' songs have become part of the Canadian cultural landscape. Among his best-known songs are "Sudbury Saturday Night", "Bud the Spud" and "The Hockey Song"; the last is played at various games throughout the National Hockey League.
STONE: A building material used in Manitoba for nearly 200 years, from trading forts to the modern-day architecture of the Canadian Museum for Human Rights, received international recognition in 2023 as a global heritage stone resource. Tyndall Stone - a fossil-laden limestone dating back 450 million years - has also been used at the parliament buildings in Ottawa, the Canadian Museum of History in Quebec and the legislative buildings in Regina and Winnipeg. Canada is the only source in the world for the stone, and Manitoba is the only place it is quarried. The designation means that the Tyndall stone is considered a culturally significant material.
STORE: The local convenience store has been the backbone of Canadian communities for generations. In fact, our convenience store roots can be traced back to Quebec in the 1600s when Samuel de Champlain founded the first store outside of Quebec City. The more than 22,500 stores across Canada act as gathering places in many communities. Those community hubs generate more than $54 billion in sales, employ more than 200,000 Canadians and sell everything from fuel, EV charging, to lottery, energy drinks, bottled water, salty snacks and in Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador, beer. Find out more about Canada’s convenience industry from its chief advocate, The Convenience Industry Council of Canada at [convenienceindustry.ca](https://convenienceindustry.ca/).
STORK: The Great Stork Derby was a decade-long baby-making contest held from 1926 to 1936. Female residents of Toronto, Ontario, Canada, competed to produce the most babies in order to qualify for an unusual bequest in the will of eccentric millionaire Charles Vance Millar. In the end, there were six women tied for first place. The winners each gave birth to nine children, and received $125,000 (worth roughly $2 million today).
STOVE: The stove was the true heart of many early Canadian pioneer homes. Cast-iron wood stoves provided the main source of heat during long, freezing winters while also serving as the primary place for cooking meals, heating water, and gathering as a family. For many settlers, the stove was more than an appliance, it was an essential part of daily life and survival in Canada’s harsh climate.
STRAW: Nothing says summer in Canada like a basket of fresh-picked strawberries! From coast to coast, strawberry season typically runs from late June to early July, with local farms offering juicy, sun-ripened berries perfect for jams, shortcakes, or snacking straight from the patch. In 2024, Canadian farmers harvested nearly 26,000 tonnes of fresh strawberries – the biggest crop in five years. Quebec leads the berry pack, producing over two-thirds of the country’s supply. Talk about a sweet success!
STRAY: The Parliament Hill cat colony was a clowder of stray cats living on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Ontario, in a cat sanctuary set aside for them. The care of the cats and maintenance of the sanctuary was carried out by volunteers, and the effort was funded by donations. The colony was closed in January 2013 after the remaining cats were adopted into homes.
STUNT: Ken Carter was a Canadian stunt driver born in Montreal, Quebec. Carter dropped out of school to perform car stunts with a team of traveling daredevils. Subsequently, he began performing as a solo act, and he jumped at racetracks all over North America. He became a notorious showman, earning the nickname "The Mad Canadian" for his death-defying antics. He travelled the country, jumping bodies of water, cars and buses. Check out the great NFB documentary about Ken Carter called "[The Devil At Your Heels](https://www.nfb.ca/film/devil_at_your_heels/)" and the [Canadian History Ehx](https://canadaehx.com/2019/12/08/daredevil-ken-carter-the-mad-canadian/) podcast episode to learn more about The Mad Canadian.
SUEDE: The [Blue Suede Music Festival](https://bluesuedemusicfestival.com/) is held in northern Alberta, Canada at the Ag Grounds in the town of Westlock. This festival was started as a way to keep the memory of Elvis and his music alive and to allow tribute artists to come and pay homage to the King of Rock and Roll in a non-competitive setting. It takes place outdoors in the province that has the most Elvis fans in Canada! This year's festival runs from July 26-28, 2024.
SUGAR: Spring is only a few weeks away, and that means it's almost sugar season! Sugar shacks ("cabanes à sucres" in French) are cabins where sap is collected from sugar maple trees and boiled into maple syrup. In 2022, over 72 million litres of maple syrup came out of sugar shacks in Quebec, accounting for over 90% of Canada's domestic production.
SUITE: [Honeymoon Suite](https://honeymoonsuiteband.com/) is a Canadian rock band that was formed in 1981 in Niagara Falls, Ontario. The band's name was inspired by the fact that Niagara Falls is the unofficial honeymoon capital of the world. Honeymoon Suite won the Juno Award for Group of the Year in 1986.
SUNNY: Canada’s North is particularly well-known as being the fabled “land of the midnight sun.” Due to its proximity to the Arctic Circle, northern days can entail up to 24 straight hours of sunlight in the summer. Calgary is the sunniest of Canada's large cities, enjoying an average of 2,400 hours of bright sun each year, spread over 333 days.
SUPER: It's a Bird... It's a Plane... It's Superman! The Superman character was co-created by Canadian artist Joseph Shuster. Born in Toronto, he is a cousin of Wayne Shuster, one-half of the beloved Canadian comedy duo Wayne and Shuster. Joseph, who passed away in 1992 at the age of 78, said Metropolis was modelled on Toronto and the Daily Planet was inspired by the Toronto Star, which he delivered as a kid.
SURGE: The [Calgary Surge](https://www.calgarysurge.ca/) is a Canadian professional basketball team based in Calgary, Alberta, that competes in the [Canadian Elite Basketball League](https://www.cebl.ca/) (CEBL). In 2023 they relocated from Guelph, where they were known as the Guelph Nighthawks. The Surge lost to the Scarborough Shooting Stars in the 2023 CEBL Championship game. The CEBL boasts the highest percentages of Canadian players of any pro league in the country with 75 percent of its players being Canadian.
SUSHI: Although sushi may not come immediately to mind when discussing Canadian food, the California Roll - evolved from the Japanese sushi tradition and given an American-sounding name - is Canadian! Vancouver sushi chef Hidekazu Tojo invented the California roll and popularized the "inside-out" sushi technique in North America. There are thousands of sushi restaurants across Canada - more than 600 of them are in Vancouver alone.
SWATH: A swath is the strip of crops cut by a scythe or combine – and it’s a familiar sight across Canada’s prairies. During harvest season, golden swaths of wheat and canola stretch for kilometres across provinces like Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba, painting the landscape with the colours of Canada’s breadbasket.
SWEAT: Sweat lodges are sacred spaces used by many First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities for ceremony, healing, and spiritual renewal. Inside the lodge, steam rises as water is poured over heated stones, creating an intense sweat that symbolizes purification and connection to the land, ancestors, and community. These ceremonies have been passed down for generations, offering a powerful way to reflect, give thanks, and restore balance.
SWEEP: In the sport of [curling](https://www.curling.ca), sweeping helps control the speed and direction of the curling stone, a skill Canadian curlers have mastered. Canada has an impressive Olympic track record in curling, with both men's and women's teams sweeping their way to Olympic glory and consistently reaching the podium. Highlights include the men's team winning gold in 2006, 2010, and 2014, and the women's team securing gold in 1998 and 2014. Canada also won gold in mixed doubles curling at the 2018 PyeongChang Olympics.
SWING: [Oscar Peterson](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/oscar-peterson) is one of Canada's most honoured musicians and is widely regarded as one of the greatest jazz pianists of all time. Born and raised in Montreal, Peterson began playing piano at the age of five. Known as the "master of swing" or the "king of inside swing," Peterson made a name for himself with his incredible dexterity, speed and ornate technique on the keys. Over the course of Peterson’s acclaimed career, he won seven Grammy Awards, was awarded the Order of Canada and the Order of Ontario, won the Martin Luther King Jr. Achievement Award, received numerous honorary degrees, and was inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame. A public statue of Oscar Peterson was unveiled by Queen Elizabeth II in Ottawa in 2007. Check out this [Heritage Minutes video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7cdXEhR9dd4) that recounts the early years of Peterson’s music career.
SYNTH: Canadian [Hugh Le Caine's electronic Sackbut](https://ingeniumcanada.org/scitech/artifact/hugh-le-caine-electronic-sackbut-synthesizer) was the world's first synthesizer, a type of musical instrument that gave 1970s pop music its distinctively electronic sound. Le Caine, a trained musician, was a physicist at the National Research Council of Canada (NRC) and began work on the Sackbut in 1945. His innovative instrument utilized oscillators and filters to produce a wide range of tones, allowing musicians to explore new creative possibilities.
TAFFY: Maple taffy (tire d'érable or tire sur la neige in French-speaking Canada) is a sugar candy made by boiling maple sap past the point where it would form maple syrup, but not so long that it becomes maple butter or maple sugar. It is part of traditional culture in Québec, Eastern Ontario, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia. In these regions, maple syrup is boiled, poured into rows on a snow-lined tray, and rolled onto sticks to make this chewy, irresistible candy.
TAILS: Today marks the start of [Winterlude](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/winterlude.html), the annual winter festival in Ottawa-Gatineau featuring ice, snow, and BeaverTails! [BeaverTails](https://beavertails.com/about-beavertails-pastries/) are world famous Canadian fried dough pastries that are individually stretched to resemble beaver's tails, with sweet toppings like cinnamon & sugar, chocolate hazelnut, and maple spread. They are the ultimate way to keep warm during Winterlude!
TANKS: 79 years ago today on D-Day, Canadian soldiers and tanks landed on Juno Beach, one of five beaches of the Allied invasion of German-occupied France in the Normandy landings on June 6, 1944 during the Second World War. June 6th is a day to remember those who fought and fell so we could be free.
TARTS: A butter tart is a delicious pastry tart, which generally consists of butter, sugar, syrup, and egg, filled into a flaky pastry. The earliest published recipe for a butter tart is from Barrie, Ontario dating back to 1900 in the Women's Auxiliary of the Royal Victoria Hospital Cookbook.
TAXES: Lottery & gambling winnings in Canada are treated as windfalls and are not subject to Canadian income tax. Turns out taxes aren't always certain after all!
TAXIS: Taxis have played an important role in Canadian urban history since the early 20th century, with cities like Winnipeg and Toronto among the first to introduce motorized taxi services. During World War II, Canadian taxi fleets were repurposed for civil defense – transporting supplies, volunteers, and even serving as emergency vehicles when needed. Today, while rideshares are popular, classic yellow cabs remain a familiar sight in many of Canada’s biggest cities.
TEAMS: Fifty [Canadian Paralympians](https://paralympic.ca/games/milano-cortina-2026/athletes/) are bound for the 2026 Winter Paralympics, which open on March 6! They’ll compete across six sports: para alpine skiing, para biathlon, para cross-country skiing, para ice hockey, para snowboarding, and wheelchair curling. From individual races to medal-contending teams on the ice and snow, they’ll challenge 665 athletes from around the world across 79 medal events. Together, these teams and athletes bring skill, strategy, and teamwork to every course and match, representing the strength and resilience of the Canada Paralympic Team.
TEETH: Did you know the humble zipper owes its "teeth" to Canadian ingenuity? In 1913, while working for the Universal Fastener Company, Gideon Sundback, a Swedish-born inventor who settled in St. Catharines, Ontario, developed the modern zipper we use today. His design - originally called the "Separable Fastener" - featured interlocking metal teeth that made it easy to open and close. Though small, this invention would go on to revolutionize fashion, camping gear, and much more. Next time you zip up, give a nod to Canada's history of clever creations!
TERRY: While 'terry' can refer to a type of soft, absorbent fabric, it also carries special meaning in Canada as the name of Terry Fox, a true Canadian hero whose Marathon of Hope continues to inspire millions. In 1980, Terry set out to run across Canada to raise money for cancer research after losing his leg to the disease. Although he was forced to stop early, his legacy lives on through the annual [Terry Fox Run](https://terryfox.org/terry-fox-run/), held every September, including this year on September 15. So, when you think of Terry, remember the determination and courage that have united Canadians from coast to coast in support of a great cause!
THEIR: [Their Opportunity](https://www.theiropportunity.com/) is a national children's charity in Canada that uses sport and generosity to educate, uplift, and support children facing barriers. Their programs break down obstacles to participation and promote a lifestyle of giving back, empowering youth to grow, belong, and thrive. Their Opportunity is one of the charities supported by the [Sach In Motion](https://sachinmotion.ca/) fund, as Sachin Latti completes his coast-to-coast run in St. John’s, Newfoundland today, raising awareness and support for mental health and community causes.
THEME: "The Hockey Theme" is a Canadian piece of instrumental theme music composed in 1968 by Dolores Claman and orchestrated by Jerry Toth. The theme was associated with CBC Television's Hockey Night in Canada and it was widely recognized as Canada's unofficial second national anthem.
THING: [The Nature of Things](https://www.cbc.ca/natureofthings/) is television’s longest-running science series that debuted on CBC on November 6, 1960. It evolved into an hour-long documentary during renowned Canadian scientist and environmental activist David Suzuki’s tenure as host (1979–2023). The groundbreaking program was among the first to present scientific findings on subjects such as HIV/AIDS and climate change. Over the course of more than 60 seasons and over 900 episodes, The Nature of Things has been seen in more than 80 countries. It has received 17 Gemini Awards and seven Canadian Screen Awards.
THIRD: In curling, the third is the player who throws the third pair of stones and helps the skip plan strategy. At the 2026 Winter Olympics, Team Canada’s thirds [Marc Kennedy](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/marc-kennedy/) and [Tracy Fleury](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/tracy-fleury/) play a crucial role in every end, delivering precise shots, calling key plays, and helping their teams chase medals on the world stage. Their decisions on the ice can change the course of an entire match.
THREE: Happy National Sisters Day! The [Three Sisters](https://www.travelalberta.com/listings/three-sisters-mountains-2010/) are a trio of peaks near Canmore, Alberta. They are known individually as Big Sister (Faith), Middle Sister (Charity) and Little Sister (Hope). These three peaks have a significant role in the town of Canmore, tourism, and hiking in the area and may be the most recognized peaks in the Bow River Valley.
TIDES: The highest tides in the world can be found in Canada at the Bay of Fundy, which separates New Brunswick from Nova Scotia.
TIGER: The [Hamilton Tiger-Cats](https://ticats.ca/) are a professional Canadian football team in the CFL based in Hamilton, Ontario. The Ticats have over 153 years of history & tradition and have won 15 Grey Cup championships. Oskee Wee Wee!
TIPSY: Sometime around World War II, people along the south coast of Newfoundland began to associate December 23rd with the phrase "Tibb's Eve" and deemed it the first night during Advent when it was appropriate to have a drink. Sometimes called Tip's Eve or Tipsy Eve, it's one of several extensions of the Christmas holidays. For many Newfoundlanders, this day is the official opening of Christmas, and it is customary to have a couple of drinks in the company of friends.
TITAN: The [Ottawa Titans](https://www.ottawatitans.com/) are one of three Canadian baseball teams that play in the MLB Partner [Frontier League](https://www.frontierleague.com/). Formed in 1993, it is the oldest currently running independent league in the United States. The Can-Am League merged with the Frontier League in 2019.
TITLE: On October 18, 1929, Canadian women gained an important new title under the law: “persons.” The landmark Persons Case was the result of the Famous Five’s fight to have women recognized as “qualified persons” eligible to serve in the Senate. Their victory paved the way for women to enter the Senate and marked a major milestone in the advancement of gender equality in Canada. October 18 is now commemorated across Canada as Persons Day.
TODAY: Today's Special is a Canadian children's television program that aired from 1981-1987. Much of the series was set in a department store based on Simpson's then-flagship location in Toronto. The magic words "Hocus pocus alimagocus!" would bring Jeff the mannequin to life on each show. The adventures of Jeff, Jodie, Sam Crenshaw and Muffy Mouse brought magic to the screen for over 120 episodes!
TOKEN: When Toronto’s first subway opened on March 30, 1954, commuters used purpose-built [metallic tokens](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/a-look-back-at-the-history-of-ttc-tickets-tokens-and-passes-1.7534088) designed to combat the counterfeiting of paper tickets. TTC tokens became one of the most recognizable objects in Toronto life, handled by generations of riders for nearly seven decades. The last tokens were sold in March 2023, ending a 69-year tradition.
TOLLS: Ontario’s [Highway 407 ETR](https://www.407etr.com/), which opened north of Toronto in 1997, was the world’s first fully electronic toll highway. Instead of toll booths, overhead cameras and transponders automatically identify vehicles and charge drivers as they travel. The 108-kilometre highway helped pioneer open-road tolling and the cashless technology now used on highways around the world.
TONIC: Ontario is the world's largest producer of [North American ginseng](https://ginsengontario.com/about/), whose distinctive, forked root has been prized for centuries as a traditional herbal tonic. Often steeped in hot water to make a restorative tonic or tea, Canadian ginseng is highly valued in Asia, where most of Ontario's crop is exported. Grown beneath shade cloth in the sandy soils near Lake Erie, ginseng is a demanding crop: once harvested, the same field may not support another successful ginseng crop for decades!
TOOLS: Happy Father's Day from Canuckle! Across Canada, tools are a familiar part of garages, workshops, and weekend projects – because if something breaks, there’s a good chance a dad has already said, “I’ve got just the tool for that!” For many, they’ve also been part of passing down practical skills, problem-solving, and hands-on learning from one generation to the next. On Father's Day we’re celebrating all the dads and father figures across the country for everything they build, fix, and figure out along the way.
TOQUE: Toque (or tuque) is the official name for a winter hat in Canada!
TOTAL: On April 8, 2024, a spectacular and rare celestial event is set to unfold over Canada, the United States and Mexico – a [total solar eclipse](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/astronomy/eclipses/total-solar-eclipse.asp). As the Moon aligns perfectly between Earth and the Sun, temporary darkness will sweep across parts of the country, captivating countless spectators. In Canada, the solar eclipse's path of totality will pass through some cities and towns in Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, plunging them into darkness for a few minutes. People outside the path of totality will be able to observe a partial solar eclipse, during which the Sun is not hidden in totality.
TOTEM: The word totem comes from the Algonquian word “odoodem“ meaning “his kinship group“.
TOUGH: The [ParaTough Cup](https://www.paratoughcup.ca/) is a half-day corporate challenge in which teams compete in Para sport and get to know Paralympians. The ParaTough Cup was created to raise awareness of the Paralympic movement and funds for Canadians with a disability to participate and excel in sport. It is the signature fundraising event of the [Paralympic Foundation of Canada](https://paralympic.ca/foundation/paralympic-foundation-canada).
TOURS: World Tourism Day, created by the United Nations World Tourism Organization, is celebrated each year on September 27th to spread awareness about the importance of tourism and its impact on our society. Canada is a country filled with famous landmarks, historical wonders, delicious food, incredible culture, and all the outdoor exploration you could want. Whether you are touring the Parliament Buildings in Ottawa, touring one of Canada's many national parks and historic sites, touring Niagara Falls, or taking a tour through the Canadian Rockies, there are so many natural and cultural wonders to enjoy in our country!
TOXIC: During the First World War, a Canadian innovation helped protect soldiers from toxic gases on the battlefield. The [Hypo Helmet](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/hypo-helmet), invented by Newfoundland doctor Captain Cluny Macpherson in 1915, was an early type of gas mask designed to filter out toxic gases like chlorine gas. It was made of a chemically treated flannel hood with a mica visor, and was a crucial development in protecting soldiers from the harmful effects of chemical warfare. This Canadian invention was an important step in the evolution of gas masks, helping to save countless lives during the war.
TRADE: Canada’s three biggest trading partners are the United States, the European Union and China. Goods and services trade with the US totaled over $800 billion in 2021.
TRAIL: The [Trans Canada Trail](https://tctrail.ca/) is Canada’s national trail and is the longest network of multi-use recreational trails in the world. Crossing Canada on the Trans Canada Trail by foot would take over two years, spanning a whopping 24,134 km!
TRAMP: The [Capilano Suspension Bridge](https://www.capbridge.com/) in Vancouver, British Columbia has been a popular destination for adventurers since the late 1890s. Back then, reaching the bridge was no easy feat. Hikers had to first cross the Burrard Inlet by steamboat, then trek through a 12km path winding through dense rainforest to get to the bridge. Those who made the long journey were said to 'tramp' their way to the bridge and were dubbed 'Capilano Tramps', earning the nickname for their determination and endurance. Today, visitors still experience the beauty of the bridge, but thankfully, they don’t have to tramp their way through the wilderness to get there!
TRASH: Harry Wasylyk was a Canadian inventor from Winnipeg, Manitoba, who together with Larry Hansen of Lindsay, Ontario, invented the disposable green polyethylene trash bag.
TRAWL: Dragging large fishing nets through the water, a method known as trawling, is widely used in Canadian fisheries along both coasts. From the Atlantic provinces to British Columbia, trawling supports important commercial fishing communities and contributes significantly to Canada’s seafood industry. But it’s not just about catching fish – sustainable trawling practices are essential for protecting marine ecosystems, helping ensure these waters remain rich and vibrant for generations to come.
TREAT: Happy Halloween from Canuckle! 🎃 While the act of going door-to-door in costume in exchange for something sweet to eat has been around since the Middle Ages, it wasn't until sometime in the last century that people started saying "trick or treat." Trick-or-treating as we know it in Canada began in the late 1920s. In fact, the earliest recorded usage of the phrase “trick or treat” comes from Blackie, Alberta, where in 1927 a newspaper article reported on pranksters demanding “trick or treat” at houses. There is also record of a variation of the phrase originating in Chatsworth, Ontario in 1917, and then appearing in [The Sault Daily Star](https://www.sootoday.com/rooted/origin-of-phrase-trick-or-treat-in-print-traced-to-the-sault-6033664) in Saut Ste. Marie, Ontario on Nov 1, 1917. "Tricks or treats you could hear the gangs call out," the article read. Either way, it has a Canadian origin story that lives on to this day!
TREES: One of the most widely-known facts about Canada is that we’ve got an abundance of trees, but did you know that Canada actually boasts 30 per cent of the world’s boreal forest and 10 per cent of the world’s total forest cover?
TRIBE: In Canada, Indigenous tribes, also called nations or bands, have rich cultures, languages, and histories that stretch back thousands of years. The name tribe has also inspired modern artists, such as the Canadian group A Tribe Called Red (now The Halluci Nation), who blend traditional Indigenous music with electronic beats to celebrate culture and community.
TROLL: Troll Falls is a scenic gem in Alberta’s Kananaskis Country, where a forest trail leads to a beautiful waterfall tucked beneath rocky cliffs. Surrounded by mountain views and towering trees, it’s a favourite for families year-round – especially in winter, when the frozen falls create a dazzling curtain of ice. With a name straight out of a storybook, this magical setting lives up to the fairy tale feel.
TROOP: The Canadian Armed Forces has personnel deployed across Canada and around the world. Since 1947, Canadian troops have completed 72 international missions.
TRUCK: The first known dump truck was developed in Saint John, New Brunswick when Canadian Robert Mawhinney attached a dump box to a flatbed truck in 1920. His idea was an instant hit, and within a decade, the dump truck was mandatory equipment wherever earth was moved.
TRUSS: Nestled on Vancouver Island, the Kinsol Trestle Bridge is a stunning example of Canadian engineering and natural beauty. Built in 1920, this towering wooden bridge uses a Howe truss design – an ingenious system of beams that supports its massive length and height. At 44 metres tall and 187 metres long, the Kinsol Trestle is one of the tallest wooden trestle bridges in the world and a lasting symbol of Canada's timber heritage.
TRUST: The [National Trust for Canada](https://nationaltrustcanada.ca/) is an independent national charity that empowers communities to save and renew heritage places. Heritage places are the backbone of resilient, diverse and sustainable communities: think of historic lighthouses and schools, rural landscapes, Indigenous heritage sites, etc. They work with partners, donors and funders to see heritage places play their part as cornerstones of climate action and social cohesion, and they spark important conversations about Canada at the places our members visit and discover.
TUNES: "What’s up, Doc?" Did you know that a Canadian is the newest voice of Bugs Bunny, Porky Pig, Daffy Duck, Tweety Bird, and Marvin the Martian for Looney Tunes Cartoons? Eric Bauza grew up in the Toronto suburb of Scarborough, Ontario and became the voice actor for these cartoon characters in December 2020. Eric recently won the Emmy Award for "Outstanding Voice Performance in an Animated Program" for his work on Looney Tunes Cartoons. "That's all Folks!"
TURTLE: Many Indigenous Peoples across the land now called Canada refer to North America as Turtle Island. In these traditional teachings, the turtle carries the world on its back, symbolizing creation, resilience, and connection to the land. The shell’s 13 large scutes are said to represent the lunar cycles, while the 28 smaller sections reflect the days between them. These teachings continue to inspire respect for the land and a sense of belonging within the natural world.
TWILL: Coast Salish peoples include a variety of First Nations living along the Northwest Pacific Coast in British Columbia. In traditional Coast Salish society, blankets held much importance. They were generally white twill-weave or twined featuring repeated geometric designs, and were thick and heavy. In addition to serving many practical functions, twill blankets were a primary medium of exchange and they held much spiritual significance.
TWINE: Today marks the start of the NHL regular season in North America! In hockey, "twine" is a common slang term for the net, and "tickling the twine" refers to scoring a goal - a thrill that no player delivered more than Canadian hockey legend Wayne Gretzky! Known as "The Great One," Gretzky tickled the twine a jaw-dropping 894 times, setting the record for the most career goals in NHL history.
TWINS: The Edison Twins is a Canadian children's television program which ran for six seasons on CBC Television from March 3, 1984 to December 17, 1986. The series featured the adventures of Tom and Annie Edison (played by Andrew Sabiston and Marnie McPhail respectively), a pair of teenage scientific prodigy siblings who face a variety of challenges which they overcome with their expertise of science. McPhail won the Gemini Award for Best Performance by a Lead Actress in a Continuing Dramatic Series in 1986.
TWIST: The new [Tundra Twister at Canada's Wonderland](https://www.canadaswonderland.com/rides-experiences/tundra-twister) is the only ride of its kind in the world. The brand new, never-been-built carnival ride has a 360-degree spinning swing with twisting gondola arms. Parkgoers are sent on a twirling journey as they twist and turn 360-degrees and upside down at heights of 47 metres and speeds of 75 kilometres per hour!
UDDER: Cows are at the heart of the [Canadian dairy industry](https://dairyfarmersofcanada.ca/), which produces everything from milk and butter to cheese and yogurt. Milk is collected from the udder, the part of the cow where it's stored before being carefully cooled and transported. Canada is home to over 10,000 dairy farms, and its farmers follow some of the highest standards in the world for quality, safety, and animal care. So the next time you pour a glass of milk or bite into a gooey grilled cheese, you can thank a Canadian cow!
UNDER: Under the Umbrella Tree is a Canadian children's television series created by Noreen Young that originally aired on CBC from 1987 to 1993.
